Lekh Lekha לֶךְ־לְךָ

BereshitNoachLekh Lekha

Genesis 12:1–17:27. Select a Hebrew word for its morphology, lemma, root, senses and the comments anchored to it. A dotted underline marks a word a commentator quotes.

12:1

The LORD said to Abram, "Go forth from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you."

and-said the-LORD to-Abram go-(you) to-you from-land-of-you and-from-birthplace-of-you and-from-house-of father-of-you to the-land that I-will-show-you

Grammar
  • לֶךְ־לְךָ is the imperative of הלך with a reflexive-looking dative. The first-letter loss in the imperative (הלך gives לֶךְ) is regular for this root. Ramban and Radak list parallel idioms: אֵלְכָה לִּי, קְחוּ לָכֶם.
  • The three prepositional phrases מֵאַרְצְךָ, וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ, וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ run from the widest circle to the narrowest: land, kin, household. The accents mark the list; the etnaḥta falls on אָבִיךָ and splits the verse between what he leaves and where he goes.
  • The destination is deliberately not named: אֶל־הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ. The hifil of ראה governs two accusatives (here the suffix and the land, which is the object of the relative clause).
  • In pause, under the silluq, the suffix of אַרְאֶךָּ is ־ֶךָּ: the dagesh in the kaf is an assimilated (energic) nun.

The narrative order is kept: the command follows 11:31–32, where Terah and Abram have already reached Haran. Rashi's reading (the command means 'move further away') fits that order; Ibn Ezra takes the command as given earlier, in Ur of the Chaldeans. The English says only 'said' and does not choose a pluperfect. 'Birthplace' is chosen for מוֹלֶדֶת because the pack's lexicon gives 'birth, kindred'; Ramban shows that the word covers the family's home. The ethical dative is dropped from the English as idiom; Rashi's reading is recorded.

Commentary (15)
Rashinormativerecords לֶךְ לְךָ֛
Rashi: לֶךְ־לְךָ means 'for your own benefit and good': there He will make you a great nation, here you do not merit children; and also so that your nature (reputation) becomes known. Ramban and Radak say instead that this is simply the idiom of the language; the English does not translate the dative.

לַהֲנָאָתְךָ וּלְטוֹבָתְךָ, שָׁם אֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָדוֹל, כָּאן אִי אַתָּה זוֹכֶה לְבָנִים, וְעוֹד שֶׁאוֹדִיעַ טִבְעֲךָ בָּעוֹלָם:
Rashinormativefollows מֵאַרְצְךָ֥
Rashi: but he had already left Ur with his father and come to Haran; so the command means 'distance yourself even further from there and leave your father's house'. The English leaves 'your land' as it stands and the verse order (Haran, then this command) is kept in the English.

Rashinormativefollows אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַרְאֶֽךָּ׃
Rashi: He did not reveal the land at once, in order to make it dear in Abram's eyes and to give him reward for every single utterance (compare Isaac in 22:2). The English keeps the destination unnamed: 'the land that I will show you'.

Ibn Ezranormativerecords לֶךְ לְךָ֛
Ibn Ezra: God commanded Abram while he was still in Ur of the Chaldeans to leave his land, his birthplace and his father's house. The reason: God knew that Terah, once he had set out for Canaan, would settle in Haran, and Terah did not die until sixty years after Abram left his father's house in Haran; Scripture simply does not give Abram's age when he left Ur. After 'that I will show you' God revealed the secret to him (12:5, 'they set out for the land of Canaan'), or 'I will show you' refers to 13:15, 'all the land that you see I will give to you'. The English does not take the verb as pluperfect, and this reading is recorded as the alternative.

Rambannot-applicable מֵאַרְצְךָ֥ וּמִמּֽוֹלַדְתְּךָ֖
Ramban quotes Rashi ('distance yourself further'), then rejects Ibn Ezra's view that the command came in Ur. Genesis 11:31 says Terah took Abram, so Abram left Ur on his father's initiative. Joshua 24:3 says 'from beyond the River', not 'from Ur'. And in Genesis 24:4, 10 'my land and my birthplace' is Aram Naharaim, the city of Nahor. His own view: Haran is Abram's land and birthplace, the land of his fathers, and the command to leave them came there. The three terms are named because each is harder to leave than the last. The comment concerns the history of the narrative and does not change the English.

Apparatus
  • 12:1.2, the divine name: MAM writes יְהֹוָה, the pack's analysis reads יְהוָה; the English is 'the LORD' in both.
  • The tense of וַיֹּאמֶר: simple past (Rashi's sequence) against pluperfect 'had said' (Ibn Ezra, Radak: he spoke to him before leaving Ur, as in 15:7).
12:2

I will make you into a great nation, I will bless you, and make your name great, and you shall be a blessing.

and-I-will-make-you to-nation great and-I-will-bless-you and-I-will-make-great name-of-you and-be (you) blessing

Grammar
  • Three first-person imperfects (וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ, וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ, וַאֲגַדְּלָה) carry the promise. None is a wayyiqtol: the vav has shewa, or pataḥ before the ḥaṭef pataḥ of the guttural א (a first-person wayyiqtol would have וָאֲ with qamets).
  • The fourth verb, וֶהְיֵה, is an imperative addressed to Abram, 'and be'. Radak takes it as an imperative standing for the future 'and you will be' (compare Deut. 32:50); Rashi reads it as a gift: the power of blessing is put into Abram's hand.
  • וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ is Piel with a suffix; וַאֲגַדְּלָה is Piel of גדל, causative 'make great', with the cohortative ending ־ָה. The root גדל recurs: גּוֹי גָּדוֹל, וַאֲגַדְּלָה.
  • In וֶהְיֵה the vav has segol because the imperative הֱיֵה begins with ה under ḥaṭef segol. Before a ḥaṭef the vav takes the matching short vowel, and the ḥaṭef becomes a silent shewa (וֶהְ־).
  • The accents: the etnaḥta on שְׁמֶךָ divides the verse. The first half holds the three promises, and the second half holds וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה alone.

Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah) reads the three promises as answering the three losses of travel, which diminishes children, wealth and name: 'nation' is children, 'bless' is wealth, 'make great your name' is fame. The English keeps 'bless' unspecified and records this. Radak agrees on wealth for 'bless' and on renown for the name. For וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה the English has 'you shall be', so that the imperative is plainly addressed to Abram. Rashi says the blessings are put in Abram's hand, Radak says the imperative stands for a future 'you will be', and Ramban says that people will invoke him in blessing.

Rashinormativefollows וְאֶֽעֶשְׂךָ֙ לְג֣וֹי גָּד֔וֹל

Apparatus

12:3

I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse, and all the families of the earth will bless themselves by you.

and-I-will-bless those-who-bless-you and-the-one-who-curses-you I-will-curse and-will-bless-themselves in-you all-of families-of the-ground

Grammar
  • The plural participle מְבָרְכֶיךָ and the singular מְקַלֶּלְךָ are kept apart in the English ('those who' / 'the one who'): many will bless, few will curse (Ibn Ezra, Radak).
  • The object מְקַלֶּלְךָ is placed first in its clause and the verb אָאֹר follows: this fronting is the Hebrew's way of setting the two outcomes against each other.
  • וְנִבְרְכוּ is Niphal. The Niphal of ברך can be reflexive ('bless oneself') or passive ('be blessed'); Rashi reads it as 'bless themselves': people will say 'may you be like Abraham' (compare 48:20, 'by you Israel will bless: may God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh').
  • The two cursing verbs differ: קלל (Piel) is 'treat lightly, curse' and ארר (Qal) is the stronger 'lay under a curse'; the English uses 'curse' for both.
  • The accents: the pashta on וַאֲבָרְכָה, the zaqef on מְבָרְכֶיךָ, the etnaḥta on אָאֹר mark the two halves of the first part, and the verse ends with the great blessing as a separate clause.

The Niphal is read as reflexive following Rashi (who says 'this is its plain sense'); the passive 'will be blessed through you' is the alternative and is recorded here. Ramban holds that both are possible and adds that all will be blessed on account of him. The English preserves the number of the participles.

The English reads the Niphal as reflexive.

12:4

So Abram went, as the LORD had spoken to him, and Lot went with him. Now Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.

and-went Abram as spoke to-him the-LORD and-went with-him Lot and-Abram son-of five years and-seventy year in-going-out-of-him from-Haran

Grammar
  • וַיֵּלֶךְ is a wayyiqtol with the weak root's first letter dropped; it is repeated at the start of the second clause with a new subject (Lot).
  • כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר ... יְהֹוָה: the perfect after כַּאֲשֶׁר refers back to the command of verse 1, hence 'had spoken'.
  • The clause וְאַבְרָם בֶּן־חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים וְשִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה is verbless: 'and Abram (was) son of five years and seventy years'. The subject comes first; the vav marks a circumstance.
  • בְּצֵאתוֹ is the preposition ב with an infinitive construct and a suffix: the Hebrew way to write a temporal clause 'when he went out'.

The pluperfect in 'as the LORD had spoken' is needed in English; the Hebrew perfect is unmarked for time. The age is given as 'seventy-five' because the Hebrew counts units before tens.

Apparatus
  • No variant readings are listed for this verse in the pack.
  • Terah was seventy at Abram's birth (11:26) and died at two hundred and five (11:32), so he died sixty years after Abram left Haran at seventy-five, though 11:32 tells of it first. Ibn Ezra on 12:1 says this: Terah did not die until sixty years after Abram left. The English translates the text as it stands.
12:5

Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all the property that they had amassed, and the people they had acquired in Haran, and they set out for the land of Canaan, and they came to the land of Canaan.

and-took Abram acc. Sarai wife-of-him and-acc. Lot son-of brother-of-him and-acc. all-of property-of-them that they-amassed and-acc. the-person that they-made in-Haran and-they-went-out to-go land-of-to Canaan and-they-came land-of-to Canaan

Grammar
  • The verse is a string of wayyiqtols (וַיִּקַּח, וַיֵּצְאוּ, וַיָּבֹאוּ), each marking the next step; the objects of וַיִּקַּח are joined by repeated וְאֶת־.
  • The two relative clauses אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ and אֲשֶׁר־עָשׂוּ use perfects that describe what had been done before Abram took them, hence the English pluperfect. The root רכשׁ is in both the noun רְכוּשׁ and the verb רָכָשׁוּ.
  • הַנֶּפֶשׁ is singular in form but collective in sense ('the persons'); the verb עָשׂוּ that follows is plural.
  • אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן uses the directional he, ־ָה, on a noun in the construct state; the same expression appears twice, in the goal (to go) and in the arrival. The repetition is deliberate: they set out for Canaan and they arrived there, unlike Terah (11:31).
  • The verb עָשָׂה, 'make', has the sense 'acquire' here; the pack's lexicon lists it as Qal II.7.

עָשׂוּ is the difficulty. Rashi gives two readings: the aggadic one (Abram converted the men, Sarai the women, and Scripture counts it as if they had made them), and what he calls the plain sense, 'servants and maidservants that they acquired'. Ibn Ezra gives 'slaves born in the house, or 'made' is 'acquired'' and, as another view, 'souls whom they taught the truth'. Radak also gives the aggadic reading and Onkelos's, 'those whom they subjected to the Torah'. The English follows the plain sense and records the other readings.

Commentary (15)
Rashinormativefollows אֲשֶׁר עָשׂ֣וּ בְחָרָ֑ן
Rashi: 'the people they had made in Haran': Abram converted the men and Sarai the women, and Scripture credits them as if they had made them; but the plain sense is servants and maidservants that they acquired, as in 'he made all this wealth for himself' (31:1) and 'Israel is making power' (Num. 24:18), a language of acquiring and gathering. The English takes the plain sense and records the homily here.

Apparatus
  • 12:5.21: the pack gives the accents of לָלֶכֶת as pashta, pashta (a repeated accent); the word is a single infinitive.
  • 12:5.18 עָשׂוּ: 'acquired' (plain sense, Rashi and Ibn Ezra) against 'converted' or 'taught' (aggadah, Onkelos, Radak, Ibn Ezra's alternative).
  • The Hebrew is 'to the land of Canaan' in both the departure and the arrival clauses; the English repeats the phrase.
12:6

Abram passed through the land as far as the site of Shechem, as far as the terebinth of Moreh. The Canaanite was then in the land.

and-passed Abram in-the-land as-far-as place-of Shechem as-far-as terebinth-of Moreh and-the-Canaanite then in-the-land

Grammar
  • The verb עָבַר takes the preposition בְּ here: 'pass through (the land)'. The verse gives two stopping places in a chain of constructs: מְקוֹם שְׁכֶם and אֵלוֹן מוֹרֶה, each introduced by עַד.
  • The first עַד carries yetiv (עַ֚ד), a disjunctive accent written before the first letter of the word. It stands in place of pashta on a word stressed on its first syllable with no conjunctive before it. The zaqef on שְׁכֶם marks a pause between the two places.
  • וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי אָז בָּאָרֶץ is a verbless clause with the vav of circumstance; the singular gentilic with the article is collective.
  • אָז 'then' is the point of the commentators' difficulty (see the note): it can mark the Canaanite's presence at that time, as distinct from later, or his recent seizure of the land (Rashi, Ibn Ezra).

Three difficulties are kept open. (1) 'The site of Shechem': Ibn Ezra says that Moses called the place by this name, since there was no Shechem in Abraham's time; Ramban holds that Shechem is the name of the city and that Shechem son of Hamor was named after it. (2) 'The terebinth of Moreh': Ibn Ezra offers 'trees' or 'a field', and says Moreh may be Mamre, the ally of Abraham, or another, the name of a place; Rashi says that Elon Moreh is Shechem. (3) 'The Canaanite was then in the land': Rashi says Canaan was then conquering it from the descendants of Shem; Ibn Ezra says Canaan may have seized it from another's hand, and if not, 'it has a secret, and the wise will keep silent'. The English leaves the clause unexplained.

אוֹמַר לְךָ כְּלָל תָּבִין אוֹתוֹ בְּכָל הַפָּרָשִׁיּוֹת הַבָּאוֹת בְּעִנְיַן אַבְרָהָם יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב, וְהוּא עִנְיָן גָּדוֹל הִזְכִּירוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ בְּדֶרֶךְ קְצָרָה וְאָמְרוּ (תנחומא ט), כָּל מָה שֶׁאֵרַע לָאָבוֹת סִימָן לַבָּנִים. וְלָכֵן יַאֲרִיכוּ הַכְּתוּבִים בְּסִפּוּר הַמַּסָּעוֹת וַחֲפִירַת הַבְּאֵרוֹת וּשְׁאָר הַמִּקְרִים, וְיַחְשֹׁב הַחוֹשֵׁב בָּהֶם כְּאִלּוּ הֵם דְּבָרִים מְיֻתָּרִים אֵין בָּהֶם תּוֹעֶלֶת, וְכֻלָּם בָּאִים לְלַמֵּד עַל הֶעָתִיד, כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר יָבוֹא הַמִּקְרֶה לְנָבִיא מִשְּׁלֹשֶׁת הָאָבוֹת יִתְבּוֹנֵן מִמֶּנּוּ הַדָּבָר הַנִּגְזָר לָבֹא לְזַרְעוֹ. וְדַע כִּי כָל גְּזֵרַת עִירִין כַּאֲשֶׁר תֵּצֵא מִכֹּחַ גְּזֵרָה אֶל פֹּעַל דִּמְיוֹן, תִּהְיֶה הַגְּזֵרָה מִתְקַיֶּמֶת עַל כָּל פָּנִים. וְלָכֵן יַעֲשׂוּ הַנְּבִיאִים מַעֲשֶׂה בַּנְּבוּאוֹת, כְּמַאֲמָר יִרְמְיָהוּ שֶׁצִּוָּה לְבָרוּךְ "וְהָיָה כְּכַלּוֹתְךָ לִקְרֹא אֶת דִּבְרֵי הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה תִּקְשֹׁר עָלָיו אֶבֶן וְהִשְׁלַכְתּוֹ אֶל תּוֹךְ פְּרָת וְאָמַרְתָּ כָּכָה תִּשְׁקַע בָּבֶל" וְגוֹ' (ירמיה נא סג סד), וְכֵן עִנְיַן אֱלִישָׁע בְּהַנִּיחוֹ זְרוֹעוֹ עַל הַקֶּשֶׁת (מלכים ב יג טז-יז) "וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלִישָׁע יְרֵה וַיּוֹר וַיֹּאמֶר חֵץ תְּשׁוּעָה לַה' וְחֵץ תְּשׁוּעָה בַאֲרָם", וְנֶאֱמַר שָׁם (מלכים ב יג ט) "וַיִּקְצֹף עָלָיו אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים וַיֹּאמֶר לְהַכּוֹת חָמֵשׁ אוֹ שֵׁשׁ פְּעָמִים אָז הִכִּיתָ אֶת אֲרָם עַד כַּלֵּה וְעַתָּה שָׁלֹשׁ פְּעָמִים תַּכֶּה אֶת אֲרָם". וּלְפִיכָךְ הֶחֱזִיק הקב"ה אֶת אַבְרָהָם בָּאָרֶץ וְעָשָׂה לוֹ דִּמְיוֹנוֹת בְּכָל הֶעָתִיד לְהֵעָשׂוֹת בְּזַרְעוֹ, וְהָבֵן זֶה. וַאֲנִי מַתְחִיל לְפָרֵשׁ הָעִנְיָנִים בִּפְרָט בַּפְּסוּקִים בְּעֶזְרַת הַשֵּׁם:
Ramban וַיַּעֲבֹ֤ר אַבְרָם֙ בָּאָ֔רֶץ עַ֚ד מְק֣וֹם שְׁכֶ֔ם
Hebrew
הִיא עִיר שְׁכֶם, כִּי זֶה שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא, וּשְׁכֶם בֶּן חֲמוֹר עַל שֵׁם עִירוֹ נִקְרָא. וְכָתַב רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ב:ו') נִכְנַס לְתוֹכָהּ עַד מְקוֹם שְׁכֶם לְהִתְפַּלֵּל עַל בְּנֵי יַעֲקֹב כְּשֶׁיָּבֹאוּ מִן הַשָּׂדֶה עֲצֵבִים. וְנָכוֹן הוּא. וַאֲנִי מוֹסִיף כִּי הֶחֱזִיק אַבְרָהָם בַּמָּקוֹם הַהוּא תְּחִלָּה וְקֹדֶם שֶׁנָּתַן לוֹ אֶת הָאָרֶץ, נִרְמַז לוֹ מִזֶּה כִּי בָּנָיו יִכְבְּשׁוּ הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא תְּחִלָּה קֹדֶם הֱיוֹתָם זוֹכִים בּוֹ, וְקֹדֶם הֱיוֹת עֲוֹן יוֹשֵׁב הָאָרֶץ שָׁלֵם לְהַגְלוֹתָם מִשָּׁם. וְלָכֵן אָמַר "וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי אָז בָּאָרֶץ". וְכַאֲשֶׁר נָתַן לוֹ הקב"ה הָאָרֶץ בְּמַאֲמָר, אָז נָסַע מִשָּׁם וְנָטַע אֹהֶל בֵּין בֵּית אֵל וּבֵין הָעַי, כִּי הוּא הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר כָּבַשׁ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בַּתְּחִלָּה. וְיִתָּכֵן שֶׁהִזְכִּיר הַכָּתוּב "וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי אָז בָּאָרֶץ" לְהוֹרוֹת עַל עִנְיַן הַפָּרָשָׁה, לוֹמַר כִּי אַבְרָם בָּא בְּאֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן וְלֹא הֶרְאָהוּ הַשֵּׁם הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר יְעָדוֹ, וְעָבַר עַד מְקוֹם שְׁכֶם, וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי הַגּוֹי הַמַּר וְהַנִּמְהָר אָז בָּאָרֶץ, וְאַבְרָם יָרֵא מִמֶּנּוּ וְלָכֵן לֹא בָּנָה מִזְבֵּחַ לַה'. וּבְבוֹאוֹ בִּמְקוֹם שְׁכֶם בְּאֵלוֹן מוֹרֶה נִרְאָה אֵלָיו הַשֵּׁם וְנָתַן לוֹ הָאָרֶץ, וְסָרָה יִרְאָתוֹ, כִּי כְּבָר הֻבְטַח בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ, וְאָז בָּנָה מִזְבֵּחַ לַה' לְעָבְדוֹ בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא:

Apparatus
  • 12:6.8 אֵלוֹן: 'terebinth' (the pack's lexicon, Ibn Ezra's first view) against 'plain' (Onkelos, Radak, Ibn Ezra's second view).
  • 12:6.9 מוֹרֶה: place name (Rashi, Ibn Ezra) against the name of a man who owned the place (Radak, Ramban).
  • 12:6.11 אָז: 'then' (at that time) against 'already' (Canaan had taken the land before); the English keeps 'then'.
12:7

The LORD appeared to Abram and said, "To your offspring I will give this land." So he built an altar there to the LORD who had appeared to him.

and-appeared the-LORD to-Abram and-said to-seed-of-you I-will-give acc. the-land the-this and-built there altar to-the-LORD the-one-appearing to-him

Grammar
  • וַיֵּרָא is the Niphal wayyiqtol of ראה, 'appeared'. The Niphal's nun is assimilated and should double the resh; resh cannot be doubled, so the yod takes tsere instead (Ibn Ezra). The final ה of the root falls away in the short form.
  • In לְזַרְעֲךָ אֶתֵּן the recipient stands before the verb. Radak's point is the contrast: the land goes to your offspring, not yet to you.
  • הַנִּרְאֶה is a Niphal participle with the article, used as a relative clause: 'who appeared'.
  • The accents: the zaqef gadol on וַיֹּאמֶר, the etnaḥta on הַזֹּאת. The words of the promise stand between them.

'Appeared' is Ibn Ezra's reading of the Niphal, 'by way of prophecy'. Ramban holds that this is the first appearance: before it Abram had been told 'go' in a dream or by the holy spirit. The 'offspring' is given as a collective singular.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows וַיִּ֤בֶן שָׁם֙ מִזְבֵּ֔חַ
Rashi on וַיִּבֶן שָׁם מִזְבֵּחַ: for the good news of the offspring and for the good news of the land of Israel. The English joins the building to the promise with 'So'.
Hebrew
עַל בְּשׂוֹרַת הַזֶּרַע וְעַל בְּשׂוֹרַת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וַיֵּרָ֤א
Ibn Ezra on וַיֵּרָא: by way of prophecy. The word is of the Niphal pattern, and the hidden quiescent between the yod and the resh (the long vowel of the yod) stands in place of the dagesh that should be in the resh, where the Niphal's nun is swallowed. The English has 'appeared'.

12:8

He moved his tent from there to the mountain east of Bethel and pitched it, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to the LORD and called on the name of the LORD.

and-moved from-there the-mountain-ward from-east to-Bethel and-pitched tent-of-him (written: tent-of-her) Bethel from-sea and-the-Ai from-east and-built there altar to-the-LORD and-called in-name-of the-LORD

Grammar
  • וַיַּעְתֵּק is Hifil, which makes the verb transitive: 'he caused (his tent) to move'. Ibn Ezra contrasts it with the intransitive Qal in Job 18:4.
  • אָהֳלֹה is written with a final he where the usual form has vav (אָהֳלוֹ); the form is the same in meaning; Rashi reads 'her tent', as a hint in the spelling.
  • מִקֶּדֶם and מִיָּם are directions given from the point of view of the land: 'east' (front) and 'sea' (the Mediterranean, to the west).
  • וַיִּקְרָא בְּשֵׁם יְהֹוָה is a fixed idiom: 'he called on the name of the LORD'. It can be a prayer (Onkelos), a proclamation to people (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Ramban), or both.
  • The accents: the etnaḥta on אָהֳלֹה closes the moving and the pitching of the tent. The second half gives the position of the camp (Bethel on the west, Ai on the east, up to the zaqef on מִקֶּדֶם) and then the altar and the calling.

The English supplies 'his tent' as the object of the Hifil (Rashi and Ibn Ezra), and repeats it as 'it' at the next verb. Ibn Ezra gives 'called on the name' two readings, prayer or calling people to the service of God; the English keeps the idiom without choosing. The detail 'with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east' is read as the positions of the camp, with the sea as the west.

Its object is אָהֳלֹה, which is also the object of וַיֵּט, and 'moved' means 'set out, travelled'. In וַיֵּט the hidden quiescent after the yod stands in place of the nun, the first root letter, as in וְיֵז נִצְחָם (Isa. 63:3); both verbs are transitive.

12:9 · פ

Abram set out, going on from stage to stage toward the Negeb.

and-set-out Abram going and-setting-out the-Negeb-ward

Grammar
  • וַיִּסַּע is a wayyiqtol; the munaḥ joins it to אַבְרָם before the zaqef.
  • הָלוֹךְ וְנָסוֹעַ: two infinitives absolute in a row, here describing continued action (going and setting out), not commands.
  • The ending ־ָה on הַנֶּגְבָּה is the directional he, 'toward'; the word means both the region Negeb and 'south'.
  • The paragraph break (פ) after the verse closes the section.

The pair of infinitive absolutes is rendered 'going on from stage to stage' with Rashi and Radak ('from place to place'), who take it as repeated moves. The Negeb is kept as a place name while Ibn Ezra's 'south' is recorded.

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי רָעָב: the wayyiqtol of הָיָה with an indefinite subject after it, 'there was a famine'.
  • מִצְרַיְמָה carries the directional he, 'to Egypt'. Pashta is written on the last letter; it is repeated on רַ because the word is stressed on the penult.
  • לָגוּר is the infinitive construct with לְ, giving the purpose; גּוּר is to live as a resident alien, not to settle (Radak, Sforno).
  • כִּי gives the reason, and the adjective כָּבֵד 'heavy' precedes its subject in the predicate.
  • The etnaḥta on the first בָּאָרֶץ divides the verse: the famine, then Abram's going down and its reason.

'Severe' renders 'heavy', which is the idiom for a famine. Rashi's reading that the famine was a test for Abram is recorded but does not change the English.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativefollows רָעָ֖ב בָּאָ֑רֶץ
Rashi: the famine was in that land alone (בְּאוֹתָהּ הָאָרֶץ לְבַדָּהּ), to test Abram whether he would question God's word, who had told him to go to Canaan and now drives him out of it. His plain point, that 'the land' is Canaan, agrees with Ibn Ezra and with the English; the motive of testing is homiletic and does not change the English.

Apparatus
  • Radak: Egypt had plenty even in famine, being watered by the Nile rather than rain; Ramban: Abram went down to keep himself alive.
12:11

As he drew near to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, "Look now, I know that you are a woman beautiful in appearance.

and-was when he-drew-near to-enter Egypt-ward and-said to Sarai his-wife behold-now I-know that woman beautiful-of appearance you

Grammar
  • The construction וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר + qatal + לְ + infinitive is a time clause that leads into וַיֹּאמֶר.
  • הִנֵּה־נָא יָדַעְתִּי: the perfect of יָדַע is a present state, 'I know', and carries the sense of 'I have long known' (Rashi's plain sense: יָדַעְתִּי זֶה יָמִים רַבִּים).
  • יְפַת־מַרְאֶה is a construct chain, 'beautiful of appearance'; in the nominal clause the predicate אִשָּׁה יְפַת־מַרְאֶה precedes the subject אָתְּ.
  • The etnaḥta on מִצְרָיְמָה divides the verse: the time clause of arrival, then Abram's speech.
  • הִקְרִיב is a Hifil used without an object: 'drew near' (or 'brought [his camp] near', Ibn Ezra, Radak).

I follow Rashi's plain sense (the moment has come to worry about her beauty) and Ibn Ezra's gloss of נָא as 'now'. The verb הִקְרִיב is rendered intransitively.

Commentary (11)
Rashinormativefollows הִנֵּה נָ֣א יָדַ֔עְתִּי
Rashi gives a midrash (until now he had not looked at her, out of modesty) and then the plain sense: 'now it is time to worry about your beauty' as they come among dark people who are not used to beautiful women. The English follows the plain sense and does not impose the midrash.
Hebrew
מִדְרַש אַגָּדָה עַד עַכְשָׁו לֹא הִכִּיר בָּהּ מִתּוֹךְ צְנִיעוּת שֶׁבִּשְׁנֵיהֶם, וְעַכְשָׁו הִכִּיר בָּה עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֶׂה. דָּבָר אַחֵר, מִנְהַג הָעוֹלָם שֶׁעַל יְדֵי טֹרַח הַדֶּרֶךְ אָדָם מִתְבַּזֶּה, וְזֹאת עָמְדָה בְּיָפְיָהּ. וּפְשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁל מִקְרָא הִנֵּה נָא הִגִּיעַ הַשָּׁעָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִדְאֹג עַל יָפְיֵךְ, יָדַעְתִּי זֶה יָמִים רַבִּים כִּי יְפַת מַרְאֶה אַתְּ, וְעַכְשָׁו אָנוּ בָאִים בֵּין אֲנָשִׁים שְׁחֹרִים וּמְכֹעָרִים, אֲחֵיהֶם שֶׁל כּוּשִׁים, וְלֹא הֻרְגְּלוּ בְאִשָּׁה יָפָה; וְדוֹמֶה לוֹ הִנֶּה נָּא אֲדֹנַי סוּרוּ נָא (בר' י"ט):

בַּעְלָהּ בַּעֲלִילָה שֶׁיָּשִׂימוּ עָלָיו. וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי כִּי זֶה דַּרְכָּם לָמוֹ מֵעֵת צֵאתָם מֵחָרָן, בְּכָל מָקוֹם הָיָה אוֹמֵר "אֲחוֹתִי הִיא", כִּי כֵן אָמַר (בראשית כ':י"ג) "וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר הִתְעוּ אֹתִי אֱלֹהִים מִבֵּית אָבִי", אֲבָל הַכָּתוּב יַזְכִּיר זֶה בַּמְּקוֹמוֹת אֲשֶׁר יִתְחַדֵּשׁ לָהֶם עִנְיָן בַּדָּבָר. וְהִנֵּה זֵרֵז אוֹתָהּ עַתָּה כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה לָהּ מִתְּחִלָּה. וְיִצְחָק לֹא פָּחַד בְּאַרְצוֹ וּבְעִירוֹ, רַק בְּבוֹאוֹ אֶל אֶרֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּים אָחַז דֶּרֶךְ אָבִיו. וְאָמַר "לְמַעַן יִיטַב לִי בַעֲבוּרֵךְ וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי בִּגְלָלֵךְ" כָּל יְמֵי הֱיוֹתֵנוּ גָּרִים בָּאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת עַד עֲבֹר הָרָעָב, כִּי אַבְרָהָם מִפְּנֵי הָרָעָב בָּא לָגוּר בָּאָרֶץ וְכַעֲבֹר הָרָעָב יָשׁוּב לָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר נִצְטַוָּה עָלֶיהָ וּנְתָנָהּ הַשֵּׁם לוֹ וּלְזַרְעוֹ, וְהָיָה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁיְּחַיּוּ נַפְשָׁם בָּרָעָב וְיָבֹא לָהֶם רֶוַח וְהַצָּלָה מֵאֵת הָאֱלֹהִים לָשׁוּב, אוֹ שֶׁיִּתָּכֵן לָהֶם לִבְרֹחַ לְאֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן בְּהִתְיָאֲשָׁם מִמֶּנָּה. וְכָתַב רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ב:י"א) "הִנֵּה נָא יָדַעְתִּי" מִדְרַשׁ אַגָּדָה, עַד עַכְשָׁו לֹא הִכִּיר בָּהּ מִתּוֹךְ צְנִיעוּתָהּ, וְעַכְשָׁו עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֶׂה. דָּבָר אַחֵר, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַדֶּרֶךְ אָדָם מִתְבַּזֶּה, וְזוֹ עָמְדָה בְּיָפְיָהּ. וּלְפִי פְּשׁוּטוֹ הִנֵּה נָא הִגִּיעַ הַשָּׁעָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִדְאֹג עַל יָפְיֵךְ, וְיָדַעְתִּי זֶה כַּמָּה יָמִים כִּי יְפַת מַרְאֶה אָתְּ, וְעַכְשָׁו אָנוּ בָאִים בֵּין בְּנֵי אָדָם שְׁחוֹרִים אֲחֵיהֶם שֶׁל כּוּשִׁים, וְלֹא הֻרְגְּלוּ בְּאִשָּׁה יָפָה, וְדוֹמֶה לוֹ "הִנֶּה נָּא אֲדֹנַי סוּרוּ נָא", כָּל זֶה לְשׁוֹן הָרַב. וְהַמִּדְרָשׁ קַבָּלָה בַּעֲנָוָה שֶׁבָּהֶם, וְנִסְמָךְ לַמִּקְרָא, אֲבָל אֵין צֹרֶךְ לְכָל הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה, שֶׁאֵין מִלַּת "נָא" מוֹרָה עַל דָּבָר שֶׁיִּתְחַדֵּשׁ בָּעֵת הַהִיא בִּלְבַד, אֲבָל עַל כָּל דָּבָר הוֹוֶה וְעוֹמֵד יֹאמְרוּ כֵן, כִּי הוּא רוֹמֵז עַל הָעִנְיָן לוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא עַתָּה כָּכָה, "הִנֵּה נָא יָדַעְתִּי כִּי אִשָּׁה יְפַת מַרְאֶה אָתְּ" מֵאָז וְעַד עַתָּה, וְכֵן "הִנֵּה נָא עֲצָרַנִי ה' מִלֶּדֶת" (בראשית ט"ז:ב'), מִנְּעוּרַי וְעַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה. וְכֵן "הִנֵּה נָא לִי שְׁתֵּי בָנוֹת" (בראשית י"ט:ח'), כִּי לֹא נוֹלְדוּ עַתָּה, וְכֻלָּם כָּכָה. וְיֵרָאֶה מִפְּשַׁט הַכְּתוּבִים כִּי שָׂרָה לֹא קִבְּלָה עָלֶיהָ לֵאמֹר כֵּן, אֲבָל הַמִּצְרִים הָיוּ רָעִים וְחַטָּאִים מְאֹד, וְכַאֲשֶׁר רָאוּ אוֹתָהּ וַיְהַלְלוּ אֹתָהּ אֶל פַּרְעֹה לֻקְּחָה אֶל בֵּיתוֹ, וְלֹא שָׁאֲלוּ בָּהֶם כְּלָל אִם אִשְׁתּוֹ הִיא אוֹ אִם אֲחוֹתוֹ הִיא, וְהִיא שָׁתְקָה וְלֹא הִגִּידָה כִּי אִשְׁתּוֹ, וְאַבְרָהָם סִפֵּר מֵעַצְמוֹ כִּי אֲחוֹתוֹ הִיא, וּלְכָךְ הֵטִיבוּ לוֹ בַּעֲבוּרָהּ. וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב "מַה זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ לִּי לָמָּה לֹא הִגַּדְתָּ לִּי כִּי אִשְׁתְּךָ הִיא" (בראשית י"ב:י"ח), הֶאֱשִׁים אוֹתוֹ כִּי בִּרְאוֹתוֹ שֶׁיִּקְחוּ אוֹתָהּ הָיָה לוֹ לְהַגִּיד לְפַרְעֹה כִּי אִשְׁתּוֹ Apparatus
  • The verse is spoken in two stages of narration: arrival time clause, then speech.
12:12

When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife,’ and they will kill me, but you they will let live.

and-will-be when they-see you the-Egyptians and-they-say his-wife this and-they-kill me and-you they-let-live

Grammar
  • וְהָיָה כִּי + yiqtol introduces a future condition; the following weqatal verbs continue it.
  • אִשְׁתּוֹ זֹאת: the predicate precedes the subject, 'his wife [is] this'.
  • וְאֹתָךְ is fronted to contrast with אֹתִי: 'me they will kill, but you they will keep alive'.
  • The Piel יְחַיּוּ means 'let live, preserve alive'.

Ibn Ezra reads 'they will let you live' as 'they will give you all you need', since it was a time of famine. The English keeps 'let live' and records his reading.

  • Radak: Egyptians were less handsome; Radak glosses 'let live' as not killing her for their enjoyment.
12:13

Say, please, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me on your account, and I may live because of you.

say-you-f please my-sister you so-that it-be-good to-me for-sake-of-you and-live my-soul on-account-of-you

Grammar
  • אִמְרִי is a feminine singular imperative; נָא makes it a request.
  • אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ: a nominal clause, predicate first. אֲחֹתִי is stressed on the penult (munaḥ on חֹ) because אָתְּ is stressed on its first syllable (Ibn Ezra; compare קָרָא לָיְלָה, 1:5).
  • לְמַעַן + yiqtol is a purpose clause, 'so that it may go well'; בַּעֲבוּרֵךְ and בִּגְלָלֵךְ are a parallel pair, 'on your account' and 'because of you'.
  • וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי is a weqatal continuing the purpose clause; נַפְשִׁי 'my soul' stands for 'I'.
  • The etnaḥta on אָתְּ divides the request from its purpose.

I keep 'it may go well with me' as the general phrase and record the commentators' sense of 'gifts' in the commentary. 'Live' is the Qal of חיה.

The dagesh in the ת of אָת is there to absorb the nun, for אַתָּה is of the same formation as אני (with nun). A remark on accent and form that does not change the English.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos: וְתִתְקַיֵּם נַפְשִׁי בְּפִתְגָּמָיְכִי, 'and my soul will be preserved through your words', taking בִּגְלָלֵךְ as 'by what you say', as Radak also explains it (בַּעֲבוּר דְּבָרֵךְ שֶׁתֹּאמְרִי).
  • Radak: the good Abram meant was only that they would not kill him, not gifts; Sforno: they would court him with bride-price and gifts.
12:14

When Abram came to Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.

and-was when-came Abram Egypt-ward and-saw the-Egyptians ACC the-woman that beautiful she very

Grammar
  • כְּבוֹא is a preposition with an infinitive construct and the subject אַבְרָם, 'at Abram's coming'.
  • The etnaḥta on מִצְרָיְמָה closes the time clause; the wayyiqtol וַיִּרְאוּ then carries the main clause, with הַמִּצְרִים between the verb and its object.
  • וַיִּרְאוּ ... אֶת־הָאִשָּׁה כִּי יָפָה הִוא: the object is named first and then described by the כִּי clause ('saw the woman, that she was beautiful'); the English joins them.
  • The pronoun הִוא is the subject of the nominal clause and מְאֹד intensifies the adjective.
  • The text speaks of Abram alone coming, although Sarai was with him (Rashi).

Rashi's explanation, that the Egyptians saw her only at the customs inspection of the chest, is recorded but not adopted.

Commentary (3)
Rashinormativerecords וַיְהִ֕י כְּב֥וֹא אַבְרָ֖ם מִצְרָ֑יְמָה
Rashi: it should have said 'when they came'; this teaches that Abram hid her in a chest, and when customs were demanded they opened it and saw her. The English follows the plain sense (the Egyptians saw her) and records this midrash.

12:15

Pharaoh's officials saw her and praised her for Pharaoh, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house.

and-saw her officials-of Pharaoh and-praised her to Pharaoh and-was-taken the-woman house-of Pharaoh

Grammar
  • The two accents zaqef and etnaḥta mark clause breaks after פַרְעֹה, and the three wayyiqtols carry the narrative.
  • וַיְהַלְלוּ is a Piel from הלל with the first lamed written without the expected doubling (Ibn Ezra).
  • וַתֻּקַּח is passive, and the agent is left unnamed; the verse says only that she was taken.
  • בֵּית פַּרְעֹה is a direction without a preposition: 'to the house of Pharaoh'.

I take אֶל־פַּרְעֹה with Rashi as 'with regard to Pharaoh': the officials praised her among themselves as fit for the king. Ramban's other reading, that they praised her to Pharaoh himself, is recorded. The passive is kept without an agent.

Apparatus
  • Radak: 'was taken' implies against her will; Sforno 12:16 on the same word: they did not first consult Abram to persuade him.
12:16

And Pharaoh treated Abram well because of her, and he came to have flocks and herds, donkeys, male and female slaves, she-donkeys, and camels.

and-to-Abram he-treated-well for-her-sake and-was to-him flock-and-herd and-donkeys and-slaves and-maidservants and-she-donkeys and-camels

Grammar
  • לְאַבְרָם, the indirect object with לְ, is fronted before the Hifil הֵיטִיב, whose unstated subject is Pharaoh (Rashi).
  • The etnaḥta on בַּעֲבוּרָהּ divides the verse: Pharaoh's favor, then what Abram came to have.
  • וַיְהִי־לוֹ expresses possession, 'he came to have'; צֹאן and בָּקָר are collective singulars.
  • Each item after the first is joined by waw. Male and female are paired: עֲבָדִים וּשְׁפָחֹת (slaves), and חֲמֹרִים and אֲתֹנֹת (donkeys), the latter pair separated in the list.

Rashi supplies 'Pharaoh' as the subject of הֵיטִיב, and the English follows him. Sheep and goats are rendered 'flocks'.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativefollows וּלְאַבְרָ֥ם הֵיטִ֖יב
Rashi's note on ולאברם היטיב is a single word, 'Pharaoh', supplying the subject. The English follows it.

12:17

Then the LORD struck Pharaoh with great plagues, and his household too, on account of Sarai, Abram's wife.

and-struck the-LORD [obj] Pharaoh plagues great and-[obj] house-his on-account-of Sarai wife-of Abram

Grammar
  • וַיְנַגַּע is a Piel wayyiqtol with a cognate accusative, נְגָעִים גְּדֹלִים: the verb and its object come from one root.
  • The darga on יְהוָה is a conjunctive accent; the vertical stroke after it is a paseq, a slight pause that keeps the divine name apart from the object marker. The tevir on פַּרְעֹה is a minor disjunctive, and the etnaḥta on בֵּיתוֹ closes the first half: both objects, Pharaoh and his household, stand in that half, and the reason clause follows.
  • עַל־דְּבַר is a compound preposition, 'on account of', with the construct chain אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם closing the verse.

Rashi's gloss (the plague of 'raathan', a disease that made intercourse painful) is a midrashic reading and does not change the plain wording, so the English says only 'plagues'. The Hebrew does not say whether 'great' applies to the household too; Sforno reads lesser plagues on the household, and the English 'and his household too' leaves the question open. On עַל־דְּבַר the English follows Ibn Ezra ('because of'); Rashi's 'at her word' is recorded.

Apparatus
  • Ramban, Radak and Sforno also read the plagues as aimed at Pharaoh, with lesser plagues on the household (Sforno).

12:18

Pharaoh summoned Abram and said, "What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she is your wife?"

and-called Pharaoh to-Abram and-said what this you-did to-me why not you-told to-me that wife-your she

Grammar
  • הִגַּדְתָּ is a Hiphil qatal of נגד. The first nun of the root assimilates to the gimel, which therefore takes a dagesh (*hingadta > higgadta); Ibn Ezra lists the verb among those with a first-radical nun (בעלי הנוני"ן).
  • מַה־זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ לִּי is a rhetorical reproach, 'what have you done to me?'.
  • כִּי here introduces the content of what should have been told: 'that she is your wife'.
  • The verse has two questions; the etnaḥta falls after לִּי, dividing them.

The 'that' clause is read as the content that Abram should have told. Ramban notes that the question may be asked in doubt, to draw out the truth.

12:19

Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her as my wife? Now, here is your wife: take her and go.

why you-said sister-my she and-I-took [obj]-her to-me as-wife and-now behold wife-your take and-go

Grammar
  • וָאֶקַּח is a wayyiqtol in first person: the narrative sequence turns into result, 'so that I took'.
  • הִנֵּה אִשְׁתְּךָ קַח וָלֵךְ: two abrupt imperatives; Rashi sees in them an order to leave without delay, unlike Abimelech's offer in chapter 20.
  • The vav of וָלֵךְ takes a qamets before the stressed one-syllable word at the pause (silluq). Ibn Ezra relates it to the accent and compares לֶחֶם וָיָיִן (14:18).
  • לִי and לְאִשָּׁה together mean 'for myself as a wife'.

Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'to be my wife' as a lawful marriage, not a liaison; Ibn Ezra adds that the plagues kept Pharaoh from touching her. The English leaves the question of whether he touched her open, as the Hebrew does.

Grammar
  • וַיְצַו is a Piel wayyiqtol; with עַל and a person it means to give orders about someone.
  • The plural וַיְשַׁלְּחוּ has no stated subject beyond אֲנָשִׁים: 'the men escorted him'.
  • The three objects, אֹתוֹ, אִשְׁתּוֹ and כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ, each take אֶת, listing Abram, his wife and his goods.
  • Ibn Ezra reads וישלחו as an honourable escort, as in 18:16.

The 'orders' are left as the Hebrew leaves them. Rashi and Radak read them as an order to guard Abram and send him off; Ibn Ezra, as a proclamation that no one touch him or his wife. The English says only 'orders concerning him'.

13:1

So Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that was his, and Lot with him, to the Negeb.

and-went-up Abram from-Egypt he and-wife-his and-all that to-him and-Lot with-him the-Negeb-ward

Grammar
  • וַיַּעַל is a Qal wayyiqtol of עלה; the verb 'go up' is used here of leaving Egypt for the land, which lies north.
  • The independent הוּא followed by two more items lists those who went up with Abram.
  • הַנֶּגְבָּה has the article and the directional ה: 'to the Negeb'.
  • The telisha gedola on הוּא is a disjunctive accent that sets the pronoun off from the list after it. The darga on אִשְׁתּוֹ is conjunctive. The tevir on לוֹ and the tipḥa on עִמּוֹ divide the rest of the verse.

Negeb means both the region and 'south'; since Egypt lies south of Canaan, the Negeb here is the southern district of the land. I use the name. Ibn Ezra defers the verb's form to his Sefer HaYesod.

13:2

Now Abram was very heavily laden with livestock, with silver and with gold.

and-Abram heavy very in-the-livestock in-the-silver and-in-the-gold

Grammar
  • וְאַבְרָם כָּבֵד is a verbless clause: 'and Abram (was) heavy'; the vav marks a new scene.
  • מְאֹד 'very' stands after the adjective.
  • The three nouns each take בְּ: 'in livestock, in silver and in gold'.
  • The etnaḥta after מְאֹד marks the first half; the three possessions follow.

כָּבֵד 'heavy' is also 'wealthy'; Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as 'burdened' (with goods), so that the travel was slow. 'Laden' keeps both: heavy with possessions and so rich. Radak compares the construction to כְּאֵלָה נֹבֶלֶת עָלֶיהָ (Isaiah 1:30).

Ibn Ezra: he had much baggage (כְּבוּדָה רַבָּה), and one who has it moves heavily. כָּבוֹד ('honour') comes from כֹּבֶד, the weight of a stone (Proverbs 27:3), as קָלוֹן ('disgrace') comes from קַל, 'light of foot' (2 Samuel 2:18). He had much livestock, and much silver and gold besides.

13:3

He went on his journeys from the Negeb as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai,

and-went to-his-journeys from-Negeb and-until Bethel until the-place which was there tent-his at-the-beginning between Bethel and-between the-Ai

Grammar
  • לְמַסָּעָיו: 'to his journeys', i.e. by stages; the noun is a plural construct with a suffix.
  • The written אָהֳלֹה (ketiv אהלה) is an old spelling of the 3ms suffix; the qere is אָהֳלוֹ.
  • בֵּין ... וּבֵין repeats בֵּין before each term: 'between Bethel and between Ai'.
  • The relative clause אֲשֶׁר־הָיָה שָׁם אָהֳלֹה refers back to 12:8.

The ketiv אהלה is read אָהֳלוֹ ('his tent'), so the English has 'his tent'. Rashi reads the travel as returning by the same lodging places on the way back; Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'journeys' as many short stages. I take 'on his journeys' with the stages and keep Rashi's reading as an alternative.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativerecords וַיֵּ֙לֶךְ֙ לְמַסָּעָ֔יו
Rashi: on the way back he lodged at the same inns where he had stayed on the way down, teaching proper conduct, not to change one's lodging; another reading is that he paid off his debts. The English says only 'on his journeys'.

Rashinormativefollows מִנֶּ֖גֶב

Apparatus
  • Ketiv אהלה (also אָהֳלֹה): the qere is אָהֳלוֹ.
  • Radak: the 'beginning' refers to 'he pitched his tent' (12:8).
  • Sforno: מסעים are the moves of shepherds from one place to another as the pasture runs out.
  • אׇֽהֳלֹה֙ — WLC reads אָֽהֳלוֹ֙ (spelling)
  • אׇֽהֳלֹה֙ — ketiv reads אהלה (ketiv-qere)
13:4

to the place of the altar that he had made there at first; and there Abram called on the name of the LORD.

to place-of the-altar which he-made there at-the-first and-called there Abram in-name-of the-LORD

Grammar
  • The verse continues the sentence of 13:3: Abram came 'to the place of the altar'.
  • בָּרִאשֹׁנָה is 'at first', with the article and the ב of time.
  • וַיִּקְרָא שָׁם אַבְרָם בְּשֵׁם יְהוָה repeats 12:8: calling on the name of the LORD is an act of worship.
  • The verb עָשָׂה is a perfect, 'had made', since it refers to the earlier time.

קָרָא בְּשֵׁם is 'call on the name', as in 12:8. Rashi first reads the calling as part of the earlier events ('and where Abram had called'), then allows a fresh calling now. The English takes the fresh calling, as Radak does ('a second time').

Commentary (4)
Rashinormativefollows אֲשֶׁר עָ֥שָׂה שָׁ֖ם בָּרִאשֹׁנָ֑ה
Rashi reads the relative clause as going on into the next words: the place 'which he had made there at first, and where Abram had called on the name of the LORD'. He also allows the plain sequence: 'and he called there now on the name of the LORD'. The English takes this second reading.
Hebrew

Apparatus
  • Radak: 'again' is meant: he called a second time on the name of the LORD; he settled in the same place to teach that a person should fix a place for prayer.
13:5

Also, Lot, who went with Abram, had flocks and herds and tents.

and-also to-Lot the-going with-Abram was flock-and-herd and-tents

Grammar
  • הָיָה with לְ expresses possession; the singular verb agrees with the first of the things possessed, צֹאן.
  • הַהֹלֵךְ אֶת־אַבְרָם: participle with the article as a relative clause; אֶת here is the preposition 'with' (not the object marker).
  • The etnaḥta on אַבְרָם divides the verse: the description of Lot, then what he had.
  • אֹהָלִים has ḥolem on the aleph. Ibn Ezra: אֹהֶל is of the קֹדֶשׁ pattern, whose plural is בָּאֳהָלִים (Jer 35:7), with ḥaṭef qameṣ; the ḥolem of אֹהָלִים points to a singular of the גּוֹרָל pattern, which is not attested.

The phrase 'who went with Abram' is kept as a relative clause because it is the cause of Lot's wealth in Rashi and Radak. The verse goes on to say that the land could not hold both. The English puts the possession as 'had'.

Commentary (6)
Rashinormativefollows הַהֹלֵ֖ךְ אֶת אַבְרָ֑ם
Rashi asks who caused him to have this, and answers: his going with Abram. The English keeps 'who went with Abram' so that the cause is visible.

מִי גָרַם שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ זֹאת? הֲלִיכָתוֹ עִם אַבְרָם:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וְאֹהָלִֽים׃
Ibn Ezra: the singular is of the קֹדֶשׁ pattern (אֹהֶל), whose plural would be בָּאֳהָלִים (Jer 35:7), like בַּקֳּדָשִׁים (Lev 22:4); אֹהָלִים, with ḥolem between aleph and he, is the plural of a singular of the גּוֹרָל pattern, even though that singular is not found. The point is the form only; the sense is 'tents'.

Apparatus

13:6

But the land could not support them to live together, for their property was great, and they could not live together.

and-not bore them the-land to-dwell together for was their-property much and-not could to-dwell together

Grammar
  • נָשָׂא takes אֶרֶץ as a masculine subject (Radak compares נֶעְתַּם אָרֶץ in Isa 9:18); Rashi reads it as a short expression, 'the land did not bear them (its pasture)', so the verb is masculine to agree with the unexpressed מִרְעֶה.
  • יַחְדָּו is repeated at both ends of the verse, framing the problem.
  • The etnaḥta on יַחְדָּו ends the first clause; the pashta on רְכוּשָׁם and the zaqef on רָב set off the reason.
  • The reason (כִּי) comes between the two statements, so the second 'could not' is the result of the great property.

Rashi says the expression is short and needs 'with the pasture of the land'. The English keeps the short form 'support them' and does not supply the word. Ibn Ezra reads יַחְדָּו as related to יָחִיד, 'as one'; the English uses 'together'.

Commentary (7)
Rashinormativefollows וְלֹא נָשָׂ֥א אֹתָ֛ם
Rashi: the land could not provide enough pasture for their livestock; the expression is short and must be completed, 'did not bear them (the pasture of) the land', which is why the verb is masculine. The English 'support them' reflects this.

13:7

So there was a quarrel between the herders of Abram's livestock and the herders of Lot's livestock. The Canaanites and the Perizzites were then living in the land.

and-was quarrel between herders-of livestock-of-Abram and-between herders-of livestock-of-Lot and-the-Canaanite and-the-Perizzite then dwelling in-the-land

Grammar
  • בֵּין ... וּבֵין: 'between ... and between', the preposition repeated before each party.
  • הַכְּנַעֲנִי וְהַפְּרִזִּי are collective singulars; the singular participle יֹשֵׁב follows.
  • The clause וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי ... is a circumstantial clause with a noun first.
  • אָז is 'at that time'. Rashi reads the whole clause, 'the Canaanite and the Perizzite were then in the land', as the verse's answer to Lot's herders: Abram had not yet come into possession of the land.

Rashi: the quarrel was because Lot's herders let the animals graze in others' fields and Abram's herders reproved them for theft; this is a midrash of the Rabbis (Gen. Rabbah). Ibn Ezra reads only of the Perizzites as possibly one of Canaan's sons with two names. The English follows the plain sense of the quarrel over grazing, and records the midrashic reason.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativerecords וַֽיְהִי רִ֗יב
Rashi gives the cause of the quarrel as the wickedness of Lot's herders, who grazed in others' fields; Abram's herders reproved them, and they replied that the land was given to Abram, who has no heir, so Lot inherits; the verse says the Canaanite was still in the land. The English does not state this cause; it is kept as a midrashic reading.

הָאָרֶץ לְאַבְרָם וְלוֹ אֵין יוֹרֵשׁ וְלוֹט יוֹרְשׁוֹ וְאֵין זֶה גָּזֵל, וְהַכָּתוּב אָמַר "וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי וְהַפְּרִזִּי אָז יֹשֵׁב בָּאָרֶץ", וְלֹא זָכָה בָהּ עֲדַיִן אַבְרָם, וּמִדְרַשׁ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ הוּא (ב"ר מא ה). וַאֲנִי תָּמֵהַּ, כִּי הַמַּתָּנָה שֶׁנֶּאֶמְרָה לְאַבְרָם לְזַרְעוֹ הָיְתָה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לְמַעְלָה (יב ז) "לְזַרְעֲךָ אֶתֵּן אֶת הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת", וְהֵיאַךְ יִירָשֶׁנּוּ לוֹט. אוּלַי שָׁמְעוּ הָרוֹעִים הַמַּתָּנָה וְטָעוּ. וְהַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר כִּי גַּם לְלוֹט גַּם לְאַבְרָם אֵינֶנָּה עַתָּה, וּלְפִי זֶה מַה שֶׁאָמַר תְּחִלָּה כִּי הָיָה רְכוּשָׁם רָב לֵאמֹר כִּי מִפְּנֵי הָרְכוּשׁ הָרַב לֹא יִשָּׂא אוֹתָם הָאָרֶץ, וְהֻצְרְכוּ רוֹעֵי לוֹט לְהַכְנִיס מִקְנֵיהֶם בְּשָׂדוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם בְּעָלִים, וְזֹאת סִבַּת הַמְּרִיבָה. וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ הַפְּשָׁט הָיְתָה הַמְּרִיבָה עַל הַמִּרְעֶה, כִּי לֹא נָשָׂא אוֹתָם הָאָרֶץ וְכַאֲשֶׁר הָיָה מִקְנֵה אַבְרָם רוֹעֶה בָּאָחוּ הָיוּ רוֹעֵי לוֹט בָּאִים בִּגְבוּלָם וְרוֹעִים שָׁם. וְהִנֵּה אַבְרָם וְלוֹט הָיוּ גֵּרִים וְתוֹשָׁבִים בָּאָרֶץ, וּפָחַד אַבְרָם פֶּן יִשְׁמַע הַכְּנַעֲנִי וְהַפְּרִזִּי יוֹשֵׁב הָאָרֶץ כֹּבֶד מִקְנֵיהֶם וִיגָרְשׁוּם אוֹ יַכּוּ אוֹתָם לְפִי חֶרֶב וְיִקְחוּ לָהֶם מִקְנֵיהֶם וּרְכוּשָׁם, כִּי יְשִׁיבַת הָאָרֶץ עַתָּה לָהֶם לֹא לְאַבְרָם. וְזֶה טַעַם "וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי וְהַפְּרִזִּי", כִּי הִזְכִּיר שֶׁהָיוּ עַמִּים רַבִּים יוֹשְׁבִים בָּאָרֶץ הַהִיא, וְלָהֶם וּלְמִקְנֵיהֶם אֵין מִסְפָּר, וְלֹא יִשָּׂא 13:8

Abram said to Lot, "Please, let there be no quarrel between me and you, or between my herders and your herders, for we are kinsmen."

and-said Abram to Lot not please let-be strife between-me and-between-you and-between my-herders and-between your-herders for men brothers we

Grammar
  • אַל + jussive (תְהִי) is a mild prohibition; נָא softens it.
  • The repeated בֵּין is distributive: me and you, my herders and your herders.
  • אֲנָשִׁים אַחִים is literally 'men, brothers', an idiom for close kin (Rashi: קרובים; the midrash: alike in appearance).
  • The zaqef on וּבֵינֶךָ divides the masters from the herders; the etnaḥta on רֹעֶיךָ ends the plea before the reason, כִּי.

Rashi reads 'men, brothers' as kinsmen (Lot was Abram's nephew); the English 'kinsmen' follows this. The midrash that they resembled each other is recorded in the commentary.

13:9

Is not the whole land before you? Please separate from me. If you go left, I will go right; and if you go right, I will go left.

is-not all-of the-land before-you separate-yourself please from-upon-me if the-left and-I-will-go-right and-if the-right and-I-will-go-left

Grammar
  • אֵימִנָה and אַשְׂמְאִילָה are denominative Hiphil verbs from יָמִין and שְׂמֹאל, 'to take the right / the left'; both cohortatives.
  • The first form is pointed with ṣere under the aleph, אֵימִנָה, where one would expect אַיְמִינָה; Rashi compares לְהֵמִין (2 Sam 14:19), pointed thus and not לְהַיְמִין.
  • The conditional clauses are elliptical: 'if (you take) the left, then I (will take) the right'.
  • Radak reads שְׂמֹאל as north and יָמִין as south, since a person faces east; the English keeps 'left' and 'right' as in the Hebrew.

The English supplies 'you go' in the conditional clauses for clarity, which the Hebrew lacks. Rashi's 'I will turn myself to the right' is kept in the literal rendering. Ibn Ezra's note on the aleph of שמאל is a grammatical remark about the root and does not affect the English.

13:10

Lot lifted up his eyes and saw the whole plain of the Jordan, that all of it was well watered, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as you come to Zoar.

and-lifted Lot [object-marker] his-eyes and-saw [object-marker] all-of plain-of the-Jordan for all-of-it irrigation before destroying-of the-LORD [object-marker] Sodom and-[object-marker] Gomorrah like-garden-of the-LORD like-land-of Egypt coming-your Zoar

Grammar
  • כִּי introduces what Lot saw: that all of it was irrigated.
  • לִפְנֵי שַׁחֵת יְהֹוָה: a time phrase with a Piel infinitive; the subject, the LORD, follows the verbal noun (Ibn Ezra: 'before he destroys', infinitive of the intensive stem).
  • כְּגַן יְהֹוָה and כְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם are two similes; the first echoes Eden (2:10), the second Egypt's irrigated fields.
  • בֹּאֲכָה צֹעַר: 'as you come to Zoar', with a 2ms suffix that the plain sense treats as a general address (Radak: the speaker addresses the reader who knows the place); Rashi: 'as far as Zoar'.

Ibn Ezra explains כִּכָּר as a place of vegetation; Rashi (at 13:11) and the Targum as a plain. The English 'plain' follows Rashi and the Targum. Rashi takes 'garden of the LORD' as trees and 'land of Egypt' as crops; the English leaves both similes as written. The clause 'before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah' is the narrator's aside and is kept in place. Rashi and Radak take בֹּאֲכָה צֹעַר as 'as far as Zoar'; Rashi records an aggadic reading against Lot. The English 'as you come to Zoar' keeps the Hebrew's form and the sense 'up to'.

Commentary (16)

Apparatus
  • The Targum renders כִּכָּר by מֵישַׁר, 'plain'.
  • BDB entry for עַיִן in the pack lists no plain sense 'eye'.
13:11

Lot chose for himself the whole plain of the Jordan, and Lot set out from the east, and they separated, one from the other.

and-chose for-him Lot [object-marker] all-of plain-of the-Jordan and-set-out Lot from-east and-separated man from-upon his-brother

Grammar
  • לוֹ after the verb is a reflexive dative: 'for himself'.
  • מִקֶּדֶם: 'from the east' or 'from of old'; Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it of direction (Sodom is west of Bethel); the aggada in Rashi reads it as 'from the Ancient One (קַדְמוֹנוֹ) of the world'.
  • אִישׁ מֵעַל אָחִיו is the idiom for 'each from the other'; the Niphal plural is reciprocal.
  • The etnaḥta on מִקֶּדֶם divides Lot's journey from the separation.

The English follows Rashi (plain sense) and Ibn Ezra: Lot set out from the east, travelling westward, because Sodom lies west of Bethel. Sforno agrees (from east to west, away from Abram near Ai). Radak takes it differently: toward the east, since the Jordan is east of Canaan. The midrash 'from the Ancient One of the world' is recorded in the commentary.

  • The pack parses וַיֶּאֱהַל as Qal, which the form bears out (prefix vowel segol before the guttural); the lexicon lists only a Piel, so no sense of the entry is cited.

13:13

Now the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners against the LORD, exceedingly.

and-men-of Sodom wicked and-sinners to-the-LORD exceedingly

Grammar
  • The verse is a verbless clause: subject אַנְשֵׁי סְדֹם, predicates רָעִים and חַטָּאִים.
  • The etnaḥta falls on וְחַטָּאִים, so the accents set לַיהוָה מְאֹד apart as a closing phrase. Radak takes it over both predicates ('all of it is sin to the LORD'). Ibn Ezra, who reads רָעִים as 'toward people', leaves it to חַטָּאִים, and the English follows him in joining 'against the LORD' to 'sinners'.
  • Rashi divides the two words: רָעִים in their bodies, חַטָּאִים in their wealth. Onkelos has the reverse.
  • מְאֹד is a noun used adverbially, 'exceedingly'.

The adjectives are kept apart, 'wicked' and 'sinners', because the normative commentators distinguish them: Rashi, wicked 'in their bodies' (בְּגוּפָם) and sinners 'in their wealth' (בְּמָמוֹנָם); Ibn Ezra, wicked 'toward people' (לִבְנֵי אָדָם). 'Against' renders ל as the context requires.

  • 13:13.5 vowels: WLC reads לַיהוָה; the base text has לַיהֹוָה. The English is the same.

13:14

The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward."

and-the-LORD said to Abram after being-separated Lot from-with-him lift please your-eyes and-see from-the-place which you there northward and-southward and-eastward and-westward

Grammar
  • The clause opens with וַיהוָה אָמַר, a fronted subject and a qatal, so it reads as background: the LORD had spoken, or spoke, once Lot was gone.
  • אַחֲרֵי הִפָּרֶד־לוֹט is a preposition with an infinitive construct and its subject.
  • שָׂא נָא עֵינֶיךָ וּרְאֵה: two imperatives; נָא makes the command a request.
  • Each of the four directions takes the directional ה, 'toward'; the sea is the west because the Mediterranean lies there.

The perfect after a fronted subject is rendered as a simple past with 'after' carrying the order. The omitted נָא is recorded in the phrase note.

  • 13:14.1 vowels: WLC reads וַיהוָה; the base text has וַיהֹוָה.

13:15

for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.

for [object-mark] all-the-land which you seeing to-you I-will-give-it and-to-your-seed until forever

Grammar
  • The object, כָּל־הָאָרֶץ, comes first, then the relative clause, then the verb, so the whole land is stressed.
  • אֶתְּנֶנָּה has a nun-energic suffix, a resumptive pronoun for the fronted object.
  • רֹאֶה is a participle: the land is what Abram is looking at.
  • The etnaḥta falls on אֶתְּנֶנָּה, so וּלְזַרְעֲךָ עַד־עוֹלָם stands apart: a second recipient and the term of the gift, added to the verb before the pause. It has no verb of its own.

The resumptive suffix on אֶתְּנֶנָּה is not repeated in English because the fronted object already stands in the sentence.

Commentary (5)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows לְךָ֣ אֶתְּנֶ֑נָּה
Ibn Ezra: לְךָ אֶתְּנֶנָּה is 'by speech': the giving is done by the spoken word, as in 'he shall put (וְנָתַן) them on the head of the goat' (Lev 16:21), where the sins are put on the goat by the spoken confession. So 'I will give' is a grant made in words, not yet a handing over.

I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if anyone can count the dust of the earth, then your offspring too can be counted.

Grammar
  • כַּעֲפַר הָאָרֶץ is a simile of number, not of substance.
  • אֲשֶׁר אִם introduces a conditional with a result sense: 'such that if ...'.
  • The apodosis גַּם־זַרְעֲךָ יִמָּנֶה has no particle of its own; גַּם marks the parallel.
  • The wordplay on the root מנה: יוּכַל ... לִמְנוֹת, then יִמָּנֶה.

'Dust' is the plain sense of עָפָר here; the verb שַׂמְתִּי is rendered 'make' in the sense 'turn into', as in 'make a nation'.

Apparatus
  • The sentence has a pause at ׀ after אֲשֶׁר (legarmeh in the base text); the reading follows the zaqef qaton after הָאָרֶץ.
13:17

Get up, walk about the land through its length and its breadth, for I will give it to you.

Grammar
  • קוּם הִתְהַלֵּךְ: a pair of imperatives; the first is a preliminary, 'get going'.
  • The hitpael of הלך gives the sense 'walk back and forth'.
  • The distributive ל on אָרְכָּהּ and רָחְבָּהּ is 'along'.
  • The etnaḥta on וּלְרָחְבָּהּ divides the command from its reason.

The land is the object of 'walk about'; the preposition ב means 'in' or 'through'.

Grammar
  • Four wayyiqtols in a row (וַיֶּאֱהַל, וַיָּבֹא, וַיֵּשֶׁב, וַיִּבֶן) give the narrative sequence of Abram's move.

I follow Rashi and Ibn Ezra on Mamre, taking it as a man's name and the oaks as the oaks in Hebron. The Hebrew verb is intransitive: 'he pitched tent', so 'moved his tent' is an interpretive rendering.

It happened in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim,

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי with a time phrase begins a long sentence whose subject-verb comes in verse 2 (עָשׂוּ מִלְחָמָה).
  • Each king is joined to his land by a construct מֶלֶךְ־; the etnaḥta on אֶלָּסָר and zaqef on שִׁנְעָר/עֵילָם group the four kings in pairs.
  • The list is asyndetic until the last member, which takes וְ.

גּוֹיִם is kept as a place name, 'Goiim', following Rashi and the first reading of Ibn Ezra; the reading 'king of nations' is recorded. The names are transliterated without comment on their meaning.

14:2

they made war on Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar.

they-made war with-Bera king-of Sodom and-with-Birsha king-of Gomorrah Shinab king-of Admah and-Shemeber king-of Zeboiim and-king-of Bela it Zoar

Grammar
  • עָשׂוּ מִלְחָמָה אֶת־ is the idiom 'make war with/against' (אֵת as 'with').
  • The five kings fall into groups: אֶת־בֶּרַע ... וְאֶת־בִּרְשַׁע, both with אֶת; then שִׁנְאָב ... וְשֶׁמְאֵבֶר, with no אֶת and with וְ only on the second; then וּמֶלֶךְ בֶּלַע, a king without a name. The etnaḥta on עֲמֹרָה divides the first pair from the rest.
  • The pashta is written on the last letter of its word; on בֶּרַע and שֶׁמְאֵבֶר it is written twice because the stress is not on the last syllable (penultimate stress of the segolate forms).
  • הִיא־צֹעַר is a gloss giving the later name of Bela.

The names are transliterated. Rashi's moral readings of the names (Bera 'evil', Birsha 'wickedness', Shinab 'hater of his father', Shemeber 'he set a wing') are homiletic and are not put into the English.

14:3

All these joined forces in the Valley of Siddim, which is the Salt Sea.

all-of these they-joined to valley-of the-Siddim it sea-of the-salt

Grammar
  • כָּל־אֵלֶּה is the subject placed first; חָבְרוּ is 3rd plural perfect, with the zaqef after it dividing verb from place.
  • אֶל־עֵמֶק with a verb of coming together: 'to' the valley, as a gathering point.
  • הוּא יָם הַמֶּלַח is a pronoun-copula gloss: 'it (is) the Salt Sea', naming the place by its later name.
  • עֵמֶק is in the construct state: 'the valley of (the Siddim)'.

אֶל־ is rendered 'in' for English idiom (Radak: אֶל here as בְּ). The name of the valley is kept as 'Siddim': Rashi says the valley was named for its many fields; Ibn Ezra derives the name from שִׂיד 'plaster', recorded. 'Which is the Salt Sea' follows Rashi, that the sea later covered the valley; Ibn Ezra's 'the Valley of the Salt Sea' is recorded.

Rashinormativefollows ה֖וּא יָ֥ם הַמֶּֽלַח׃

twelve year they-served ACC-Chedorlaomer and-thirteen year they-rebelled

Grammar
  • The duration (שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה) stands first, an accusative of time, and is set against the second period.
  • Both verbs are perfect qatal with the same plural subject, the five kings of verse 2.
  • וּשְׁלֹשׁ־עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה has no preposition; English supplies 'in', following Ibn Ezra.

The cardinal numbers are written out in words. The preposition 'in' is added before the thirteenth year following Ibn Ezra.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows שְׁתֵּ֤ים עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה עָבְד֖וּ
Rashi: 'these five kings served Chedorlaomer'; the subject of עָבְדוּ is the five kings of verse 2.
Hebrew
חֲמִשָּׁה מְלָכִים הַלָּלוּ אֶת כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows the whole verse
Ibn Ezra: וּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה means 'in the thirteenth', the preposition understood, as in 'for in six days the LORD made' (Exod 20:11). The author of Seder Olam added the two periods together (twelve years of service, then thirteen of rebellion); Ibn Ezra defers to him: 'his knowledge is wider than ours'.

בשלש עשרה כמו "כי ששת ימים עשה ד'" (שמות כ יא), ובעל סדר סדר עולם חברם ודעתו רחבה מדעתנו:

Apparatus
  • וּשְׁלֹשׁ־עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה מָרָדוּ: Ibn Ezra and Radak, 'in the thirteenth year they rebelled'; Seder Olam, followed by Rashi on 14:5 (לְמִרְדָּן), 'for thirteen years they rebelled', with the fourteenth year of verse 5 counted from the rebellion.
14:5

In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, and the kings who were with him, and they struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim at Ham, and the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim,

and-in-four ten year came Chedorlaomer and-the-kings who with-him and-they-struck ACC-Rephaim in-Ashteroth Karnaim and-ACC-the-Zuzim in-Ham and-ACC the-Emim in-Shaveh Kiriathaim

Grammar
  • בָּא is singular: a verb that stands before a compound subject often agrees with the first member, and Rashi says Chedorlaomer was the chief party. וְהַמְּלָכִים is added after him, then the plural wayyiqtol וַיַּכּוּ takes over.
  • Three peoples are struck at three places, each with אֵת + people and בְּ + place.
  • The zaqef on אִתּוֹ ends the account of who came, and the etnaḥta on בְּהָם ends the second people-and-place pair.
  • רְפָאִים (here without the article), הַזּוּזִים and הָאֵימִים are gentilic names of ancient peoples; אֵימִים also means 'terrors'.

The ancient peoples are named by transliteration: Rephaim, Zuzim, Emim. The English 'In the fourteenth year' follows the Hebrew order. 'Came' is singular because the verb stands before its compound subject, of which Chedorlaomer, the leader, is the first member.

Commentary (10)
Rashinormativerecords וּבְאַרְבַּע֩ עֶשְׂרֵ֨ה שָׁנָ֜ה
Rashi on 'in the fourteenth year': לְמִרְדָּן, 'of their rebellion'. He counts the year from the rebellion, so with Seder Olam he takes 14:4 as 'for thirteen years they rebelled'. The English follows Ibn Ezra, 'in the thirteenth year', and counts from the start of their service.
Hebrew
לְמִרְדָּן:
Rashinormativefollows בָּ֣א כְדׇרְלָעֹ֗מֶר
Rashi: Chedorlaomer alone is named as coming because he was the chief party to the affair; 'he entered into the thickness of the beam', an idiom for being most deeply involved. The English, with the singular verb, names him first and then the kings with him.

Rashinormativefollows וְהַמְּלָכִים֙

Ibn Ezra: they are called Rephaim because whoever saw them, his heart would die and he would be counted among the Rephaim, which are the dead. He derives the name from רְפָאִים 'shades of the dead'.

14:6

and the Horites in their mountain, Seir, as far as El-paran, which is by the wilderness.

and-ACC-the-Horite in-their-mountain Seir as-far-as terebinth-of Paran which on the-wilderness

Grammar
  • הַחֹרִי is a singular gentilic with the article used as a collective, 'the Horite(s)'.
  • בְּהַרְרָם has a doubled resh; Rashi 'their mountain', Ibn Ezra a different reading (see commentary).
  • The yetiv on עַד and the zaqef on פָּארָן bound the geographical phrase.
  • עַל־הַמִּדְבָּר: 'on' the wilderness means 'beside' it.

אֵיל פָּארָן is kept as the proper name El-paran; the lexicon gives 'terebinth of Paran', and Rashi argues that אֵיל is part of a name, not 'plain'. עַל rendered 'by' following Rashi.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows בְּהַרְרָ֣ם
Rashi on בְּהַרְרָם: 'in their mountain'; the English reads 'in their mountain'.
Hebrew
בְּהַר שֶׁלָּהֶם:
Rashinormativefollows אֵ֣יל פָּארָ֔ן
Rashi: the Targum renders אֵיל as 'plain', but Rashi thinks אֵיל is not 'plain'; it is the name of the plain of Paran, as Elonei is that of Mamre and Kikkar of the Jordan. The English keeps El-paran as a name.
Hebrew
כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ מִישׁוֹר. וְאוֹמֵר אֲנִי שֶׁאֵין אֵיל לְשׁוֹן מִישׁוֹר, אֶלָּא מִישׁוֹר שֶׁל פָּארָן אֵיל שְׁמוֹ, וְשֶׁל מַמְרֵא אֵלוֹנֵי שְׁמוֹ, וְשֶׁל יַרְדֵּן כִּכָּר שְׁמוֹ, וְשֶׁל שִׁטִּים אָבֵל שְׁמוֹ, אָבֵל הַשִּׁטִּים, וְכֵן בַּעַל גָּד בַּעַל שְׁמוֹ; וְכֻלָּם מְתֻרְגָּמִין מִישׁוֹר, וְכָל א' שְׁמוֹ עָלָיו:
Rashinormativefollows עַל הַמִּדְבָּֽר׃
Rashi: עַל הַמִּדְבָּר means 'beside the wilderness', like 'and beside him the tribe of Manasseh' (Num 2); the English has 'by the wilderness'.

אָבֵל שְׁמוֹ, וְכֻלָּם מְתֻרְגָּמִין מֵישְׁרָא, וְכָל אֶחָד שְׁמוֹ עָלָיו, לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ד:ו'). וְאִלּוּ הָיָה כֵן הָיָה אוּנְקְלוֹס (תרגום אונקלוס על בראשית י"ד:ו') מְתַרְגֵּם בִּשְׁמָם "אֵילָא דְּפָארָן", "אֵלוֹנֵי דְּמַמְרֵא", כְּמִנְהָגוֹ בַּשֵּׁמוֹת, וּמִי הִגִּיד לוֹ בַּמְּקוֹמוֹת הָרַבִּים הָהֵם הֲמִישׁוֹר הֵם כֻּלָּם אוֹ הָרִים הַגְּבוֹהִים. וּ"מַמְרֵא" שֵׁם הָאִישׁ הָאֱמֹרִי, אֲחִי אֶשְׁכֹּל וַאֲחִי עָנֵר בַּעֲלֵי בְּרִית אַבְרָם, וְהַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא שֶׁלּוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר (בראשית י"ד:י"ג) "אֵלוֹנֵי מַמְרֵא הָאֱמֹרִי" כַּאֲשֶׁר פֵּרַשְׁתִּי (רמב"ן על בראשית י"ב:ו'). אֲבָל "אֵיל פָּארָן" מְקוֹם אֵילִים, "כִּי יֵבֹשׁוּ מֵאֵילִים אֲשֶׁר חֲמַדְתֶּם" (ישעיהו א כט), וְ"אֵלוֹנֵי" מְקוֹם אַלּוֹנִים "כָּאֵלָה וְכָאַלּוֹן" (שם ו יג), "אַלּוֹנִים מִבָּשָׁן" (יחזקאל כז ו), וְהַנָּהוּג בָּהֶם לִהְיוֹתָם נְטוּעִים בְּמִישׁוֹר לִפְנֵי הַמְּדִינוֹת לִהְיוֹת לָעִיר כְּמוֹ מִגְרָשׁ. וְכֵן תַּרְגּוּם "אַלּוֹן בָּכוּת" (בראשית ל"ה:ח') "מִישׁוֹר בְּכוּתָא", וְשָׁם אֵינֶנּוּ שֵׁם הָעֶצֶם לַמָּקוֹם רַק הוּא שֵׁם לָאַלּוֹן הַנָּטוּעַ שָׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמְּפֹרָשׁ (שם) "תַּחַת הָאַלּוֹן", אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא רוֹדֵף הָעִנְיָן לֹא הַמִּלּוֹת. וְהַתַּרְגּוּם הַיְּרוּשַׁלְמִי אָמַר בְּ"אֵיל פָּארָן" וְ"אֵלוֹנֵי מַמְרֵא" – "מֵישְׁרָא", כְּדִבְרֵי אוּנְקְלוֹס, וְאָמַר בְּ"אַלּוֹן בָּכוּת" – "בַּלּוּט בְּכוּתָא", כִּי "אַלּוֹן בָּכוּת" אֶצְלוֹ שֵׁם לָאִילָן, לֹא לַמָּקוֹם. וְאוּנְקְלוֹס סָבַר שֶׁהוּא שֵׁם לַמָּקוֹם, כִּי הָיוּ בּוֹ אַלּוֹנִים רַבִּים, כְּמוֹ "אֵלוֹנֵי מַמְרֵא", וּלְכָךְ אָמַר "הָאַלּוֹן". וְהִנֵּה כֻּלָּם שְׁמוֹת תֹּאַר, אֲבָל "כִּכַּר הַיַּרְדֵּן" לְשׁוֹן מִישׁוֹר מַמָּשׁ הוּא, כִּי כֵן יִקָּרֵא בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקֹּדֶשׁ הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁהַנְּהָרוֹת מִתְפַּשְּׁטִין בָּהֶם בִּמְרוּצַת הַמַּיִם הַנִּגָּרִים הַשּׁוֹטְפִים שָׁם, וְלָכֵן אָמַר (בראשית י"ט:י"ז) "וְאַל תַּעֲמֹד בְּכָל הַכִּכָּר הָהָרָה הִמָּלֵט", וְכֵן "כַּר נִרְחָב" (ישעיהו ל כג), "לָבְשׁוּ כָרִים הַצֹּאן וַעֲמָקִים יַעַטְפוּ בָר" (תהלים סה יד), פְּעָמִים יִכְפְּלוּ הַמִּלָּה וּפְעָמִים יָסִירוּ הַכֶּפֶל, כְּמוֹ "בַּת עָיִן" (שם יז ח) וְזוּלָתָם רַבִּים. וְיִקָּרְאוּ גַּם כֵּן הַשְּׁלוּחִים הַמְּהִירִים בַּשֵּׁם הַזֶּה, "לַכָּרִי וְלָרָצִים" (מלכים ב יא ד), "שָׂרֵי הַמֵּאוֹת וְאֶת הַכָּרִי" (שם יט), וְכֵן "בַּכִּרְכָּרוֹת" (ישעיהו סו כ), שֵׁם לַגְּמַלִּים הַמְּרִיצִין שֶׁהִזְכִּירוּם בַּתַּלְמוּד (מכות ה) "גַּמְלָא פַּרְחָא", וּמִמֶּנּוּ "מְכַרְכֵּר", כְּפוּלִים. וְ"אָבֵל הַשִּׁטִּים" (במדבר לג מט) וְכֵן "אָבֵל מְחוֹלָה" (שופטים ז כב) תִּרְגְּמוּ אוֹתוֹ "מֵישַׁר", הוּא הַמָּקוֹם הַנֶּחֱרָב אֵין בּוֹ נֶטַע וְלֹא בִּנְיָן, כִּי הַלָּשׁוֹן אֶצְלָם לְשׁוֹן חֲרֵבָה וּשְׁמָמָה, כְּמוֹ "וַיַּאֲבֶל חֵיל וְחוֹמָה" (איכה ב ח), "אָבַל תִּירוֹשׁ אֻמְלְלָה גָפֶן" (ישעיהו כד ז):

Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat, which is Kadesh, and struck all the territory of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar.

and-they-returned and-they-came to Spring-of Judgment it Kadesh and-they-struck ACC-all-of field-of the-Amalekite and-also ACC-the-Amorite the-dwelling in-Hazazon Tamar

Grammar
  • Two wayyiqtols, וַיָּשֻׁבוּ and וַיָּבֹאוּ, are joined and carry the campaign on. The telisha gedola stands on the first letter of its word; it is written a second time on וַיָּשֻׁבוּ to mark the stressed syllable.
  • הוּא/הִוא קָדֵשׁ is a gloss, with feminine הִוא (Pentateuch) agreeing with the place.
  • שְׂדֵה הָעֲמָלֵקִי is 'the field' in the sense of 'territory', in the construct.
  • הַיֹּשֵׁב is an active participle with article, a relative clause: 'who lived'.

שְׂדֵה is rendered 'territory', as the whole country of the Amalekites. Rashi notes that Amalek was not yet born, so the name is given in anticipation; the English keeps the text's wording.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativerecords עֵ֤ין מִשְׁפָּט֙ הִ֣וא קָדֵ֔שׁ
Rashi: En-mishpat is named for the future, since Moses and Aaron would be judged there in the matter of the spring, the waters of Meribah; Onkelos translates it simply, as the place where the people of the district gathered for every judgment. The English transliterates and follows the plain sense of the name.
Hebrew
עַל שֵׁם הֶעָתִיד, שֶׁעֲתִידִין מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן לְהִשְָּׁפֵט שָׁם עַל עִסְקֵי אוֹתוֹ הָעַיִן וְהֵם מֵי מְרִיבָה. וְאֻנְקְלוֹס תִּרְגְּמוֹ כִפְשׁוּטוֹ מָקוֹם שֶׁהָיוּ בְנֵי הַמְּדִינָה מִתְקַבְּצִים שָׁם לְכָל מִשְׁפָּט:
Rashinormativefollows שְׂדֵ֖ה הָעֲמָלֵקִ֑י
Rashi: Amalek was not yet born; the territory is called by the future name. The English keeps 'Amalekites' and notes this.

עֲדַיִן לֹא נוֹלַד עֲמָלֵק, וְנִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הֶעָתִיד:
Rashinormativefollows בְּחַֽצְצֹ֥ן תָּמָֽר׃
Rashi: Hazazon-tamar is En-gedi; a verse says so explicitly (מִקְרָא מָלֵא) in Chronicles, in the story of Jehoshaphat (2 Chr 20:2).

Ramban אֶל עֵ֤ין מִשְׁפָּט֙
Hebrew
עַל שֵׁם הֶעָתִיד, שֶׁעֲתִידִים מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן לְהִשְָּׁפֵט שָׁם עַל עִסְקֵי אוֹתוֹ הָעַיִן, לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ד:ז') מִדִּבְרֵי אַגָּדָה (במד"ר יט יד). וְלֹא הֲבִינוֹתִי זֶה, כִּי "קָדֵשׁ" זֶה הוּא "קָדֵשׁ בַּרְנֵעַ", כִּי הוּא בְּ"אֵיל פָּארָן אֲשֶׁר עַל הַמִּדְבָּר", וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִשְׁתַּלְּחוּ מְרַגְּלִים בְּשָׁנָה שְׁנִיָּה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (במדבר יג כו) "אֶל מִדְבַּר פָּארָן קָדֵשָׁה", וְכָתוּב (דברים א יט כב) "וַנָּבֹא עַד קָדֵשׁ בַּרְנֵעַ" "וַתֹּאמְרוּ נִשְׁלְחָה אֲנָשִׁים לְפָנֵינוּ", וְשָׁם יָשְׁבוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל יָמִים רַבִּים. אֲבָל "קָדֵשׁ" שֶׁשָּׁם מִשְׁפַּט הַצַּדִּיקִים הוּא בְּמִדְבַּר צִן, שֶׁבָּאוּ שָׁם בִּשְׁנַת הָאַרְבָּעִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (במדבר כ א) "וַיָּבֹאוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּל הָעֵדָה מִדְבַּר צִן בַּחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן וַיֵּשֶׁב הָעָם בְּקָדֵשׁ" וּגְמַר הַפָּרָשָׁה. אוּלַי הַמִּדְרָשׁ עַל הַשֵּׁם בִּלְבַד הוּא, רָמַז הַכָּתוּב כִּי הַשֵּׁם הַזֶּה "קָדֵשׁ" הוּא יִהְיֶה עֵין מִשְׁפָּט. וְאוּנְקְלוֹס (תרגום אונקלוס על בראשית י"ד:ז') אָמַר "מֵישַׁר פִּלּוּג דִּינָא", וְלֹא יָדַעְתִּי מַהוּ, אוּלַי הוּא מִלְּשׁוֹן "פְּלָגִים יִבְלֵי מָיִם" (ישעיהו ל כה), "מִי פִלַּג לַשֶּׁטֶף תְּעָלָה" (איוב לח כה), וְכֵן בִּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים (אסתר רבה ה) "פַּלְגּוֹ שֶׁל יָם", יֹאמַר כִּי בַּמִּישׁוֹר הַהוּא מַעְיָן הַמִּשְׁפָּט וְעֹמֶק הַדִּין, כִּי הָיָה מִישׁוֹר נָאֶה מְעֻתָּד לַמְּלָכִים, שָׁם יָשְׁבוּ לִשְׁפֹּט אֶת כָּל הַגּוֹיִם בָּאֲרָצוֹת הָהֵם:

14:8

Then the king of Sodom went out, and the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar, and they drew up battle lines against them in the Valley of Siddim.

and-went-out king-of Sodom and-king-of Gomorrah and-king-of Admah and-king-of Zeboiim and-king-of Bela it Zoar and-they-arranged with-them war in-valley-of the-Siddim

Grammar
  • The singular וַיֵּצֵא comes first, with all five kings listed after it in a series of וּמֶלֶךְ.
  • עָרַךְ מִלְחָמָה is the idiom 'draw up battle lines', here with אִתָּם 'against them'.
  • The ketiv צביים and qere צְבוֹיִם concern the vowel pattern; the name is the same as in verse 2.
  • The verse resumes the place named in verse 3, בְּעֵמֶק הַשִּׂדִּים, closing the frame.

In the Hebrew אִתָּם 'with them' stands between the verb and מִלְחָמָה; the English puts 'against them' after 'battle lines'.

Apparatus
  • 14:8.9 ketiv-qere: the ketiv reads צביים; the base text has צְבוֹיִם.

14:9

with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar: four kings against the five.

with-Chedorlaomer king-of Elam and-Tidal king-of Goim and-Amraphel king-of Shinar and-Arioch king-of Ellasar four kings with-the-five

Grammar
  • The verse is a long apposition continuing verse 8: the four kings are listed with their lands, each as 'king of X', and the list ends with the totals 'four kings against the five'.
  • אֵת is the preposition 'with' (compare עִם): Ibn Ezra glosses אֵת כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר as 'with'. It is not the object marker here.
  • The accents set each name-and-land pair apart: geresh/revia after Elam, pashta/zaqef qaton for the next two pairs, tipha and etnahta at Arioch and Ellasar; the merkha-tipha pair carries 'four kings' and silluq closes 'the five'.
  • The numerals contrast four against five; the word order 'four kings against the five' sets the few against the many.

Both אֵת in the verse (14:9.1, 14:9.16) are the preposition 'with', as the pack parses them and as Ibn Ezra glosses the first (כמו עם); in a battle 'with' the five means 'against' them. Goim (גּוֹיִם) is left as a name, as the lexicon gives it; the word is also 'nations', and Onkelos translates it 'of the peoples' (דְעַמְמִין). Onkelos reads 'Babel' for Shinar.

Rashi: the few nevertheless won, to show they were mighty, and Abram was not deterred from pursuing them. This is a moral about the numbers, not a reading of the words.

14:10

The Valley of Siddim was pit upon pit of bitumen, and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell there, and the survivors fled into the hills.

and-valley-of the-Siddim pits-of pits-of bitumen and-fled king-of Sodom and-Gomorrah and-fell-there and-the-remaining to-hill fled

Grammar
  • The doubled בֶּאֱרֹת בֶּאֱרֹת is idiomatic: 'pits and pits', that is, pit after pit. Both words are in the construct state, with חֵמָר 'bitumen' as the last member.
  • The verb וַיָּנֻסוּ is plural although מֶלֶךְ־סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה looks like a single king 'of Sodom and Gomorrah'. The sense is the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah.
  • הֶרָה and שָׁמָּה take the directional ה, a locative ending without a preposition. Rashi says הֶרָה means 'to a mountain' (indefinite), unlike הָהָרָה with the article, 'to the mountain'.
  • The word order changes at the end: 'and the remaining ones, to-the-hills they fled', with the subject and place fronted to contrast with the two kings who fell.
  • Zaqef qaton on חֵמָר ends the first clause; etnahta on שָׁמָּה ends the second.

I take חֵמָר as the lexicon gives it ('bitumen'); Rashi and Radak read 'clay, mud' for the building mortar, a reading the English does not adopt. וַיִּפְּלוּ־שָׁמָּה is kept open between 'fell into the pits' and 'threw themselves down there' (Ibn Ezra); the English line says only 'fell there'. הֶרָה is rendered 'into the hills', following Rashi's indefinite reading; Ibn Ezra's 'to the mountain' is recorded. Sforno takes the survivors to be the three remaining kings.

Commentary (14)
Rashinormativefollows בֶּֽאֱרֹ֤ת בֶּאֱרֹת֙ חֵמָ֔ר
Rashi: there were many pits there, from which earth was taken for the mortar of buildings. The aggadic midrash: the mud was thick in them, and a miracle was done for the king of Sodom, who came out of it, because some among the nations did not believe that Abraham had been saved from the furnace at Ur Kasdim; once this king came out of the mud, they believed in Abram after the fact. The English takes his 'many pits' but keeps the lexicon's 'bitumen' for the material.
Hebrew
בְּאֵרוֹת הַרְבֵּה הָיוּ שָׁם, שֶׁנּוֹטְלִין מִשָּׁם אֲדָמָה לְטִיט שֶׁל בִּנְיָן. וּמִדְרַש אַגָּדָה שֶׁהָיָה הַטִּיט מֻגְבָּל בָּהֶם, וְנַעֲשָׂה נֵס לְמֶלֶךְ סְדוֹם שֶׁיָּצָא מִשָּׁם, לְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ בָאֻמּוֹת מִקְצָתָן שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ מַאֲמִינִין שֶׁנִּצַּל אַבְרָהָם מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים מִכִּבְשַׁן הָאֵשׁ, וְכֵיוָן שֶׁיָּצָא זֶה מִן הַחֵמָר, הֶאֱמִינוּ בְאַבְרָם לְמַפְרֵעַ:
Rashinormativefollows הֶ֥רָה נָּֽסוּ׃
Rashi: הֶרָה is like לְהָר, 'to a mountain', with the ה replacing the לָמֶד at the front; it names no particular mountain, since each fled to whichever he found first, unlike הָהָרָה, which means a known mountain. The English adopts the indefinite reading.

Ibn Ezranormativerecords בֶּֽאֱרֹ֤ת
Ibn Ezra: בְּאֵר everywhere in Scripture is a well with flowing water, and its form here (בֶּאֱרֹת) is changed because of the construct. The English accepts the construct, but where he and Rashi differ on the sense it takes Rashi's pits dug for earth rather than wells; his 'wells' is kept here.

Apparatus
  • WLC reads הַשִׂדִּים with a different vowel pointing; MAM reads הַשִּׂדִּים (14:10.2).
  • Onkelos: 'the plain of the field was pits, pits of clay; the king of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell there, and those who remained fled to the mountain.'
  • הַשִּׂדִּ֗ים — WLC reads הַשִׂדִּ֗ים (vowels)
14:11

They took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and went away.

and-took all-of goods-of Sodom and-Gomorrah and all-of their-food and-went

Grammar
  • The verse is a simple chain of wayyiqtol verbs with the plural subject of the four kings.
  • רְכֻשׁ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה is a construct chain with a double genitive: 'the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah'.
  • The repetition of אֶת־כׇּל, 'all', stresses the completeness of the plunder: goods and food.
  • The telisha gedola on the first word is a prepositive accent, written twice on וַיִּקְחוּ.

וַיִּקְחוּ is rendered 'took' with the sense of plundering. Radak says 'their food' includes what was in the houses and the people in them; the English keeps 'food'. The entry for הלך lists no plain-'go' sense in the pack.

Commentary (3)
Radakfollows וַ֠יִּקְח֠וּ אֶת כׇּל רְכֻ֨שׁ סְדֹ֧ם וַעֲמֹרָ֛ה
Radak: the Valley of Siddim lay within the border of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the battle was there; Admah, Zeboiim and Bela were not on that side. So the kings took the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah from those cities and their villages, and רְכֻשׁ includes movable property and livestock. The English 'goods' carries this.
Hebrew
כִּי עֵמֶק הַשִּׂדִּים הוּא בִּגְבוּלָם וְשָׁם הָיְתָה הַמִּלְחָמָה, אֲבָל אַדְמָה וּצְבוֹיִם וּבֶלַע לֹא הָיוּ מֵאוֹתוֹ הַצַּד; וְלָקְחוּ אֶת כָּל רְכֻשׁ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה מֵהֶעָרִים הָאֵלֶּה וּבְנוֹתֵיהֶם, וּרְכֻשׁ כּוֹלֵל הַמִּטַּלְטְלִים וְהַמִּקְנֶה.
Radakrecords וְאֶת כׇּל אׇכְלָ֖ם
