וּשְׁבוֹ יָת כָּל קִנְיָנָא דִסְדוֹם וַעֲמוֹרָה וְיָת כָּל מֵיכָלְהוֹן וַאֲזָלוּ:
14:12

They took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, and his goods, and went away; he was living in Sodom.

and-took [obj] Lot and [obj] goods-his son-of brother-of Abram and-went and-he dwelling in-Sodom

Grammar
  • וְהוּא יֹשֵׁב is a circumstantial clause: a pronoun plus a participle that states a situation, not a sequence.
  • בֶּן־אֲחִי אַבְרָם is a double construct chain in apposition to לוֹט, although in the Hebrew it stands after 'and his goods'; the English moves it next to Lot.
  • The qadma on וַיִּקְחוּ and the darga on לוֹט are conjunctive and lead to the tevir on רְכֻשׁוֹ; the merkha on אֲחִי leads to the tipḥa on אַבְרָם, and the etnaḥta on וַיֵּלֵכוּ ends the first half.
  • In the second half the merkha on וְהוּא joins the pronoun to its participle, and tipḥa and silluq close the verse: the narrator adds where Lot was living.

Ibn Ezra adds that Lot was living in Sodom 'on that day'; the English does not add a 'then'. Rashi's remark that his dwelling in Sodom was the cause is moral and is not a reading of the words.

Commentary (5)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וְה֥וּא יֹשֵׁ֖ב בִּסְדֹֽם׃
Rashi: 'Who caused him this? His living in Sodom.' This is a moral comment on the clause, not a reading of its words.
Hebrew

Ibn Ezranormativefollows וְה֥וּא יֹשֵׁ֖ב
Ibn Ezra: 'he was on that day living in Sodom', which takes the participle as a state of affairs at the time of the capture. The English renders it as a circumstantial clause.

Sforno וַיִּקְח֨וּ אֶת ל֧וֹט בֶּן אֲחִ֥י אַבְרָ֖ם
Hebrew
הִתְאַמְּצוּ לִשְׁבּוֹת אֶת לוֹט מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה בֶּן אֲחִי אַבְרָם, שֶׁיָּדְעוּ עָשְׁרוֹ וְהָיוּ מְצַפִּים שֶׁיִּפְדֵּהוּ אַבְרָם בְּהוֹן רַב:
14:13

The fugitive came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the terebinths of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner; they were allies of Abram.

and-came the-fugitive and-told to-Abram the-Hebrew and-he dwelling in-terebinths-of Mamre the-Amorite brother-of Eshcol and-brother-of Aner and-they masters-of covenant-of Abram

Grammar
  • וְהוּא שֹׁכֵן is a circumstantial clause (pronoun plus participle) about Abram.
  • 'Brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner' stands in apposition to מַמְרֵא; the accents (revia, then mahpakh and pashta) attach it to Mamre, not to Abram.
  • בַּעֲלֵי בְרִית is an idiom: 'masters of a covenant', that is, allies. The same construction pairs a person with a thing owned.
  • הַפָּלִיט has the article: 'the fugitive', one particular person known to the story; הָעִבְרִי is its only appearance as a title for Abram.
  • Etnahta on הָעִבְרִי separates the report from the circumstantial clause that follows.

Rashi's plain-sense identification of the fugitive as Og is recorded, not adopted in the English line. הָעִבְרִי is rendered 'the Hebrew'; Rashi's 'from across the river' is a gloss on the name, not an alternative translation. 'Eshcol' has a sense in its entry for a valley; here it is a personal name.

Commentary (12)
Rashinormativerecords וַיָּבֹא֙ הַפָּלִ֔יט
Rashi: on the plain sense this is Og, who escaped the war (Deuteronomy 3), since Amraphel and his allies did not kill him when they struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim. The English says only 'the fugitive'.
Hebrew
לְפִי פְשׁוּטוֹ זֶה עוֹג, שֶׁפָּלַט מִן הַמִּלְחָמָה, וְהוּא שֶׁכָּתוּב כִּי רַק עוֹג נִשְׁאַר מִיֶּתֶר הָרְפָאִים (דבר' ג') וְזֶהוּ נִשְׁאַר, שֶׁלֹּא הֲרָגוּהוּ אַמְרָפֶל וַחֲבֵרָיו כְּשֶׁהִכּוּ הָרְפָאִים בְּעַשְׁתְּרוֹת קַרְנַיִם, תַּנְחוּמָא וּמִדְרַשׁ בְּ"רַ זֶה עוֹג, שֶׁפָּלַט מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל; וְזֶהוּ מִיֶּתֶר הָרְפָאִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר הַנְּפִלִים הָיוּ בָאָרֶץ וְגוֹ' (לְעֵיל ו') וּמִתְכַּוֵּן שֶׁיֵּהָרֵג אַבְרָם וְיִשָּׂא אֶת שָׂרָה:
Rashinormativefollows הָעִבְרִ֑י
Rashi, after Genesis Rabbah: הָעִבְרִי means one who came from across the river. The English keeps 'the Hebrew', which can carry that sense.
Hebrew

14:14

When Abram heard that his brother had been taken captive, he armed his trained men, those born in his household, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued as far as Dan.

and-heard Abram that was-taken-captive his-brother and-armed [obj] his-trained-men born-of his-house eight ten and-three hundreds and-pursued up-to Dan

Grammar
  • וַיִּשְׁמַע ... כִּי introduces the content of what Abram heard: 'that his brother was taken captive'. The Niphal נִשְׁבָּה is passive.
  • וַיָּרֶק is Hiphil of רִיק, 'empty out'. The verb is used of drawing a sword (Leviticus 26:33) or a spear (Psalm 35:3), and so here 'armed'; its object is 'his trained men'.
  • חֲנִיכָיו is the plural of חָנִיךְ with the suffix 'his', from the root חנך, 'train, initiate' (compare 'train up a child', Proverbs 22:6). Rashi cites a singular written form חנכו, which the MAM text does not have.
  • The number is written 'eight ten and three hundreds': שְׁמֹנָה עָשָׂר 'eighteen' first, then שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת 'three hundred', with the short form of 'three' because מֵאָה is feminine. English reverses the order.
  • Etnahta on אָחִיו divides the verse into the news and Abram's response.

For וַיָּרֶק I choose 'armed' on the combined view of Rashi (armed, as Onkelos וְזָרִיז) and Ibn Ezra's first reading ('gave them weapons'); his second reading, 'drew out the swords from the sheath', is kept in the commentary entry. Rashi's singular spelling חנכו is recorded in the apparatus. Rashi's midrash that the three hundred and eighteen are Eliezer alone is not adopted, and Rashi's remark on Dan (the later calf-idol) is not a reading of the words.

Commentary (14)
Rashinormativefollows וַיָּ֨רֶק
Rashi: וַיָּרֶק means 'armed', as Onkelos renders it (וְזָרִיז); so 'I will unsheathe (וַהֲרִיקֹתִי) the sword after you' (Leviticus 26:33) means 'I will arm myself with my sword against you', and so 'I will draw my sword' (Exodus 15:9) and 'draw out the spear and close' (Psalm 35:3). The English takes 'armed'.

The word means a person's or a vessel's first entry into the craft it is to serve, as in 'train up a child' (Proverbs 22:6), 'the dedication of the altar' (Numbers 7) and 'the dedication of the house' (Psalm 30). The English renders the plural of the MAM text, 'trained men', in this sense.

Apparatus
  • Rashi reports the spelling חנכו, singular, 'his trained one', which he reads as Eliezer; the MAM text reads חֲנִיכָיו and the pack records no Ketiv/Qere at this word (14:14.8).
14:15

He and his servants divided themselves against them by night and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is north of Damascus.

and-divided-himself against-them night he and-his-servants and-struck-them and-pursued-them up-to Hobah which from-left to-Damascus

Grammar
  • The singular verb וַיֵּחָלֵק is followed by הוּא וַעֲבָדָיו: the subject 'he and his servants' comes after the verb and the adverb 'by night', which is why Rashi says the verse is transposed.
  • וַיִּרְדְּפֵם and וַיַּכֵּם have the suffix מ, 'them': the verbs are wayyiqtols and the verb 'pursue' is repeated from verse 14.
  • מִשְּׂמֹאל לְדַמָּשֶׂק is 'from the left of Damascus' and names the north, taken from the person facing east.
  • The qadma and darga lead into the tevir on לַיְלָה, which sets 'by night' apart from the pronoun that follows.

I follow Rashi's plain-sense reordering: 'he and his servants divided themselves against them by night', as pursuers split up after fugitives who scatter. His aggadic reading, that the night itself was divided in two, is not adopted. For מִשְּׂמֹאל I write 'north of', the sense 3 in the entry. Rashi's remark that no place is called Hobah and that Dan is meant is a midrash and is not adopted; the English keeps the name Hobah.

Commentary (12)
Rashinormativefollows וַיֵּחָלֵ֨ק עֲלֵיהֶ֧ם
Rashi: on the plain sense the verse is transposed: 'he and his servants divided themselves against them at night', as pursuers split into parties after fugitives who flee in different directions. The English adopts this order.
Hebrew

Rashinormativefollows לַ֛יְלָה
Rashi: 'night' means that even after dark he did not hold back from pursuing them; the English 'by night' follows this plain sense. The aggadic midrash, that the night was divided, with a miracle done for him in its first half while the second half was kept for the midnight of Egypt, is not adopted.

14:16

He brought back all the goods, and also brought back Lot his brother and his goods, and also the women and the people.

and-brought-back [obj] all-of the-goods and-also [obj] Lot his-brother and-his-goods brought-back and-also [obj] the-women and [obj] the-people

Grammar
  • The first verb, וַיָּשֶׁב, is the Hiphil wayyiqtol of שׁוּב, 'bring back': after the wayyiqtol prefix the long form יָשִׁיב is shortened and its vowel becomes segol. Do not confuse it with וַיֵּשֶׁב 'and he sat, dwelt', from יָשַׁב.
  • In the second clause the verb is placed last (הֵשִׁיב, perfect), after its double object; this emphasis on Lot sets him apart from the general goods.
  • וְגַם ... וְגַם ... repeats 'and also' in the verse, as the narrator widens the list from goods to Lot and then to the captives.
  • The etnaḥta on הָרְכֻשׁ divides the verse in two: the goods, then the persons.

הָעָם is rendered 'the people' with the entry sense 4, the persons taken from Sodom. 'Brother' for Lot is as in 14:14.

14:17

The king of Sodom went out to meet him, after his return from striking down Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, to the Valley of Shaveh, that is, the King's Valley.

and-went-out king-of Sodom to-meet-him after return-his from-striking [obj] Chedorlaomer and-[obj] the-kings who with-him to valley-of Shaveh it valley-of the-king

Grammar
  • וַיֵּצֵא is a wayyiqtol: the narrative resumes after the battle report, with the king of Sodom as the new subject.
  • אַחֲרֵי שׁוּבוֹ and מֵהַכּוֹת are infinitives with suffix or preposition and form one time clause: 'after his returning from the striking of'.
  • The zinor on סְדֹם and the segol on לִקְרָאתוֹ set 'the king of Sodom ... to meet him' apart from the time clause; the etnaḥta on אִתּוֹ ends the first half.
  • הוּא עֵמֶק הַמֶּלֶךְ glosses the place name: 'that is, the King's Valley'.

The English follows Rashi in taking עֵמֶק שָׁוֵה as the name of the place; Rashi and the Targum also give its sense as a cleared, level plain. The identity of 'the king' in הַמֶּלֶךְ is not stated; the name is kept as 'the King's Valley'.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos renders עֵמֶק שָׁוֵה 'a cleared plain' and עֵמֶק הַמֶּלֶךְ 'the place Beth Risa of the king'.
  • כְּדׇרְלָעֹ֔מֶר — WLC reads כְּדָרלָעֹ֔מֶר (vowels)
14:18

Now Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine. He was a priest of God Most High.

and-Malki-Tsedeq king-of Shalem brought-out bread and-wine and-he priest to-God Most-High

Grammar
  • The proper name has two parts joined by maqqef, מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק. The pashta is written on the last letter of its word; because צֶדֶק is stressed on its first syllable, the accent is written a second time on the stressed syllable. The name can be read 'my king is Ṣedeq' or 'king of righteousness'.
  • הוֹצִיא is a hifil perfect, 'brought out'; the verb comes after its subject, so the clause is a new scene, not the next step in a chain of wayyiqtols.
  • וְהוּא כֹהֵן is a circumstantial clause giving his office: the pronoun opens the clause and the noun without article is the predicate.
  • אֵל עֶלְיוֹן: 'God Most High', the first appearance of the title.

I give שָׁלֵם as Salem and record Jerusalem (Ibn Ezra, Ramban, Radak, citing Psalm 76:3). Rashi's 'Shem son of Noah' (so Radak) is recorded, not adopted, since it identifies the man and does not change the English. Rashi holds that the bread and wine were what one gives those weary from war (so also Radak and Sforno); Ibn Ezra does not comment on them. The Targum's 'ministered' (מְשַׁמֵּשׁ) for כֹהֵן, which Ibn Ezra adopts, is rendered 'was a priest'.

Commentary (16)
Rashinormativerecords וּמַלְכִּי צֶ֙דֶק֙
Rashi: according to the aggada, Melchizedek is the name of Shem son of Noah (Nedarim 32). The English keeps the name only.
Hebrew
מִ"אַ הוּא שֵׁם בֶן נֹחַ (נדרים ל"ב):

Rashi: so one treats those weary from battle, and he showed Abram he bore no grudge for killing his sons; the aggada has it hint at the offerings and libations. The English takes the plain sense of a meal for the weary.
Hebrew
כָּךְ עוֹשִׂים לִיגִיעֵי מִלְחָמָה, וְהֶרְאָה לוֹ שֶׁאֵין בְּלִבּוֹ עָלָיו עַל שֶׁהָרַג אֶת בָּנָיו. ומִ"אַ רָמַז לוֹ עַל הַמְּנָחוֹת וְעַל הַנְּסָכִים שֶׁיַּקְרִיבוּ שָׁם בָּנָיו:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows וּמַלְכִּי צֶ֙דֶק֙
Ibn Ezra: he was so called because he was king over a place of righteousness, though some say it is a personal name. The English keeps the name.

נקרא כן בעבור שהוא מלך על מקום צדק וי"א כי הוא שם

לְהוֹדִיעַ כִּי אַבְרָהָם לֹא הָיָה נוֹתֵן מַעֲשֵׂר לְכֹהֵן לֵאלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים, אֲבָל מִפְּנֵי שֶׁיָּדַע בּוֹ שֶׁהוּא כֹּהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן נָתַן לוֹ הַמַּעֲשֵׂר לִכְבוֹד הַשֵּׁם. וְהָרֶמֶז לְאַבְרָהָם מִזֶּה כִּי שָׁם יִהְיֶה בֵּית אֱלֹהִים, וְשָׁם יוֹצִיא זַרְעוֹ הַמַּעֲשֵׂר וְהַתְּרוּמָה, וְשָׁם יְבָרְכוּ אֶת ה'. וְעַל דַּעַת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (נדרים לב) שֶׁאוֹמְרִים כִּי מַלְכִּי צֶדֶק הוּא שֵׁם בֶן נֹחַ, הָלַךְ מֵאַרְצוֹ לִירוּשָׁלִַם לַעֲבֹד שָׁם אֶת ה', וְהָיָה לָהֶם לְכֹהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן, כִּי הוּא אֲחִי אֲבִיהֶם הַנִּכְבָּד, כִּי יְרוּשָׁלַיִם מִגְּבוּל הַכְּנַעֲנִי הִיא מֵעוֹלָם. וְרַשִׁ"י כָּתַב לְמַעְלָה (יב ו) "וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי אָז בָּאָרֶץ", הָיָה הוֹלֵךְ וְכוֹבֵשׁ אֶת אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִזַּרְעוֹ שֶׁל שֵׁם זְקֵנוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁבְּחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל שֵׁם נָפְלָה כְּשֶׁחִלֵּק נֹחַ לְבָנָיו אֶת הָאָרֶץ (ספרא קכו), שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וּמַלְכִּי צֶדֶק מֶלֶךְ שָׁלֵם". וְאֵין זֶה נָכוֹן, כִּי "גְּבוּל הַכְּנַעֲנִי מִצִּידוֹן" (בראשית י':י"ט) יִכְלֹל כָּל אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּגְבוּל בְּנֵי שֵׁם בַּמִּזְרָח מִמַּשָּׂא רָחוֹק מֵאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל. אֲבָל אִם חִלֵּק נֹחַ לְבָנָיו הָאֲרָצוֹת וְנָתַן לְשֵׁם אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, הָיָה זֶה כִּ"מְחַלֵּק נְכָסָיו עַל פִּיו", וְיָשְׁבוּ בָּהּ בְּנֵי כְּנַעַן עַד אֲשֶׁר יַנְחִיל אוֹתָהּ הַשֵּׁם לְזֶרַע אוֹהֲבוֹ, כַּאֲשֶׁר הִזְכַּרְתִּי כְּבָר (רמב"ן על בראשית י':ט"ו):

14:19

He blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth."

and-blessed-him and-said blessed Abram to-God Most-High maker-of heavens and-earth

Grammar
  • וַיְבָרְכֵהוּ is a piel wayyiqtol with the object suffix, followed by a second wayyiqtol that introduces the blessing itself.
  • בָּרוּךְ is a passive participle; there is no verb 'be', so the wish is a verbless clause 'blessed Abram to God Most High'.
  • קֹנֵה is a construct participle of קנה; it can mean 'buyer', 'owner', or 'maker', the last attested for the root in Deuteronomy 32:6 and Psalm 139:13.
  • The accents divide the blessing: the zaqef on עֶלְיוֹן separates the blessing from the title 'maker of heaven and earth'.

קֹנֵה is read 'maker' with Rashi (קֹנֶה like עֹשֶׂה, and by making them he acquired them as his own) and Radak (not one who buys from another, but one who makes or brings into being). Ramban holds the main sense is ownership, 'whose possession they are', and says Onkelos meant this by דִּקִנְיָנֵיהּ; that reading is recorded in the apparatus. בָּרוּךְ is a Qal passive participle.

כָּתַב רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ד:י"ט), קוֹנֶה כְּמוֹ עֹשֶׂה, עַל יְדֵי עֲשִׂיָּתוֹ קְנָאָן לִהְיוֹת לוֹ. וְאֵלֶּה שְׁנֵי פָּנִים הֵם, וְאוּלַי כֵּן הַדָּבָר שֶׁיָּבֹא לְשׁוֹן קִנְיָן בְּעִנְיָן הָעֲשִׂיָּה, וְכֵן "כִּי אַתָּה קָנִיתָ כִלְיֹתָי" (תהלים קלט יג), שֶׁיִּכְפֹּל "תְּסוּכֵנִי בְּבֶטֶן אִמִּי", וְכֵן "הֲלֹא הוּא אָבִיךָ קָּנֶךָ הוּא עָשְׂךָ וַיְכֹנְנֶךָ" (דברים לב ו), כִּי הַלָּשׁוֹן יֹאמַר "קִנְיָן" בַּעֲשִׂיָּה, וְהַהֵפֶךְ "אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן" (בראשית י"ב:ה'), קָנוּ, "וּמֵאֲשֶׁר לְאָבִינוּ עָשָׂה" (בראשית ל"א:א'). וְהַנָּכוֹן מָה שֶׁאָמַר עוֹד קְנָאָן לִהְיוֹת לוֹ, כִּי כָל אֲשֶׁר לָאָדָם יִקָּרֵא קִנְיָנוֹ, וְיִקְרְאוּ הַצֹּאן "מִקְנֶה" בַּעֲבוּר הֱיוֹתוֹ עִקַּר רְכוּשׁ הָאָדָם. וּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים (ב"מ י), הַמַּגְבִּיהַּ מְצִיאָה לַחֲבֵרוֹ קָנָה חֲבֵרוֹ, הַבָּטָה בְּהֶפְקֵר קַנְיָא (שם קיח), חֲצֵרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם קוֹנָה לוֹ שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ (שם יא), וְכֵן בְּכָל מָקוֹם תָּבוֹא לָהֶם בִּמְקוֹם זְכִיָּה, כְּלוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא שֶׁלּוֹ. וְלָזֶה נִתְכַּוֵּן אוּנְקְלוֹס (תרגום אונקלוס על בראשית י"ד:י"ט) שֶׁתִּרְגֵּם "דְּקִנְיָנֵהּ" וְלֹא אָמַר "קָנָה":

Apparatus
  • Onkelos has 'to God Most High whose possession is heaven and earth' (דִּקִנְיָנֵיהּ); Radak says 'make or provide'; Sforno 'heaven and earth are a possession for him'.
14:20

And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand. And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.

and-blessed God Most-High who delivered your-foes in-your-hand and-gave to-him tenth from-all

Grammar
  • מִגֵּן is a piel perfect, 'delivered up', as Rashi (הִסְגִּיר, Hosea 11:8) and Ibn Ezra (like נָתַן, Proverbs 4:9) say, not 'shielded'. The lexicon files it under the root גנן, which gives מָגֵן 'shield'; Ibn Ezra holds that the מ is a root letter.
  • צָרֶיךָ is a plural construct (צָרֵי) with the suffix ךָ: 'your adversaries'.
  • The pashta on בָּרוּךְ and the zaqef on עֶלְיוֹן divide the blessing from its relative clause.
  • וַיִּתֶּן־לוֹ has no stated subject; the reader must decide who gives to whom, and Rashi says Abram gave.

Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that מִגֵּן means 'handed over', like נָתַן, and the English follows them rather than 'shielded'. The subject of וַיִּתֶּן is Abram (Rashi, Ibn Ezra); the other reading, that Melchizedek gave Abram a tithe, is a real alternative that the Hebrew does not exclude, and I do not adopt it.

Rashinormativefollows וַיִּתֶּן ל֥וֹ

14:21

The king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the people, and take the goods for yourself."

and-said king-of Sodom to Abram give to-me the-person and-the-goods take for-you

Grammar
  • נֶפֶשׁ with the article is a collective singular, 'the persons'; the word does not mean 'soul' here but the living captives.
  • The two imperatives תֶּן and קַח are set against each other: the king asks for the people and offers the goods.
  • הָרְכֻשׁ is placed before its verb for contrast with הַנֶּפֶשׁ.
  • לָךְ is the pausal form of לְךָ 'to you' (masculine singular): at the silluq the suffix is written ךְ with qamets under the ל. The same form returns at the etnaḥta in 14:23.

The pack parses the suffix of לָךְ as feminine; the form is the pausal ךְ spelling, and the sense is addressed to Abram. I keep the pack's data and note it here. 'The people' follows Rashi's 'the bodies alone'.

Commentary (3)
Rashinormativefollows תֶּן לִ֣י הַנֶּ֔פֶשׁ

14:22

Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I raise my hand in oath to the LORD, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth:

and-said Abram to king-of Sodom I-raise my-hand to YHWH God Most-High maker-of heavens and-earth

Grammar
  • הֲרִמֹתִי is a hifil perfect with a performative sense: the act of raising the hand is the oath, as Rashi's parallel with 'I have sworn' (22:16) shows.
  • The name יְהוָה is added to Melchizedek's title: Abram says 'the LORD, God Most High', identifying the two.
  • The oath continues through verse 24 and does not end at the silluq.
  • The qadma on הֲרִמֹתִי and the mahpakh on יָדִי hold the oath formula together.

The English renders the gesture and gives its sense, an oath, with Rashi and Ibn Ezra, who agree. Abram adds the divine name יְהוָה to the title used by Melchizedek (Ibn Ezra: 'I swore by the name by which this priest blessed me').

Commentary (8)

Rashi: the phrase is the language of an oath: 'I raise my hand to God Most High', like 'I have sworn by myself' (22:16) and 'I give you the field' (23:13). The English says 'in oath'.

  • 14:22.6: MAM writes הֲרִמֹתִי (defective); WLC writes הֲרִימֹתִי (plene), the spelling of Ibn Ezra's and Ramban's lemmas. The sense is the same.

14:23

I will not take so much as a thread or a sandal strap, nor anything that is yours, so that you cannot say, 'I made Abram rich.'

if from-thread and-up-to strap-of sandal and-if I-take from-all who to-you and-not you-say I I-enriched [obj] Abram

Grammar
  • The oath formula אִם ... אִם takes a negative sense: 'if I take ... may I be ...', that is 'I will not take'; the penalty is left unsaid.
  • מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ־נַעַל is an idiom for 'the smallest thing', from a thread to a shoe strap.
  • הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי is the hifil of עָשַׁר, the causative of the Qal 'be rich': 'I made rich'. The pronoun אֲנִי, not needed with a finite verb, stresses the claim: 'I, I made'.
  • The etnaḥta on לָךְ ends the oath, and וְלֹא תֹאמַר starts the clause giving the purpose.

אִם is the elliptical oath, 'not' (so Rashi's 'I will keep back for myself nothing from the captives'). Rashi reads the second clause as 'if you offer me a reward from your treasury, I will not take it' and the third as God's promise to enrich Abram (12:2), which is the reason; both bear on the sense but not on the wording of the English.

14:24 · ס

Not for me, only what my servants have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol and Mamre. They may take their share."

apart-from-me only what ate the-lads and-share-of the-men who went with-me Aner Eshcol and-Mamre they let-them-take share-their

Grammar
  • בִּלְעָדַי is a preposition with suffix meaning 'apart from me'; it opens the verse without a verb, as a stand-alone refusal.
  • רַק limits what follows: only the food eaten and the allies' portion are excepted from the oath.
  • The names עָנֵר אֶשְׁכֹּל וּמַמְרֵא stand in apposition to הָאֲנָשִׁים; the zaqef on וּמַמְרֵא closes the list, and the tipḥa on הֵם and the silluq end the closing clause 'they shall take their share'.
  • יִקְחוּ is jussive in sense: 'let them take'; הֵם adds emphasis, 'let them, for their part'.

Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that הַנְּעָרִים are Abram's servants, so the English says 'my servants' (literally 'the lads'). Rashi adds that though the servants fought, Aner and his companions stayed with the baggage, yet they take a share (David learned from this).

15:1

After these events the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, saying: Do not be afraid, Abram. I am a shield for you; your reward is very great.

after the-things the-these came word-of LORD to Abram in-the-vision to-say not you-fear Abram I shield to-you your-reward making-great exceedingly

Grammar
  • הָיָה דְבַר־יְהֹוָה אֶל־: the standard formula for the arrival of a prophetic word. Here it is joined to בַּמַּחֲזֶה, a rare word for the medium of the revelation.
  • The two sentences אָנֹכִי מָגֵן לָךְ and שְׂכָרְךָ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד are verbless. The English present tense is a choice: Ibn Ezra takes the first as a past 'I was a shield' (see commentary), but the Hebrew has no tense.
  • הַרְבֵּה is the hifil infinitive absolute of רבה, 'making much', used with מְאֹד as the predicate of the clause: 'very much, very great'.
  • The etnaḥta on לֵאמֹר ends the narrative frame. In the speech the zaqef qaton on לָךְ closes the prohibition and its first ground; within that part the revia on אַבְרָם divides 'Do not be afraid, Abram' from 'I am a shield for you'. The pashta on אָנֹכִי is a lesser division inside 'I am a shield for you'.

The speech is placed in a vision (בַּמַּחֲזֶה), which Ibn Ezra glosses as 'the visions of prophecy' and Radak says shows Abram an action, not only words. The present 'I am a shield' takes the verbless clause as Rashi does, of protection from punishment to come; Ibn Ezra's past reading, 'I was a shield to you (against the kings)', is recorded in the commentary.

Commentary (14)
Rashinormativefollows אַחַ֣ר הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה
Rashi: אחר means close in time (אחרי a remote interval). The reference is to the victory over the kings: Abram feared he had used up his reward or would be punished for the lives he took, so God says 'I am a shield' against punishment and 'your reward is great'.

Apparatus
  • The pack parses לָךְ as having a feminine suffix; the pausal ָךְ is the pausal form of the masculine suffix, since Abram is addressed. The data is kept.
  • Onkelos has 'my Memra will be a strong shield for you' (מֵימְרִי תְּקוֹף לָךְ), a paraphrase of the shield image; it does not change the Hebrew sense.
15:2

Abram said, My Lord, the LORD, what will you give me, when I go on childless, and the steward of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?

and-said Abram my-lords LORD what you-will-give to-me and-I going childless and-son-of charge-of my-house he Damascus Eliezer

Grammar
  • וְאָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי: a circumstantial clause with a participle ('while I am going about without ...'). The sense of הוֹלֵךְ ('go on living' or 'go to my death') is open, see the note.
  • בֶּן־מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי הוּא דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר: a difficult verse. מֶשֶׁק is a hapax, understood by Rashi and the Targum as 'one who manages (my house)', by Ibn Ezra as from שׁקק 'run about'. The English follows the sense 'steward' which both give.
  • אֲדֹנָי יֱהֹוִה: the Masoretic pointing יֱהֹוִה tells the reader to say Elohim, not Adonai, after אֲדֹנָי. Radak says the title precedes the name because the name is the essence.
  • The etnaḥta on עֲרִירִי divides the verse between Abram's complaint and its explanation.

דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר is rendered 'Eliezer of Damascus' with the Targum and Radak (who supplies the missing relational yod). Another reading in Radak is that the man's own name was Damascus. For הוֹלֵךְ the English keeps the neutral 'go on'.

Commentary (18)
Rashinormativefollows הוֹלֵ֣ךְ עֲרִירִ֑י
Rashi gives Menahem ben Saruq's view that עֲרִירִי means 'without an heir', lacking sons (he joins it to עֵר וְעֹנֶה, Malachi 2:12, with a privative sense like תְשָׁרֵשׁ 'uproot', Job 31:12); his own view joins עֵר to 'awake' (Song 5:2) and takes עֲרִירִי as 'desolation', as עָרוּ עָרוּ (Psalm 137:7). The English 'childless' gives Menahem's sense, which the plain context requires on either view.
Hebrew

The Talmud reads דמשק as an acrostic: he 'draws and gives drink' (דולה ומשקה) of his master's teaching to others. The English takes the plain sense, 'of Damascus'.

Rambanrecords מַה תִּתֶּן לִ֔י וְאָנֹכִ֖י הוֹלֵ֣ךְ עֲרִירִ֑י
Ramban cites an interpretation (marked יב"ע) that הולך ערירי means 'I am dying childless', as in הולך האדם אל בית עולמו (Ecclesiastes 12:5). He prefers: Abram complains, what will my reward be when I have no sons, and I go wandering alone in a foreign land like a juniper in the desert, with none coming and going in my house but Eliezer, a stranger I took from Damascus. The English 'go on' does not narrow to either.

15:3

Abram said, Look, you have given me no offspring, and so a member of my household is my heir.

and-said Abram lo to-me not you-gave seed and-behold son-of my-house inheriting me

Grammar
  • הֵן לִי לֹא נָתַתָּה זָרַע: 'to me you have not given seed'. The word order puts 'to me' first, against the promises Abram has heard.
  • וְהִנֵּה בֶן־בֵּיתִי יוֹרֵשׁ אֹתִי: the participle יוֹרֵשׁ describes a state near at hand. Verbs of inheriting normally take the thing inherited as object, not the person, so 'inheriting me' means 'inheriting from me'.
  • זֶרַע is singular but collective, 'offspring', and the English uses a singular noun for it.

Rashi takes the opening as asking 'what good is all that you give me?', continuing the complaint of verse 2. The English keeps the sentence as a complaint with 'Look'.

and-behold word-of LORD to-him to-say not he-will-inherit-you this but-if who he-will-come-out from-your-innards he he-will-inherit-you

Grammar
  • וְהִנֵּה דְבַר־יְהֹוָה אֵלָיו: a verbless clause, 'and behold, the word of the LORD to him'; וְהִנֵּה marks the sudden arrival of the word (Ramban: while Abram was still speaking). The qadma on וְהִנֵּה is conjunctive; the first divisions fall at the pashta on אֵלָיו and the zaqef qaton on לֵאמֹר.
  • לֹא יִירָשְׁךָ זֶה: the verb has the 2nd person masculine suffix and the same verb occurs again at the end, so the verse is built around a contrast between two heirs. The etnaḥta on זֶה divides the rejected heir from the true one.
  • כִּי־אִם after a negative means 'but rather', not 'if'.
  • יִירָשׁ with an object of person means 'be the heir of' that person, here 'inherit from you'.

מֵעֶיךָ is rendered 'your own body', keeping the euphemism that Ibn Ezra identifies (Radak adds that it is the 'vessel of seed', cf. צאצאי מעיך Isaiah 48:19).

Commentary (6)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows מִמֵּעֶ֔יךָ
Ibn Ezra: מִמֵּעֶיךָ is a 'kinuy', a euphemism for the limb, because it is near; hence 'from your own body'.
Hebrew
כנוי לאבר בעבור היותו קרוב:
Rambanrecords וְהִנֵּ֨ה דְבַר יְהֹוָ֤ה אֵלָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר לֹ֥א יִֽירָשְׁךָ֖ זֶ֑ה
Ramban: because the son who would inherit him would come only after his old age, God promised him here only about the inheritance, that he should not worry: his own seed will inherit him. וְהִנֵּה means that while Abram was still saying 'my household member is my heir', the word of the LORD came to him suddenly.
Hebrew
בַּעֲבוּר הֱיוֹת לוֹ הַבֵּן הַיּוֹרֵשׁ אַחֲרֵי זִקְנָתוֹ לֹא הִבְטִיחוֹ רַק עַל הַיְּרֻשָּׁה, שֶׁלֹּא יִדְאַג כִּי זַרְעוֹ יִירָשֶׁנּוּ. וְטַעַם "וְהִנֵּה דְבַר ה' אֵלָיו" כִּי עוֹד בְּפִיו "וְהִנֵּה בֶן בֵּיתִי יוֹרֵשׁ אֹתִי" וּבָא אֵלָיו פִּתְאוֹם דְּבַר הַשֵּׁם לֵאמֹר "לֹא יִירָשְׁךָ זֶה":
Radak וְהִנֵּ֨ה דְבַר יְהֹוָ֤ה
Hebrew
הָיָה לוֹ דְּבַר ה׳ לַעֲנוֹתוֹ עַל אֲשֶׁר שָׁאַל, לֵאמֹר:
Radakfollows לֹ֥א יִֽירָשְׁךָ֖ זֶ֑ה
Radak: the verse limits the earlier promise, 'to you and to your seed', to a true descendant who comes from your innards.
Hebrew
, בֶּן בֵּיתְךָ, כִּי אִם אֲשֶׁר יֵצֵא מִמֵּעֶיךָ, וְלֹא תִטְעֶה בְּמַה שֶׁאָמַרְתִּי ״לְךָ וּלְזַרְעֲךָ״, כִּי לֹא אָמַרְתִּי אֶלָּא עַל זַרְעֲךָ מַמָּשׁ שֶׁיֵּצְאוּ מִמֵּעֶיךָ. וְכָל אֲשֶׁר בְּתוֹךְ הַגּוּף נִקְרָא מֵעַיִם, וְכָאן כִּוֵּן עַל כְּלִי הַזֶּרַע, וְכֵן ״וְצֶאֱצָאֵי מֵעֶיךָ״ (ישעיה מח:יט).

וְהָא פִּתְגָּמָא דַּיְיָ עִמֵּיהּ לְמֵימַר לָא יִרְתִנָּךְ דֵּין אֱלָהֵין בַּר דְּתוֹלִיד הוּא יִרְתִנָּךְ:
Sforno לֹ֥א יִֽירָשְׁךָ֖ זֶ֑ה כִּי אִם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יֵצֵ֣א מִמֵּעֶ֔יךָ

כִּי הַבֵּן יִצְלַח בְּהַנְהָגַת הַמָּמוֹן בְּחַיֶּיךָ, כְּאָמְרוֹ (בראשית כה:ה-ו): "וַיִּתֵּן אַבְרָהָם אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ לְיִצְחָק" וַיְשַׁלְּחֵם מֵעַל יִצְחָק בְּנוֹ בְּעוֹדֶנּוּ חַי.

15:5

He brought him outside and said, Look toward the sky, please, and count the stars, if you are able to count them. Then he said to him, So will your offspring be.

and-brought-out him the-outside and-said look please the-heavenward and-count the-stars if you-are-able to-count them and-said to-him thus he-will-be your-seed

Grammar
  • וַיּוֹצֵא אֹתוֹ הַחוּצָה: a hifil wayyiqtol. The subject is God, the object Abram. הַחוּצָה has the article and the directional ה together.
  • הַבֶּט־נָא הַשָּׁמַיְמָה: שָׁמַיִם with the article and the directional ending ָה, 'skyward'. The imperative with נָא is courteous.
  • אִם־תּוּכַל לִסְפֹּר: אִם introduces a conditional clause whose result is implied (the answer is no). The verb סָפַר is used twice (imperative and infinitive) in the one speech.
  • כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ: the adverb כֹּה refers to the stars in sight; the verb is future and 'offspring' is collective.
  • The pashta on וַיֹּאמֶר is written twice because the word is stressed on its first syllable: one mark shows the stress, the other is the accent's usual place on the last letter. It is one accent. The etnaḥta on אֹתָם ends the first speech, and the second begins with a new וַיֹּאמֶר.

Rashi gives the plain sense (God took Abram out of his tent to see the stars) and the midrash (go out of your astrology; 'look down' from above the stars). The English follows the plain sense, with the midrashic alternatives recorded.

Commentary (6)
Rashinormativefollows וַיּוֹצֵ֨א אֹת֜וֹ הַח֗וּצָה
Rashi: by its plain sense He brought him out of his tent to see the stars. By the midrash He told him, go out of your astrology, since you saw in the constellations that you will not have a son: 'Abram has no son, but Abraham will; Sarai will not bear, but Sarah will'. Another midrash lifted him above the stars, hence the sense of looking down.
Hebrew
לְפִי פְּשׁוּטוֹ הוֹצִיאוֹ מֵאָהֳלוֹ לַחוּץ לִרְאוֹת הַכּוֹכָבִים, וּלְפִי מִדְרָשׁוֹ אָמַר לוֹ צֵא מֵאִצְטַגְנִינוּת שֶׁלְּךָ שֶׁרָאִיתָ בַּמַּזָּלוֹת שֶׁאֵינְךָ עָתִיד לְהַעֲמִיד בֵּן, אַבְרָם אֵין לוֹ בֵן, אֲבָל אַבְרָהָם יֵשׁ לוֹ בֵן, שָׂרַי לֹא תֵלֵד, אֲבָל שָׂרָה תֵלֵד; אֲנִי קוֹרֵא לָכֶם שֵׁם אַחֵר וְיִשְׁתַּנֶּה הַמַּזָּל. דָּ"אַ הוֹצִיאוֹ מֵחֲלָלוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם וְהִגְבִּיהוֹ לְמַעְלָה מִן הַכּוֹכָבִים, וְזֶהוּ לְשׁוֹן הַבָּטָה מִלְמַעְלָה לְמַטָּה:
Rambanrecords וַיּוֹצֵ֨א אֹת֜וֹ הַח֗וּצָה
Ramban quotes Rashi's plain sense (He brought him out of his tent to see the stars) and the midrash (go out of your astrology), and objects that Abram, while still Abram, fathered Ishmael; he explains the midrash as meaning that Abram was seeking a son who would be his heir.
Hebrew
לְפִי פְּשׁוּטוֹ הוֹצִיאוֹ מֵאָהֳלוֹ אֶל הַחוּץ לִרְאוֹת הַכּוֹכָבִים. וּלְפִי מִדְרָשׁוֹ אָמַר לוֹ צֵא מֵאִצְטַגְנִינוּת שֶׁלְּךָ, שֶׁרָאִיתָ בַּמַּזָּלוֹת שֶׁאֵינְךָ עָתִיד לְהַעֲמִיד בֵּן, אַבְרָם אֵין לוֹ בֵּן, אַבְרָהָם יֵשׁ לוֹ בֵּן, שָׂרַי לֹא תֵלֵד, שָׂרָה תֵּלֵד, לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית ט"ו:ה'). וְהִנֵּה אַבְרָם הוֹלִיד אֶת יִשְׁמָעֵאל. אֲבָל פֵּרוּשׁ הַמִּדְרָשׁ כִּי אַבְרָם מְבַקֵּשׁ בֵּן יוֹרֵשׁ אוֹתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר
Radakfollows וַיּוֹצֵ֨א אֹת֜וֹ הַח֗וּצָה
Radak: the word came to him in his tent, and in the vision He brought him outside, as in Ezekiel 8:3 'he brought me to Jerusalem in visions of God'. The stars after the dust of the earth in the earlier promise are both hyperbole.
Hebrew
בְּאָהֳלוֹ בָּאָה לוֹ הַנְּבוּאָה וְהוֹצִיאוֹ מֵאָהֳלוֹ בְּמַרְאֵה הַנְּבוּאָה לַחוּץ לִרְאוֹת אֶת הַכּוֹכָבִים, וְכֵן ״וַתָּבֵא אֹתִי יְרוּשָׁלַיְמָה בְּמַרְאוֹת אֱלֹהִים״ (יחזקאל ח:ג). וּמִתְּחִלָּה אָמַר לוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כַּעֲפַר הָאָרֶץ וְעַכְשָׁיו אָמַר לוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כְּכוֹכְבֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם, וְהַכֹּל דֶּרֶךְ הַפְלָגָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְנוּ, וְגַם כָּתַבְנוּ הַדְּרָשׁ. וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר עוֹד שֶׁרָמַז לוֹ כִּי בְּסוֹף כְּשֶׁיִּהְיוּ יְמֵי הַמָּשִׁיחַ יִהְיוּ כְּכוֹכְבֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם שֶׁלֹּא תִשְׁלֹט בָּהֶם יַד אָדָם עוֹד, וְיִהְיוּ בְּאוֹרָם לְעוֹלָם. וּבְבֵרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה:
Radak וַיּוֹצֵ֨א אֹת֜וֹ

Apparatus

15:6

He trusted in the LORD, and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.

and-he-trusted in-the-LORD and-he-reckoned-it to-him righteousness

Grammar
  • וְהֶאֱמִן: the waw with a perfect (weqatal) after a string of wayyiqtols; it gives the narrator's comment on Abram's state of trust, not a new event in the sequence. The hifil of אמן means 'consider firm', 'put trust in'.
  • וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה: the verb takes an object suffix (feminine, 'it') and a double complement, 'to him' and 'as righteousness'. The feminine suffix refers to his faith or to the promise.
  • The subject of וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ is not named. Rashi and Sforno take it to be God. Ramban's preferred reading takes Abram as the subject: he reckoned that God would give him seed out of God's righteousness; his second reading has God count the promise to him as righteousness (cf. Psalm 106:31 of Pinhas).

The English names the LORD as the subject of 'reckoned', following Rashi and Sforno; the ambiguity of the Hebrew (Abram, or God) is kept in the phrase note and the commentary. צְדָקָה is 'righteousness'; Ibn Ezra explains it by Deuteronomy 6:25 and sets it apart from the Sages' sense 'charity'.

Commentary (9)
Rashinormativefollows וְהֶאֱמִ֖ן
Rashi: Abram did not ask for a sign about this (the son); but about inheriting the land he asked for a sign, 'by what shall I know'. So 'he trusted' refers to the son.
Hebrew
לֹא שָׁאַל לוֹ אוֹת עַל זֹאת; אֲבָל עַל יְרֻשַּׁת הָאָרֶץ שָׁאַל לוֹ אוֹת וְאָמַר לוֹ בַּמָּה אֵדַע.
Rashinormativefollows וַיַּחְשְׁבֶ֥הָ לּ֖וֹ צְדָקָֽה׃
Rashi: the Holy One, blessed be He, counted it to Abram as merit and as righteousness for the trust he showed. A second reading takes בַּמָּה אֵדַע as asking in what merit Israel will endure, and God answers, by the merit of sacrifices.
Hebrew
הַקָּבָּ"ה חֲשָׁבָהּ לאַבְרָם לִזְכוּת וְלִצְדָקָה עַל הַאֲמָנָה שֶׁהֶאֱמִין בּוֹ. דָּבָר אַחֵר בַּמָּה אֵדַע, לֹא שָׁאַל לוֹ אוֹת אֶלָּא אָמַר לְפָנָיו, הוֹדִיעֵנִי בְּאֵיזֶה זְכוּת יִתְקַיְּמוּ בָּהּ, אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּבָּ"ה, בִּזְכוּת הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת:
Ibn Ezranormativefollows צְדָקָֽה׃
Ibn Ezra: צדקה is as in וצדקה תהיה לנו (Deuteronomy 6:25) and like צדק ומשפט; he adds that the Sages' sense of צדקה as charity is different.
Hebrew
כמו וצדקה תהיה לנו (דבר' ו כה) וצדק ומשפט אחים רק בדברי קדמונינו ז"ל דרך צדקה אחרת
Rambanrecords וְהֶאֱמִ֖ן וַיַּחְשְׁבֶ֥הָ לּ֖וֹ צְדָקָֽה׃
Ramban does not understand Rashi's 'merit' (why would Abram not trust a God of truth?), and suggests Abram trusted that God would give him a child out of His own righteousness, not Abram's; or that God counted the promise itself as righteousness.

פֵּרֵשׁ רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית ט"ו:ו'), הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא חָשַׁב לוֹ צְדָקָה וּזְכוּת עַל הַאֲמָנָה שֶׁהֶאֱמִין בּוֹ. וְאֵינִי מֵבִין מָה הַזְּכוּת הַזֹּאת, לָמָּה לֹא יַאֲמִין בֵּאלֹהֵי אָמֵן וְהוּא הַנָּבִיא בְּעַצְמוֹ, וְלֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיכַזֵּב, וּמִי שֶׁהֶאֱמִין לִשְׁחֹט אֶת בְּנוֹ הַיָּחִיד הָאָהוּב וּשְׁאָר הַנִּסְיוֹנוֹת אֵיךְ לֹא יַאֲמִין בִּבְשׂוֹרָה טוֹבָה. וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי כִּי יֹאמַר שֶׁהֶאֱמִין בַּה' וְחָשַׁב כִּי בְּצִדְקוֹ שֶׁל הקב"ה יִתֵּן לוֹ זֶרַע עַל כָּל פָּנִים, לֹא בְּצִדְקַת אַבְרָם וּבִשְׂכָרוֹ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ "שְׂכָרְךָ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד", וּמֵעַתָּה לֹא יִירָא פֶּן יִגְרֹם הַחֵטְא, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבַּנְּבוּאָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה חָשַׁב שֶׁתִּהְיֶה עַל תְּנַאי כְּפִי שְׂכַר מַעֲשָׂיו, עַתָּה כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִבְטִיחוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יִירָא מִן הַחֵטְא וְיִתֵּן לוֹ זֶרַע הֶאֱמִין כִּי נָכוֹן הַדָּבָר מֵעִם הָאֱלֹהִים, אֱמֶת לֹא יָשׁוּב מִמֶּנָּה, כִּי צִדְקַת ה' הִיא וְאֵין לָהּ הֶפְסֵק, כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁכָּתוּב (ישעיהו מה כג) בִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי נְאֻם ה' יָצָא מִפִּי צְדָקָה דָּבָר וְלֹא יָשׁוּב. אוֹ יֹאמַר כִּי אַבְרָהָם הֶאֱמִין שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לוֹ זֶרַע יוֹרֵשׁ עַל כָּל פָּנִים, והקב"ה עוֹד חָשַׁב לוֹ הַהַבְטָחָה הַזּוֹ שֶׁהִבְטִיחוֹ צְדָקָה, כִּי בְּצִדְקַת ה' יַעֲשֶׂה כֵּן, כְּמוֹ "אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטוֹבָה" (בראשית נ':כ'), וְכֵן "וַתֵּחָשֶׁב לוֹ לִצְדָקָה" (תהלים קו לא) דְּפִנְחָס, שֶׁחָשַׁב לוֹ הַבְטָחָתוֹ זוֹ שֶׁבָּטַח בַּשֵּׁם בַּמַּעֲשֶׂה הַהוּא לִצְדָקָה לְדוֹר וָדוֹר, כִּי לְעוֹלָם יִשְׁמֹר לוֹ הָאֵל בַּעֲבוּרָהּ צִדְקָתוֹ וְחַסְדּוֹ, כְּדֶרֶךְ "לְעוֹלָם אֶשְׁמָר לוֹ חַסְדִּי" (שם פט כט):

15:7

He said to him, I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to take possession of it.

and-said to-him I LORD who I-brought-you-out from-Ur Chaldeans to-give to-you [object-mark] the-land the-this to-possess-it

Grammar
  • אֲנִי יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ: the formula of self-introduction, 'I am the LORD who ...', that recalls the earlier act as grounds for the promise.
  • The relative אֲשֶׁר takes a 1st person verb, 'who I brought you out', and the English turns it into a normal relative clause with 'who brought'.
  • לָתֶת לְךָ ... לְרִשְׁתָּהּ: two infinitives with ל expressing purpose. The first is of נתן, the second of ירשׁ with the feminine suffix referring to הָאָרֶץ.
  • The zaqef qaton on כַּשְׂדִּים closes 'I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans'. In what follows the tevir on לְךָ divides 'to give you' from 'this land', and the tipḥa on הַזֹּאת sets the last word, לְרִשְׁתָּהּ, apart. The darga on לָתֶת is conjunctive and joins it to לְךָ.

אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים is rendered 'Ur of the Chaldeans', the familiar English name; Ibn Ezra points out that the promise names Ur and not Haran because it was in Ur that the call came, as the Lekh Lekha section shows.

Ibn Ezra: Abram trusted God that his son would inherit; for the inheritance of the land he asked for a sign, as Gideon did, since every prophecy is conditional unless sworn. It bears on verse 8 and the sense of 'by what will I know', not on this verse.

15:8

He said, My Lord, the LORD, by what will I know that I shall take possession of it?

and-said my-lord LORD by-what I-will-know that I-will-possess-it

Grammar
  • בַּמָּה אֵדַע: the interrogative with ב asks for the means or sign by which knowledge will come; it is not a statement of doubt, and Radak says Abram did not doubt that his sons would inherit.
  • כִּי אִירָשֶׁנָּה: the כִּי introduces the content of the knowledge, 'that I shall inherit it'. The suffix -נָּה, with the nun, is an energic form on a feminine object.
  • The etnaḥta falls on the first word, וַיֹּאמַר, which takes its pausal form (patah for the segol of וַיֹּאמֶר); it sets the speech apart from the narrative.

There are no normative comments on this verse. Radak and Sforno agree that Abram asks for knowledge that the inheritance will be lasting, since his descendants might sin and lose the land; the English 'by what will I know' keeps the question open, as the Hebrew does.

Commentary (4)
Radakfollows בַּמָּ֥ה אֵדַ֖ע כִּ֥י אִֽירָשֶֽׁנָּה׃
Radak: Abram did not doubt that his sons would inherit, for he had trusted the LORD (15:6); he asked whether they would inherit it for ever, since they might sin and be exiled, and 'by what' asks in what way it will be made known to him, as the stars were shown for the offspring.

15:9

He said to him, "Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon."

and-said to-him take for-me heifer tripled and-she-goat tripled and-ram tripled and-turtledove and-young-bird

Grammar
  • קְחָה is the imperative with the paragogic ה, a mark of urgency or courtesy.
  • מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת / מְשֻׁלָּשׁ is a Pual participle (feminine, then masculine) of שָׁלַשׁ; it agrees in gender with each animal.
  • The accents group the three large animals, each with its participle, and the etnaḥta falls on מְשֻׁלָּשׁ; the two birds follow as a separate pair.
  • The list is in a fixed order of three animals and two birds; the birds take no participle.

מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת can mean 'three-year-old' (BDB: Pu three years old; Ibn Ezra's choice) or 'threefold', i.e. three of each (Rashi, Onkelos). I read 'three-year-old' and record the other in the commentary. הַגּוֹזָל is any young bird; Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as the young of the dove, which fits the pairing with the turtledove.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos reads three of each ('three heifers, three goats, three rams'), against Ibn Ezra's three-year-old.
  • Radak notes that גּוֹזָל can name the young of any bird, citing Deut 32:11, but takes it here as the young dove.
15:10

He took all these for him, cut them in the middle, and set each half opposite the other; but the birds he did not cut in two.

and-took for-him OBJ all-of these and-cut them in-the-midst and-gave man piece-his to-meet fellow-his and-OBJ the-bird not cut

Grammar
  • The object is fronted in וְאֶת־הַצִּפֹּר לֹא בָתָר, which sets the birds against the animals: the animals were cut, the birds were not.
  • אִישׁ בִּתְרוֹ לִקְרַאת רֵעֵהוּ is a distributive phrase, 'each one its piece opposite its fellow', as in Exod 26:3 (Ibn Ezra).
  • The root בתר occurs three times: the Piel verb וַיְבַתֵּר 'he cut in two', the noun בִּתְרוֹ 'his piece', and the Qal verb בָתָר. From it the scene is called בְּרִית בֵּין הַבְּתָרִים, 'the covenant between the pieces'.
  • The etnaḥta at רֵעֵהוּ closes the first half: the cutting and setting out of the animals.

The text does not say who commanded the cutting; the commentators take it as part of the covenant rite. צִפֹּר is a collective singular; Ibn Ezra reads it as the turtledove and the young pigeon of v. 9, which I follow. The pointing הַצִּפֹּר is that of the base text; WLC reads הַצִפֹּר without the dagesh. בֶּתֶר at 15:10.11 is listed in the lexicon only with the sense 'cleft mountains', which does not fit here; I give no sense number and read 'piece, half', as the lexicon's gloss says.

Commentary (11)
Rashinormativefollows וַיְבַתֵּ֤ר אֹתָם֙
Rashi: he divided each into two parts, for he was making a covenant, and covenant-makers divide animals and pass between the pieces (Jer 34:18). The smoking oven and flaming torch that pass between the pieces are the messenger of the Presence.

So it is used of animals as well, and of curtains, 'one to her sister' (Exod 26:3). He set the piece of each one opposite its fellow, 'for beast and man are two', meaning the word serves for both.

Apparatus
  • 15:10.15 vowels: WLC reads הַצִפֹּ֖ר (no dagesh in the צ); base text הַצִּפֹּ֖ר. Meaning unchanged.
  • Ramban records that the birds were not cut because of the rule of Lev 1:17 (the bird burnt offering is not divided) and notes Bereshit Rabbah on the difference between burnt-offering and sin-offering birds; not adopted as the plain sense.

15:11

The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them off.

and-came-down the-bird-of-prey upon the-carcasses and-caused-to-blow them Abram

Grammar
  • וַיַּשֵּׁב is a Hifil wayyiqtol of נשב ('to blow'), with the doubled shin standing for the assimilated nun; it means 'he blew them off'.
  • הָעַיִט is a collective singular with a singular verb: 'the birds of prey'.
  • The etnaḥta on הַפְּגָרִים divides the verse; the second half gives Abram's response.
  • The pronoun object אֹתָם comes before the named subject אַבְרָם. This is the usual order when the object is a pronoun and the subject a noun, so no emphasis is implied.

הַפְּגָרִים are the bodies of the animals that Abram had just cut up (Rashi: 'the pieces'; Ibn Ezra: 'the bodies'), so I write 'carcasses'. Radak argues that פְּגָרִים are whole bodies, i.e. the two birds; not adopted. For וַיַּשֵּׁב, Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take 'to blow away, make fly off'; Ibn Ezra also offers 'he made the carcasses return to drive off the bird', recorded in the apparatus.

Apparatus
  • Ibn Ezra's alternative: וַיַּשֵּׁב from שׁוּב, 'he put the carcasses back' to scare off the bird; the English keeps the נשב reading, the one the lexicon lists.

15:12

As the sun was about to go down, a deep sleep fell on Abram, and suddenly dread, a great darkness, was falling on him.

and-was the-sun to-go-in and-deep-sleep fell upon Abram and-behold dread darkness great falling upon-him

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי with a time clause (הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ לָבוֹא) is a standard way to open a new scene: 'the sun was about to set'.
  • The verb forms move from the qatal נָפְלָה, after its fronted subject וְתַרְדֵּמָה, to the participle נֹפֶלֶת: the deep sleep has fallen, and the dread is falling, still in progress.
  • אֵימָה חֲשֵׁכָה גְדֹלָה: three words in a row, 'terror, darkness, great'; the adjective is feminine and may modify חֲשֵׁכָה alone or both nouns.
  • הִנֵּה brings the reader into Abram's experience.

The three nouns אֵימָה חֲשֵׁכָה גְדֹלָה can be read as a list ('a dread, a darkness, great') or as 'a dread of great darkness' or 'a great, dark dread'. The English keeps the apposition: 'dread, a great darkness'. The lexicon lists no sense for גָּדוֹל that matches 'great' (it lists 'loud', 'do great things', 'greatness'), so I give none at 15:12.11.

15:13

He said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not theirs, and they will serve them, and they will oppress them, for four hundred years.

and-said to-Abram knowing you-will-know that sojourner will-be your-seed in-land not to-them and-they-will-serve-them and-they-will-oppress OBJ-them four hundreds year

Grammar
  • יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע is the infinitive absolute before the finite verb of the same root: 'you shall surely know'.
  • The accents join the clause 'your offspring will be a sojourner in a land not theirs' and then close it at the zaqef; the next verbs are a new clause, whose subject shifts without being named.
  • The perfects with wāw (וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ) continue the future: 'and they will serve, and will afflict'.
  • אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה is the number of years in apposition: the period comes at the end.

In וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ אֹתָם the subject and object are not named; 'they will serve them … and they will oppress them' keeps that ambiguity, where 'they' is the people of the land. Whether 'four hundred years' counts the whole period or only the oppression is also open: Rashi counts four hundred years from the birth of Isaac, and Ibn Ezra counts from the day of the vision; the English keeps the number without fixing its starting point. Rashi's point that 'a land not theirs' is not only Egypt is followed.

Commentary (14)
Rashinormativerecords כִּי גֵ֣ר יִהְיֶ֣ה זַרְעֲךָ֗
Rashi: the four hundred years run from the birth of Isaac until Israel left Egypt (Isaac sixty at Jacob's birth, Jacob 130 at the descent, 210 years in Egypt), and he shows that the time in Egypt alone was less. The English does not fix the starting point.
Hebrew

15:14

And also the nation that they will serve, I will judge; and afterward they will come out with great wealth.

and-also OBJ the-nation that they-will-serve judging I and-after thus they-will-go-out with-property great

Grammar
  • The object וְגַם אֶת־הַגּוֹי is placed first, before the subject אָנֹכִי; this puts the weight on the nation that will be judged.
  • דָּן is a participle ('judging'), which here gives a near-future sense: 'I am about to judge'.
  • אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ is a relative clause without a resumptive pronoun: 'the nation that they will serve'.
  • בִּרְכֻשׁ גָּדוֹל, 'with great property', looks ahead to the Exodus, and the verb יֵצְאוּ 'they will go out' is the verb later used of it.

The word order of the Hebrew puts the object first, and the English follows it. Rashi takes גַּם to add the four kingdoms to Egypt; this is recorded rather than adopted. Ibn Ezra's gloss for אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ ('so that they have servants') fits the plain sense of the nation as master.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativerecords וְגַ֧ם אֶת הַגּ֛וֹי
Rashi: 'also' adds the four kingdoms, since they too will be destroyed for enslaving Israel. The English keeps 'also' without naming the kingdoms.

עָוֹן, גַּם אֶת הַגּוֹי אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ אָדִין עַל הֶחָמָס אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשׂוּ לָהֶם. וְהַנָּכוֹן בְּעֵינַי כִּי טַעַם "וְגַם", אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֲנִי גָּזַרְתִּי עַל זַרְעֲךָ לִהְיוֹת גֵּרִים בְּאֶרֶץ לֹא לָהֶם וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ אוֹתָם, אַף עַל פִּי כֵן אֶשְׁפֹּט אֶת הַגּוֹי אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ עַל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשׂוּ לָהֶם, וְלֹא יִפָּטְרוּ בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁעָשׂוּ גְּזֵרָתִי. וְהַטַּעַם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב (זכריה א יד), "וְקִנֵּאתִי לִירוּשָׁלִַם וּלְצִיּוֹן קִנְאָה גְדוֹלָה וְקֶצֶף גָּדוֹל אֲנִי קֹצֵף עַל הַגּוֹיִם הַשַּׁאֲנַנִּים אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי קָצַפְתִּי מְּעָט וְהֵמָּה עָזְרוּ לְרָעָה", וְאוֹמֵר (ישעיהו מז ו) "קָצַפְתִּי עַל עַמִּי חִלַּלְתִּי נַחֲלָתִי" וְגוֹ'. וְכֵן הָיָה בְּמִצְרַיִם, שֶׁהוֹסִיפוּ לְהָרַע כִּי הִשְׁלִיכוּ בְּנֵיהֶם לַיְּאוֹר וַיְמָרְרוּ אֶת חַיֵּיהֶם, וְחָשְׁבוּ לִמְחוֹת אֶת שְׁמָם. וְזֶה טַעַם "דָּן אָנֹכִי", שֶׁאָבִיא אוֹתָם בְּמִשְׁפָּט אִם עָשׂוּ כַּנִּגְזַר עֲלֵיהֶם אוֹ הוֹסִיפוּ לְהָרַע לָהֶם. וְזֶהוּ מַה שֶׁאָמַר יִתְרוֹ "כִּי בַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר זָדוּ עֲלֵיהֶם" (שמות יח יא), כִּי הַזָּדוֹן הוּא שֶׁהֵבִיא עֲלֵיהֶם הָעֹנֶשׁ הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁאִבְּדָם מִן הָעוֹלָם, וְכֵן "כִּי יָדַעְתָּ כִּי הֵזִידוּ עֲלֵיהֶם" (נחמיה ט י). וְהָרַב נָתַן טַעַם בְּסֵפֶר הַמַּדָּע (הלכות תשובה ו ה), לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא גָּזַר עַל אִישׁ יָדוּעַ, וְכָל אוֹתָם הַמְּרֵעִים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אִלּוּ לֹא רָצָה כָּל אֶחָד מֵהֶם הָרְשׁוּת בְּיָדוֹ, לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא נִגְזַר עַל אִישׁ יָדוּעַ. וְלֹא נִתְכְּנוּ דְּבָרָיו אֶצְלִי, שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ גָּזַר שֶׁאֶחָד מִכָּל הָאֻמּוֹת יָרֵעַ לָהֶם בְּכָךְ וְכָךְ, וְקָדַם זֶה וְעָשָׂה גְּזֵרָתוֹ שֶׁל הקב"ה, זָכָה בִּדְבַר מִצְוָה, וּמָה טַעַם בִּדְבָרָיו כַּאֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ בְּנֵי מְדִינָה פְּלוֹנִית מַעֲשֶׂה מִן הַמַּעֲשִׂים, הַמִּתְרַשֵּׁל וּמַטִּיל הַדָּבָר עַל הָאֲחֵרִים חוֹמֵס וְחוֹטֵא נַפְשׁוֹ, וְהָעֹשֶׂה יָפִיק רָצוֹן מִמֶּנּוּ. וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁהַכָּתוּב אָמַר "וְגַם אֶת הַגּוֹי אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ", שֶׁיַּעַבְדוּ הַגּוֹי כֻּלּוֹ, וְהֵם הָלְכוּ מֵעַצְמָם לְמִצְרַיִם. אֲבָל הַטַּעַם כַּאֲשֶׁר כָּתַבְתִּי, וּכְבָר הִזְכִּירוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ הָעִנְיָן הַזֶּה, אָמְרוּ בִּוְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (שמות רבה ל':ט"ו), מָשָׁל לְאָדוֹן שֶׁאָמַר לִבְנוֹ "יַעֲשֶׂה עִם פְּלוֹנִי וְלֹא יְצַעֲרֶנּוּ", הָלַךְ וְעָשָׂה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעָשָׂה עִמּוֹ חִנָּם לֹא הִנִּיחַ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה מְצַעֲרוֹ. כְּשֶׁנִּתְרַצָּה הָאָדוֹן לִבְנוֹ גָּזַר עַל מְצַעֲרָיו הֲרִיגָה. כָּךְ גָּזַר הקב"ה שֶׁיִּהְיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מְשֻׁעְבָּדִין בְּמִצְרַיִם, עָמְדוּ עֲלֵיהֶם וְשִׁעְבְּדוּם בְּחֹזֶק. אָמַר הקב"ה הָיָה לָכֶם לִנְהֹג בָּם כַּעֲבָדִים וְיַעֲשׂוּ צָרְכֵיכֶם, "אֲנִי קָצַפְתִּי מְּעָט וְהֵמָּה עָזְרוּ לְרָעָה" (זכריה א טו), עַד כָּאן לְשׁוֹנָם. וְדָבָר בָּרוּר הוּא כִּי הַשְׁלָכַת בְּנֵיהֶם לַיְּאוֹר אֵינָהּ בִּכְלַל "וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ אוֹתָם", אֲבָל הִיא עֲקִירָתָם לְגַמְרֵי. וְכֵן מָה שֶׁאָמְרוּ תְּחִלָּה "הָבָה נִתְחַכְּמָה לוֹ פֶּן יִרְבֶּה" (שמות א י), אֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל עַבְדוּת וְעִנּוּי, מִלְּבַד מָה שֶׁהוֹסִיפוּ בָּעִנּוּי עַצְמוֹ "וַיְמָרְרוּ אֶת חַיֵּיהֶם בַּעֲבֹדָה קָשָׁה" וְגוֹ'. וְהוּא מָה שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב (דברים כו ז), "וַיַּרְא אֶת עָנְיֵנוּ וְאֶת עֲמָלֵנוּ וְאֶת לַחֲצֵנוּ". וְדַע וְהָבֵן כִּי הָאִישׁ שֶׁנִּכְתַּב וְנֶחְתַּם בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לַהֲרִיגָה, לֹא יִנָּקֶה הַלִּסְטִים הַהוֹרֵג אוֹתוֹ בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁעָשָׂה מָה שֶׁנִּגְזַר עָלָיו, הוּא רָשָׁע בַּעֲוֹנוֹ יָמוּת וְדָמוֹ מִיָּד הָרוֹצֵחַ יְבֻקַּשׁ, אֲבָל כַּאֲשֶׁר תֵּצֵא הַגְּזֵרָה עַל פִּי נָבִיא יֵשׁ בָּעֹשֶׂה אוֹתָהּ דִּינִים, כִּי אִם שָׁמַע אוֹתָהּ וְרָצָה לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן בּוֹרְאוֹ כַּנִּגְזָר, אֵין עָלָיו חֵטְא, אֲבָל יֵשׁ לוֹ זְכוּת בּוֹ, כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר בְּיֵהוּא (מלכים ב י ל) "יַעַן אֲשֶׁר הֱטִיבֹתָ לַעֲשׂוֹת הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינַי כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר בִּלְבָבִי עָשִׂיתָ לְבֵית אַחְאָב בָּנִים רְבִעִים יֵשְׁבוּ לְךָ עַל כִּסֵּא יִשְׂרָאֵל". אֲבָל אִם שָׁמַע הַמִּצְוָה וְהָרַג אוֹתוֹ לְשִׂנְאָה אוֹ לִשְׁלֹל אוֹתוֹ, יֵשׁ עָלָיו הָעֹנֶשׁ, כִּי הוּא לַחֲטֹא נִתְכַּוֵּן וַעֲבֵרָה הוּא לוֹ, וְכֵן הַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר בְּסַנְחֵרִיב (ישעיהו י ה) "הוֹי אַשּׁוּר שֵׁבֶט אַפִּי וְגוֹ' בְּגוֹי חָנֵף אֲשַׁלְּחֶנּוּ וְעַל עַם עֶבְרָתִי אֲצַוֶּנּוּ", וְאָמַר הַכָּתוּב "וְהוּא לֹא כֵן יְדַמֶּה וּלְבָבוֹ לֹא כֵן יַחְשֹׁב כִּי לְהַשְׁמִיד בִּלְבָבוֹ", וְעַל כֵּן הֶעֱנִישׁוֹ בַּסּוֹף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שם י יב) "וְהָיָה כִּי יְבַצַּע ה' אֶת כָּל מַעֲשֵׂהוּ אֶפְקֹד עַל פְּרִי גֹדֶל לְבַב מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר וְעַל תִּפְאֶרֶת רוּם עֵינָיו" וְגוֹ', וְאָמַר בּוֹ "שֶׂה פְזוּרָה יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲרָיוֹת הִדִּיחוּ הָרִאשׁוֹן אֲכָלוֹ מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר וְזֶה הָאַחֲרוֹן עִצְּמוֹ נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּר מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל לָכֵן כֹּה אָמַר ה' וְגוֹ' הִנְנִי פֹקֵד אֶל מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל וְאֶל אַרְצוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר פָּקַדְתִּי עַל מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר" (ירמיהו נ יז), וְהִנֵּה זוֹ רְאָיָה שֶׁנֶּעֱנַשׁ מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר עַל הָרָעָה שֶׁעָשָׂה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל. וְהִנֵּה נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּר שָׁמַע כִּי הַנְּבִיאִים פֶּה אֶחָד קוֹרְאִים אוֹתוֹ לְהַחְרִיב יְרוּשָׁלַיִם, וְהוּא וְכָל עַמּוֹ נִצְטַוּוּ עַל כָּךְ מִפִּי הַנָּבִיא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (ירמיהו כה ט) "הִנְנִי שׁוֹלֵחַ לְךָ וְלָקַחְתִּי אֶת כָּל מִשְׁפְּחוֹת צָפוֹן נְאֻם ה' וְאֶל נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּר מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל עַבְדִּי וַהֲבִאֹתִים עַל הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת וְעַל יוֹשְׁבֶיהָ וְהַחֲרַמְתִּים", וּכְתִיב (שם לב כח) "הִנְנִי נֹתֵן אֶת הָעִיר הַזֹּאת בְּיַד הַכַּשְׂדִּים וּבְיַד נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּר מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל וְהִצִּיתוּ אֶת הָעִיר בָּאֵשׁ", וְאַף עַל בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ עַצְמוֹ אָמַר (שם כו ו), "וְנָתַתִּי אֶת הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה כְּשִׁלֹה", וְהֵם יוֹדְעִים כִּי מִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם הִיא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר נְבוּזַרְאֲדָן לְיִרְמְיָהוּ (שם מ ב) "ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ דִּבֶּר אֶת הָרָעָה הַזֹּאת אֶל הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה וַיָּבֵא וַיַּעַשׂ ה' כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֵּר כִּי חֲטָאתֶם לַה'", וְאַף עַל פִּי כֵן נֶעֶנְשׁוּ הַכַּשְׂדִּים כֻּלָּם בַּסּוֹף, וְהָיָה זֶה מִפְּנֵי שְׁנֵי טְעָמִים, הָאֶחָד שֶׁגַּם הוּא נִתְכַּוֵּן לְהַשְׁמִיד כָּל הָאָרֶץ לְהַגְדִּיל מֶמְשַׁלְתּוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בּוֹ (ישעיהו יג יא) "וְהִשְׁבַּתִּי גְּאוֹן זֵדִים וְגַאֲוַת עָרִיצִים אַשְׁפִּיל", וּכְתִיב (שם יד יג) "וְאַתָּה אָמַרְתָּ בִלְבָבְךָ הַשָּׁמַיִם אֶעֱלֶה" וְגוֹ' וְכָתוּב "אֶעֱלֶה עַל בָּמֳתֵי עָב אֶדַּמֶּה לְעֶלְיוֹן", וּכְתִיב בְּאֻמָּתוֹ (שם מז ח) "הָאוֹמֶרֶת בִּלְבָבָהּ אֲנִי וְאַפְסִי עוֹד", וְאָמַר בּוֹ חֲבַקּוּק (חבקוק ב ט), "הוֹי בֹּצֵעַ בֶּצַע רָע לְבֵיתוֹ לָשׂוּם בַּמָּרוֹם קִנּוֹ" וְגוֹ', וְהִנֵּה זֶה כְּעָנְשׁוֹ שֶׁל סַנְחֵרִיב. וּלְכָךְ אָמַר הַכָּתוּב (ירמיהו נ יח) "לָכֵן כֹּה אָמַר ה' הִנְנִי פֹקֵד אֶל מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל וְאֶל אַרְצוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר פָּקַדְתִּי עַל מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר". אֲבָל הָיָה בְּמֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל עֹנֶשׁ אַחֵר, שֶׁהוֹסִיף עַל הַגְּזֵרָה וְהֵרַע לְיִשְׂרָאֵל יוֹתֵר מְאֹד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר בּוֹ (ישעיהו מז ו) "קָצַפְתִּי עַל עַמִּי חִלַּלְתִּי נַחֲלָתִי וָאֶתְּנֵם בְּיָדֵךְ לֹא שַׂמְתְּ לָהֶם רַחֲמִים עַל זָקֵן הִכְבַּדְתְּ עֻלֵּךְ מְאֹד", וְעַל כֵּן בָּא עֲלֵיהֶם עֹנֶשׁ כָּפוּל וּמְכֻפָּל, שֶׁנִּשְׁמַד זַרְעוֹ לְגַמְרֵי וְלֹא יִהְיֶה לְבָבֶל שֵׁם וּשְׁאָר נִין וָנֶכֶד (ישעיהו יד כב), וְנִשְׁמְדָה עִירוֹ לְעוֹלָמִים, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שם יג יט) "וְהָיְתָה בָבֶל צְבִי מַמְלָכוֹת תִּפְאֶרֶת גְּאוֹן כַּשְׂדִּים כְּמַהְפֵּכַת אֱלֹהִים אֶת סְדֹם וְאֶת עֲמֹרָה לֹא תֵשֵׁב לָנֶצַח וְלֹא תִשְׁכֹּן עַד דּוֹר וָדוֹר וְרָבְצוּ שָׁם צִיִּים וּשְׂעִירִים יְרַקְּדוּ שָׁם", וְאָמַר בּוֹ הַכָּתוּב (ירמיהו נא יא) "כִּי נִקְמַת ה' הִיא נִקְמַת הֵיכָלוֹ", וּכְתִיב (שם נא לה לו) "חֲמָסִי וּשְׁאֵרִי עַל בָּבֶל תֹּאמַר יֹשֶׁבֶת צִיּוֹן וְדָמִי אֶל יֹשְׁבֵי כַשְׂדִּים תֹּאמַר יְרוּשָׁלִָם לָכֵן כֹּה אָמַר ה' הִנְנִי רָב אֶת רִיבֵךְ וְנִקַּמְתִּי אֶת נִקְמָתֵךְ", וּפְסוּקִים רַבִּים כָּאֵלֶּה:

15:15

As for you, you will go to your fathers in peace; you will be buried at a good old age.

and-you you-will-come to your-fathers in-peace you-will-be-buried in-old-age good

Grammar
  • וְאַתָּה with the separate pronoun contrasts Abram with his descendants, who suffer in the previous verses.
  • תָּבוֹא אֶל־אֲבֹתֶיךָ is a euphemism for death, 'come to your fathers' (Ibn Ezra).
  • תִּקָּבֵר is a Nifal, 'you will be buried', passive of קבר.
  • בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה means 'in a good old age'; the adjective follows the noun and agrees in gender.

תָּבוֹא is rendered 'you will go': Hebrew בוא is 'come' or 'go in', and English 'go to your fathers' is the usual idiom for death. The lexicon sense used is Qal 4, 'go'. Rashi's comments on the repentance of Terah and Ishmael use the verse for homily and do not bear on the plain sense.

Commentary (10)
Rashinormativefollows וְאַתָּ֛ה תָּב֥וֹא
Rashi: 'and you will come [to your fathers]': and you will not see all this. The emphatic וְאַתָּה sets Abram apart from the exile foretold for his offspring. The English 'As for you' follows.

Rashi: Terah served idols, so 'to your fathers' teaches that Terah repented; a homily.

15:16

and-generation fourth they-will-return hither for not complete iniquity-of the-Amorite until hither

Grammar
  • וְדוֹר רְבִיעִי is a singular noun with a plural verb (יָשׁוּבוּ): the 'generation' stands for its members.
  • הֵנָּה ('here') appears twice in the verse, once of place (in the land) and once of time (up to now: עַד־הֵנָּה).
  • The reason clause כִּי לֹא־שָׁלֵם עֲוֺן הָאֱמֹרִי states why the promise is delayed: the Amorites' guilt is not yet full.
  • The etnaḥta on הֵנָּה ends the first half, the return; the second half gives the reason.

I follow Rashi in taking דּוֹר as 'generation' (BDB sense 2), so four generations: Jacob and his sons into Egypt, then the fourth generation returns. Ibn Ezra reads דּוֹר as 'a dwelling' of the lifetime of a person and also counts to the fourth after the sojourn; I record this. The Amorites are a collective singular; the word 'iniquity' is kept, and not softened to 'guilt'.

Hebrew
וְדָרָא רְבִיעָאָה יְתוּבוּן הָכָא אֲרֵי לָא שְׁלִים חוֹבָא דֶּאֱמוֹרָאָה עַד כְּעָן:
Apparatus
  • Ibn Ezra rejects deriving הָאֱמֹרִי from אמר ('to say'); the Amorites are named for their strength, as in Amos 2:9.
15:17

When the sun had set and it was thick darkness, there was a smoking furnace and a flaming torch that passed between these pieces.

and-was the-sun came and-thick-darkness was and-behold furnace-of smoke and-torch-of fire which passed between the-pieces the-these

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי opens a time clause; both clauses that follow put the subject before the verb: הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בָּאָה, וַעֲלָטָה הָיָה (Rashi: וַיְהִי דָּבָר זֶה, 'and this thing happened').
  • בָּאָה is accented on the first syllable (zaqef qaton on a mil'el form), so it is a perfect, 'had come', not a participle 'is coming' (Rashi, Radak).
  • הָיָה is masculine although עֲלָטָה is feminine; the clause is impersonal: 'it was thick darkness'.
  • תַּנּוּר and לַפִּיד are in the construct before עָשָׁן and אֵשׁ; Radak reads עָשָׁן as an adjective ('a smoky furnace').
  • אֲשֶׁר עָבַר is singular after two nouns. That fits one apparition, a smoking furnace with the torch inside it (Ibn Ezra, Ramban); Radak has the torch pass between the pieces.
  • The etnaḥta on הָיָה divides the scene (sunset, darkness) from the vision.

Followed Rashi (and Radak) on בָּאָה: a perfect, the sun had set. Ibn Ezra agrees: in v. 12 (לָבוֹא) the sun had not yet set, and here it has. עֲלָטָה is a thick darkness. The verb עָבַר is singular: for Ibn Ezra and Ramban one figure passes, a furnace with a torch of fire inside it; Radak has the torch pass, to confirm the covenant of the next verse.

Apparatus
  • גֶּזֶר: the plural גְּזָרִים occurs elsewhere only in Ps 136:13; Ibn Ezra and Radak equate it with the בְּתָרִים of v. 10.
15:18

On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying: To your offspring I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:

in-the-day the-that cut the-LORD with-Abram covenant to-say to-your-seed I-have-given the-land the-this from-river-of Egypt until the-river the-great river-of Euphrates

Grammar
  • כָּרַת בְּרִית is the idiom 'cut a covenant'; the verb's basic sense is 'cut' (cf. the pieces of v. 17).
  • לֵאמֹר (ל + infinitive construct of אמר) introduces the speech; לְזַרְעֲךָ stands before its verb, which puts the weight on 'to your offspring'.
  • נָתַתִּי is a perfect of certainty: the promise is spoken as already given (Rashi: the saying of the Holy One is as if done).
  • מִנְּהַר מִצְרַיִם עַד־הַנָּהָר הַגָּדֹל: the boundaries are given as two rivers; נְהַר־פְּרָת stands in apposition to 'the great river'.
  • יְהֹוָה is read 'the LORD' (decisions).

'I have given' keeps the perfect. נְהַר מִצְרַיִם is rendered 'the river of Egypt' because Ibn Ezra identifies it as the Shiḥor and not the Nile (היאור); the Hebrew word is unchanged. The token אֶת־ at 15:18.5 is parsed as a preposition (BDB a.gn.aa, 'with'): kept as given, the sense list of that entry has 'together with' but Abram here is the party with whom the covenant is cut, so 'with' is the reading.

  • The verse continues the list of objects of נָתַתִּי (v. 18); each name is a singular gentilic with the article, read collectively.

קַדְמֹנִי is 'Kadmonites' (BDB 'Easterners'), a name for a people, kept as a name. The list of names resumes in v. 20.

15:20

the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Rephaim;

and-(OBJ)-the-Hittite and-(OBJ)-the-Perizzite and-(OBJ)-the-Rephaim

Grammar
  • The list continues with the objects of נָתַתִּי; the ו of each וְאֶת is rendered by the commas and the final 'and'.
  • הַחִתִּי, הַפְּרִזִּי are singular collective gentilics; הָרְפָאִים is plural.
  • The merkha, tipḥa and silluq accents mark the three names.

רְפָאִים is kept as 'Rephaim'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra identify it with the land of Og ('the land of Rephaim', Deut 3:13). Ibn Ezra explains that the ten nations are all Canaanite in a wide sense.

Commentary (5)
Rashinormativefollows וְאֶת הָרְפָאִֽים׃

Do not wonder that the Canaanite and the Jebusite follow: the seven nations are all Canaanites, Canaan had eleven sons, and after six are named 'the Canaanite' covers the rest; here the nations are listed one by one, elsewhere as a whole, as 'Judah and Israel' (1 Kgs 4:20) although Judah is part of Israel.

16:1

Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had not borne him a child. She had an Egyptian maidservant, and her name was Hagar.

and-Sarai wife-of Abram not bore to-him and-to-her maidservant Egyptian and-name-her Hagar

Grammar
  • The sentence opens with waw + subject, not a wayyiqtol: it gives background, not a new event.
  • Possession is expressed with the preposition ל: וְלָהּ שִׁפְחָה 'and to her (there was) a maidservant'.
  • The accents pair מִצְרִית with שִׁפְחָה under a tipha and divide the verse at the etnahta after לוֹ.

The negated perfect יָלְדָה is rendered 'had not borne' since it reports the state at the time of the story. 'A child' supplies the unexpressed object.

Commentary (4)
Rashinormativerecords שִׁפְחָ֥ה מִצְרִ֖ית
Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: Hagar was Pharaoh's daughter. When Pharaoh saw the miracles done for Sarah, he said: better that my daughter be a maidservant in this house than a mistress in another. The English keeps the plain 'Egyptian maidservant' and records this identification.

Sarai said to Abram, "Look, the LORD has kept me from bearing children. Please go in to my maidservant; perhaps I shall be built up through her." And Abram listened to Sarai's voice.

Grammar
  • אִבָּנֶה is a Niphal imperfect 1cs of בנה (a III-ה verb): the dagesh in ב is the assimilated נ of the Niphal (from *ʾinbāneh). The sound-play with בֵּן 'son' is the point.
  • בֹּא־נָא is a polite imperative: 'come now, please'.
  • שָׁמַע לְקוֹל, 'to listen to the voice of', means to obey.
  • The zaqef on מִלֶּדֶת and the etnahta on מִמֶּנָּה mark the two halves of her speech.

The English keeps 'built up' so that the connection with 'son' is preserved in the notes. 'Listened to' keeps the idiom; 'obeyed' is the sense.

Apparatus
  • Ramban: Abram did not seek to be built up from Hagar himself; he consented only to do Sarai's will, and took no step without her (not normative).
  • Radak: the plan seemed right to Abram, since he thought that, Sarai having ceased to bear, the promised seed would come through Hagar; he did not wait for God's word (not normative).
16:3

Then Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her maidservant, at the end of ten years of Abram's dwelling in the land of Canaan, and gave her to Abram her husband to be his wife.

and-took Sarai wife-of Abram [obj] Hagar the-Egyptian maidservant-her from-end-of ten years to-dwell Abram in-land-of Canaan and-gave [obj]-her to-Abram husband-her to-him as-wife

Grammar
  • Two wayyiqtols, וַתִּקַּח and וַתִּתֵּן, carry the narrative; the intervening phrases are all attached to the first.
  • מִקֵּץ is a construct 'from the end of'; לְשֶׁבֶת is an infinitive construct of ישב with ל.
  • The accents separate 'ten years' (zaqef) from 'of Abram's dwelling' (tipha).

The English ties the ten years to Abram's dwelling in the land of Canaan, as Rashi reads it (years outside the land do not count). Ibn Ezra takes the verse as a support (asmakhta) for the rule of ten years; he says nothing about where they were counted. 'Took' is kept as plain narrative; Rashi's 'took her with words' is recorded.

Rashi: ten years is the fixed term for a woman who has lived ten years without bearing to her husband, after which he must marry another. This explains the mention of ten years.

Apparatus
  • Ramban accepts that years outside the land do not count, but rejects Rashi's reason (the promise 'I will make you a great nation'): the rule holds for everyone, and a couple who come to the land are given ten years from their arrival, as Abram and Sarai counted (not normative).
16:4

He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. She saw that she had conceived, and her mistress became of little account in her eyes.

and-went-in to Hagar and-conceived and-saw that conceived and-was-slight mistress-her in-eyes-her

Grammar
  • A chain of wayyiqtols (וַיָּבֹא, וַתַּהַר, וַתֵּרֶא, וַתֵּקַל) moves the story at speed.
  • וַתֵּרֶא כִּי הָרָתָה: ראה + כִּי 'saw that', with the perfect הָרָתָה giving the state seen.
  • בְּעֵינֶיהָ 'in her eyes' is the idiom for her estimate of things.

The data parse וַתֵּקַל as Qal of קלל ('be slight'). Ibn Ezra takes the form as Niphal, with the doubled letter absorbed; the pack's parse is kept and the difference is noted. The meaning 'was lightly regarded' is the same either way.

Apparatus
  • Radak: Hagar thought that since Abraham's seed would come from her she would be the mistress, so she ignored Sarai's commands.
16:5

Sarai said to Abram, "The wrong done to me is on you! I myself gave my maidservant into your arms, and when she saw that she had conceived, I became of little account in her eyes. May the LORD judge between me and you."

and-said Sarai to Abram my-violence upon-you I gave maidservant-my in-bosom-your and-saw that conceived and-I-was-slight in-eyes-her may-judge the-LORD between-me and-between-you

Grammar
  • חֲמָסִי עָלֶיךָ: 'my violence is on you'; the suffix is objective ('wrong done to me').
  • אָנֹכִי is an emphatic subject pronoun before the perfect.
  • וָאֵקַל is a wayyiqtol in the first person: 'and I became slight'.
  • The extraordinary dots on the yod of וּבֵינֶיךָ are a scribal mark noted in the data.

Rashi and Radak agree that חמסי עליך means the wrong done to me is laid on you, so 'The wrong done to me is on you' is adopted. The puncta extraordinaria on the yod of וּבֵינֶיךָ are recorded in the apparatus.

Apparatus
  • The yod of וּבֵינֶיךָ carries puncta extraordinaria (WLC note 4); Radak takes it as a full spelling, and Rashi as a hint at a miscarriage.
16:6

Abram said to Sarai, "Here, your maidservant is in your hand. Do to her what is good in your eyes." Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her presence.

and-said Abram to Sarai behold maidservant-your in-hand-your do to-her the-good in-eyes-your and-afflicted-her Sarai and-fled from-faces-her

Grammar
  • 'In your hand' means in your power.
  • The Piel of ענה means to afflict or oppress; the suffix is the object.
  • מִפָּנֶיהָ is literally 'from her faces'; idiomatically 'from before her'.
  • The imperative עֲשִׂי is feminine singular.

The English 'dealt harshly with her' follows Rashi's 'she subjected her harshly' for וַתְּעַנֶּהָ; 'afflicted' is the lexical sense.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativefollows וַתְּעַנֶּ֣הָ שָׂרַ֔י
Rashi: she kept her in harsh subjection. The English 'dealt harshly with her' follows this.

16:7

Then the angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, by the spring on the way to Shur.

Grammar
  • וַיִּמְצָאָהּ carries the 3fs suffix -āh directly on the wayyiqtol; the regular form would be -ehā, as in וַיִּשְׂנָאֶהָ (Deut 22:16), so Ibn Ezra calls it a strange word.
  • עַיִן here is 'spring', a different entry from 'eye'.
  • The second 'by the spring' defines which spring.

The lexicon entry for עַיִן 'spring' lists only the place-name senses 'b' and 'd', which do not apply, so the two tokens carry no sense. Shur is a place name.

16:8

He said, "Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?" She said, "I am fleeing from Sarai my mistress."

and-said Hagar maidservant-of Sarai where from-this you-came and-whither you-go and-said from-face-of Sarai mistress-my I fleeing

Grammar
  • אֵי־מִזֶּה בָאת: 'where from this (place) did you come'.
  • The participle בֹּרַחַת gives a present state: 'I am fleeing'.
  • The pausal vowel on בֹּרַחַת is unusual; Ibn Ezra explains it by the guttural.
  • Hagar is addressed by name and by her status.

The question is rhetorical: the angel knows the answer and uses it to open a conversation. The apparatus keeps the Ibn Ezra and Radak points on form.

16:9

The messenger of the LORD said to her, "Go back to your mistress, and submit to her authority."

and-said to-her messenger-of LORD return-(f) to mistress-your and-humble-yourself-(f) under hands-of-her

Grammar
  • שׁוּבִי is a feminine singular imperative; the final -י marks the feminine.
  • הִתְעַנִּי is hitpael, 'humble yourself, submit'; it recalls וַתְּעַנֶּהָ (16:6), where Sarai afflicted her.
  • תַּחַת יָדֶיהָ, literally 'under her hands', means in her power.
  • The etnaḥta falls on גְּבִרְתֵּךְ and divides the command into 'return' and 'submit'.

מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה is 'messenger of the LORD'; the pack's sense 3 (theophanic angel) is followed. Rashi's note that a different angel spoke each time is a homily and is kept in commentary.

Commentary (6)
Rashinormativenot-applicable וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָהּ֙ מַלְאַ֣ךְ
Rashi: a different angel was sent for each speech, which is why 'angel' is written each time; a homiletic reading that does not alter the plain sense.

16:10

The messenger of the LORD said to her, "I will greatly multiply your offspring, so that they cannot be counted for their multitude."

Grammar
  • הַרְבָּה אַרְבֶּה pairs an infinitive absolute with a finite verb of the same root, for emphasis.
  • זַרְעֵךְ is a singular collective; the English plural 'they' follows the sense.
  • מֵרֹב: מִן expresses cause, 'from (sheer) abundance'.
  • The speaker is the messenger, but he speaks as the LORD himself: first person 'I will multiply'.

The narrator makes the messenger speak in the LORD's first person; Radak explains this. Radak also reads 'cannot be counted' as hyperbole.

Grammar
  • וְיֹלַדְתְּ is an unusual form, perhaps a blend of perfect and participle; here it is future, 'you will bear'.
  • וְקָרָאת keeps the older ending -ת of the 2fs; it is read as a command, 'you are to call'.
  • הִנָּךְ has the 2fs suffix; the final ךְ is feminine.
  • יִשְׁמָעֵאל, 'God hears', has a silent א in its spelling; Ibn Ezra says the aleph is dropped in pronunciation to ease the tongue.
  • שָׁמַע ... אֶל: the LORD has heard 'to' (that is, regarding) her affliction.

Rashi takes הִנָּךְ הָרָה as 'when you return you will conceive'. The English keeps 'you are pregnant' because 16:4 says Hagar had already conceived and Radak reads it so; Rashi's reading is recorded. The name is explained by the clause 'the LORD has heard', not in the English line.

He will be a wild ass of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he will dwell over against all his kin.

and-he will-be wild-ass-of man hand-his in-the-all and-hand-of all in-him and-upon face-of all brothers-his he-will-dwell

Grammar
  • פֶּרֶא אָדָם is a construct: 'wild ass of man'. Ibn Ezra reports other readings: free among men (Job 39:5), or two items, 'wild ass and man'.
  • יָדוֹ בַכֹּל, 'his hand in everything', is read by Rashi as a robber; יַד כֹּל בּוֹ, 'everyone's hand against him', answers it.
  • עַל־פְּנֵי is 'in the face of, over against'; 25:18 uses נָפַל in the same phrase.
  • The etnaḥta on בּוֹ divides the verse after the double saying about the hand.

'Wild ass of a man' keeps the construct. Rashi and Ibn Ezra differ on 'upon the face of all his brothers': Rashi sees a great offspring; Ibn Ezra identifies the brothers as the sons of Keturah. The English 'over against' is neutral to both.

16:13

She called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are El Roi," for she said, "Have I even here seen, after the one who sees me?"

and-called(f) name-of LORD the-speaking to-her you God-of seeing for said(f) also-here have-I-seen after seeing-me

Grammar
  • אֵל רֳאִי is 'God of seeing': רֳאִי is a noun, and Rashi explains the ḥaṭef qamets as marking a noun.
  • הֲגַם הֲלֹם is a rhetorical question; Rashi: she is amazed to see even here; Ibn Ezra: 'also here'.
  • אַחֲרֵי רֹאִי has a participle with 1cs suffix, 'after my seer', the text's hardest phrase.
  • הַדֹּבֵר אֵלֶיהָ is a participle with the article: 'the one who spoke to her'.

The last clause is obscure. The English 'after the one who sees me' follows the grammar (a participle with suffix). Ibn Ezra reads: have I seen the LORD's angel here after He saw my affliction? Rashi reads: did I see a messenger of God even here after seeing them in Abraham's house? Radak: she saw nothing after he left, so he was an angel.

16:14

Therefore the well is called Beer Lahai Roi; there it is, between Kadesh and Bered.

upon-so he-called to-the-well well-of living seeing-me behold between Kadesh and-between Bered

Grammar
  • עַל־כֵּן, 'therefore', gives the origin of the place name; קָרָא is impersonal, 'one called'.
  • בְּאֵר לַחַי רֹאִי, 'well of the Living One who sees me', is a place name; Ibn Ezra reads לַחַי differently.
  • בֵּין ... וּבֵין is the Hebrew way to say 'between X and Y'.
  • הִנֵּה points to the well as a landmark.

The name is transliterated; its sense, 'Well of the Living One who sees me' (BDB), is given in the glosses. Rashi refers to the Targum, 'the well at which the living angel appeared'; Radak links the name to Hagar's 'You are God of seeing' and to the angel who lives forever. Ibn Ezra reads לַחַי as 'to one who will be alive next year'; recorded.

Grammar

Grammar
  • בֶּן־שְׁמֹנִים שָׁנָה is the Hebrew idiom for age: 'son of eighty years'.
  • בְּלֶדֶת־הָגָר: preposition plus infinitive construct with the subject in the genitive: 'in Hagar's bearing'.
  • The singular שָׁנָה after the tens, and the plural שָׁנִים after the units, is regular.
  • The sign ס after the verse is a paragraph break.

The ס after the verse is a setumah, a closed paragraph break (an open one, petuḥah, is marked פ).

and-was Abram son-of ninety year and-nine years and-appeared the-LORD to-Abram and-said to-him I El Shaddai walk before-me and-be whole

Grammar
  • וַיְהִי with a time clause (בֶּן־תִּשְׁעִים שָׁנָה וְתֵשַׁע שָׁנִים) sets the scene: Abram is ninety-nine, thirteen years after 16:16.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׁנִים closes the age clause; the verse then divides at זָקֵף קָטָן on שַׁדַּי between the self-introduction and the two commands.
  • הִתְהַלֵּךְ is Hithpael imperative: continuous walking to and fro; וֶהְיֵה is a second imperative joined by ו, not a result clause.
  • Rashi and Targum Onkelos take הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי as "serve before me" (פְּלַח קֳדָמַי).

אֵל שַׁדַּי is kept as the name by decision. Rashi derives שַׁדַּי from דַּי "enough" (there is sufficiency in my divinity for every creature); Ibn Ezra takes it as an adjectival title meaning "mighty"; Ramban and Radak derive it from שׁדד "overpower". The English does not choose among these. תמים is rendered "whole" (complete, without lack), which covers Rashi's "whole in all my trials" and Ibn Ezra's "do not ask why circumcision".
