וְלִפְדּוֹתָם בְּמִלְחָמָה מִיַּד חֶרֶב, כְּכָל הַנִּסִּים הַנַּעֲשִׂים לְאַבְרָהָם וְלָאָבוֹת, וּכְכָל הַבָּאִים בַּתּוֹרָה בְּפָרָשַׁת אִם בְּחֻקֹּתַי (ויקרא כו ג-מו) וּבְפָרָשַׁת וְהָיָה כִּי תָבֹא (דברים כח א-סח) בַּבְּרָכוֹת וּבַקְּלָלוֹת, שֶׁכֻּלָּם נִסִּים הֵם, כִּי אֵין מִן הַטֶּבַע שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ הַגְּשָׁמִים בְּעִתָּם בְּעָבְדֵנוּ הָאֱלֹהִים, וְלֹא שֶׁיִּהְיוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם כַּבַּרְזֶל כַּאֲשֶׁר נִזְרַע בַּשָּׁנָה הַשְּׁבִיעִית, וְכֵן כָּל הַיִּעוּדִים שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה, אֲבָל כֻּלָּם נִסִּים, וּבְכֻלָּם תִּתְנַצֵּחַ מַעֲרֶכֶת הַמַּזָּלוֹת, אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם שִׁנּוּי מִמִּנְהָגוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם כַּנִּסִּים הַנַּעֲשִׂים עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ בְּעֶשֶׂר הַמַּכּוֹת וּבִקְרִיעַת הַיָּם וְהַמָּן וְהַבְּאֵר וְזוּלָתָם, שֶׁהֵם מוֹפְתִים מְשַׁנִּים הַטֶּבַע בְּפִרְסוּם, וְהֵם שֶׁיֵּעָשׂוּ בַּשֵּׁם הַמְיֻחָד אֲשֶׁר הִגִּיד לוֹ. וְלָכֵן אָמַר עַתָּה לְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ כִּי הוּא הַתַּקִּיף הַמְּנַצֵּחַ שֶׁיִּגְבַּר עַל מַזָּלוֹ וְיוֹלִיד, וְיִהְיֶה בְּרִית בֵּינוֹ וּבֵין זַרְעוֹ לְעוֹלָם, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה חֵלֶק ה' עַמּוֹ וּבִרְצוֹנוֹ יַנְהִיגֵם, לֹא יִהְיוּ תַּחַת מֶמְשֶׁלֶת כּוֹכָב וּמַזָּל. וְדַע וּרְאֵה כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ לֹא הִזְכִּיר בִּדְבָרָיו שֵׁם יוֹ"ד ה' רַק בְּצֵרוּף הַשֵּׁם הַכָּתוּב בְּאָלֶ"ף דָּלֶ"ת אוֹ בְּצֵרוּף אֵל עֶלְיוֹן עִמּוֹ, וְיַזְכִּיר בְּעִנְיָנָיו "אֱלֹהִים", וְכֵן יֹאמַר "ה' אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם" (בראשית כ"ד:ז'), וְאָמַר "ה' יִרְאֶה" (בראשית כ"ב:י"ד) עַל מְקוֹם הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הֶעָתִיד, וְיַעֲקֹב הִזְכִּיר תָּמִיד "אֵל שַׁדַּי" (להלן מג יד מח ג), וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ לֹא יַזְכִּיר כֵּן לְעוֹלָם. וְאִם תִּזְכֶּה תָּבִין זֶה כֻּלּוֹ מִמָּה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמַסֶּכֶת יְבָמוֹת (יבמות מ"ט), כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים נִסְתַּכְּלוּ בְּאִסְפַּקְלַרְיָא שֶׁאֵינָהּ מְאִירָה, וּלְפִיכָךְ אָמַר יְשַׁעְיָה "וָאֶרְאֶה אֶת ה'" (ישעיהו ו א), וּמֹשֶׁה נִסְתַּכֵּל בְּאִסְפַּקְלַרְיָא הַמְּאִירָה, וּלְפִיכָךְ אָמַר "כִּי לֹא יִרְאַנִי הָאָדָם וָחָי" (שמות לג כ). "וָאֶרְאֶה אֶת ה'" כָּתוּב בְּאָלֶ"ף דָּלֶ"ת. וְעוֹד אַזְכִּיר זֶה בְּפָרָשַׁת וָאֵרָא (שמות ו ב) אִם יִרְאֶה אֱלֹהִים בְּעָנְיִי:
Ramban הִתְהַלֵּ֥ךְ לְפָנַ֖י
Hebrew
לָלֶכֶת בַּדֶּרֶךְ אֲשֶׁר אוֹרֶה אוֹתְךָ, כְּטַעַם "אַחֲרֵי ה' אֱלֹהֵיכֶם תֵּלֵכוּ וְאֹתוֹ תִירָאוּ" (דברים יג ה), כִּי הַמְצַוֶּה לֶאֱחֹז דַּרְכּוֹ קֹדֶם שֶׁיּוֹרֶנּוּ יֹאמַר "הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי", וְהַבָּא אַחֲרֵי הַצַּוָּאָה יֹאמַר "אַחֲרֵי ה' תֵּלֵכוּ". וְהָעִנְיָן בִּשְׁנֵיהֶם לָלֶכֶת אַחֲרֵי הַשֵּׁם לִירֹא מִמֶּנּוּ לְבַדּוֹ וְלַעֲשׂוֹת מַה שֶׁיְּצַוֶּה:
Ramban וֶהְיֵ֥ה תָמִֽים׃
Hebrew
מִצְוָה אַחֶרֶת עוֹד בָּעִנְיָן הַזֶּה, כְּטַעַם "תָּמִים תִּהְיֶה עִם ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ" (דברים יח יג) אַחֲרֵי אַזְהָרַת הַשֵּׁם "לֹא יִמָּצֵא בְךָ קֹסֵם קְסָמִים מְעוֹנֵן וּמְנַחֵשׁ וּמְכַשֵּׁף" וְגוֹ' (שם יח י). וְהָעִנְיָן בִּשְׁנֵיהֶם שֶׁיַּאֲמִין בְּלִבּוֹ כִּי הקב"ה לְבַדּוֹ הוּא בַּעַל הַיְּכֹלֶת בַּתְּחִלָּה וּבַסּוֹף, הוּא הַיָּכוֹל לַעֲשׂוֹת וּלְבַטֵּל, וְלֹא יִשְׁמְעוּ אֶל מְעֹנְנִים וְאֶל קֹסְמִים אוֹ לִמְנַחֵשׁ וּמְכַשֵּׁף, וְלֹא יַאֲמִין שֶׁיָּבֹאוּ דִּבְרֵיהֶם עַל כָּל פָּנִים, אֲבָל יִגְזֹר בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁהַכֹּל בְּיַד עֶלְיוֹן הָעֶלְיוֹנִים, שֶׁהוּא "אֵל" וְהוּא "אֵל שַׁדַּי", עוֹשֶׂה טוֹבָה שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בַּמַּזָּל וּמֵבִיא רָעָה בִּהְיוֹת הַמַּזָּל טוֹב וְיָפֶה, כְּפִי שֶׁיִּתְהַלֵּךְ הָאָדָם לְפָנָיו, "מֵפֵר אֹתוֹת בַּדִּים וְקֹסְמִים יְהוֹלֵל" (ישעיהו מד כה). וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שבת קנו) צֵא מֵאִצְטַגְנִינוּת שֶׁלְּךָ וְכוּ'. וְרַשִׁ"י פֵּרֵשׁ (רש"י על בראשית י"ז:א') "וֶהְיֵה תָמִים", הֱיֵה שָׁלֵם בְּכָל הַנִּסְיוֹנוֹת. וְרַבִּי אַבְרָהָם אָמַר שֶׁלֹּא יִשְׁאַל עַל הַמִּילָה לָמָּה, וְהוּא כְּטַעַם "יְהִי לִבִּי תָמִים בְּחֻקֶּיךָ לְמַעַן לֹא אֵבוֹשׁ" (תהלים קיט פ). וְהַנָּכוֹן מָה שֶׁפֵּרַשְׁתִּי:
Radak וַיְהִ֣י אַבְרָ֔ם בֶּן תִּשְׁעִ֥ים וְתֵ֣שַׁע
Hebrew
אַחַר עוֹד שְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה מִלְּצַוּוֹתוֹ עַל הַמִּילָה, כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּזְקִין יוֹתֵר וְיַגִּיעַ עַד מֵאָה וְיִהְיֶה הַנֵּס יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל שֶׁיּוֹלִיד וְהוּא בֶּן מֵאָה, וּלְהַרְאוֹת אַהֲבַת אַבְרָם לָאֵל לַעֲשׂוֹת כָּל אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֵּהוּ, שֶׁצִּוָּהוּ לָמוּל בְּשַׂר עָרְלָתוֹ וְהוּא זָקֵן בֶּן תִּשְׁעִים וָתֵשַׁע שָׁנָה, וְכֹחוֹ תָּשַׁשׁ, וְצִוָּהוּ לָמוּל קֹדֶם לֵדַת יִצְחָק כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה יִצְחָק מִזֶּרַע כָּשֵׁר יוֹתֵר עַל יְדֵי מִצְוַת הָאֵל שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה בָּאֵבָר הַהוּא וּלְהַגְדִּיל הַפֶּלֶא, כִּי הַמִּילָה מְחַלֶּשֶׁת הָאֵבָר, וְהָיָה נֵס עַל נֵס שֶׁיּוֹלִיד בֶּן מֵאָה, וְעוֹד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אֵבָרוֹ חָלוּשׁ יוֹתֵר מִשֶּׁהָיָה קֹדֶם הַמִּילָה.
Radak אֲנִי אֵ֣ל שַׁדַּ֔י
Hebrew
פֵּרַשׁ: חָזָק, מְנַצֵּחַ, וְכֵן אוֹמֵר ״כְּקוֹל מַיִם רַבִּים כְּקוֹל שַׁדַּי בְּלֶכְתָּם״ (יחזקאל א:כד), ״כְּקוֹל אֵל שַׁדַּי בְּדַבְּרוֹ״ (יחזקאל י:ה). רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר לוֹ: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאִשְׁתְּךָ עֲקָרָה וּזְקֵנָה וְאֵינָהּ רְאוּיָה לֵילֵד, וְאַף כִּי אַתָּה זָקֵן וְחָלוּשׁ כֹּחֲךָ כִּי בֶּן תִּשְׁעִים וְתֵשַׁע אַתָּה, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁתַּחֲלִישׁ כֹּחַ הַזֶּרַע עוֹד, אֲנִי מְנַצֵּחַ הַכֹּל, כִּי אֲנִי־אֵל שַׁדַּי, וְהַטֶּבַע וְהַתּוֹלָדָה מִיָּדִי הוּא וּבְיָדִי לַעֲשׂוֹת וּלְשַׁנּוֹת כַּאֲשֶׁר אֶרְצֶה. וְכֵן אָמַר ״וָאֵרָא אֶל אַבְרָהָם וְגוֹ׳ בְּאֵל שַׁדַּי״ (שמות ו:ג), כִּי שְׁלָשְׁתָּם הָיוּ נְשֵׁיהֶם עֲקָרוֹת וְנִפְקְדוּ בִּרְצוֹן הָאֵל, כִּי שָׁמַע אֵל תְּפִלַּת הַצַּדִּיקִים וְשִׁנָּה טֶבַע נְשֵׁיהֶם וְיָלָדוּ. וְשַׁדַּי שֵׁם תֹּאַר, רָאוּי בְּתַשְׁלוּמוֹ שַׁדְּדַי בְּפַלֵּס ״מוֹכִיחַ אָדָם אַחֲרַי״ (משלי כח:כג).
Radak הִתְהַלֵּ֥ךְ לְפָנַ֖י
Hebrew

Apparatus
  • No variant readings in the pack. MAM writes the divine name with holem (יְהֹוָה); the morphology gives יְהוָה.
17:2

I will set my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly.

and-I-will-set my-covenant between-me and-between-you and-I-will-multiply [obj]-you in-muchness muchness

Grammar
  • Both verbs are cohortatives (אֶתְּנָה, אַרְבֶּה) and express the speaker's resolve.
  • וְאֶתְּנָה follows the two imperatives of verse 1. A ו-cohortative after an imperative often gives the purpose or the consequence ('walk … be whole, and I will set'). Rashi's 'by means of this commandment' reads the covenant as following on the command.
  • בֵּין is repeated before each party: בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ.
  • בִּמְאֹד מְאֹד doubles מְאֹד for the superlative; Radak says the doubling intensifies the increase.

נתן with בְּרִית is rendered "set", the sense "put, establish"; Targum has "I will give my covenant" (אֶתֵּן קְיָמִי).

Commentary (4)
Rashinormativefollows וְאֶתְּנָ֥ה בְרִיתִ֖י
Rashi: a covenant of love and the covenant of the land, to give it to you by means of this commandment. This bears on what the covenant contains, not on the translation of the words.

17:3

Abram fell on his face, and God spoke with him, saying:

and-fell Abram on his-faces and-spoke with-him God to-say

Grammar
  • פָּנִים is a plural noun used of one face; עַל־פָּנָיו 'on his face' is the idiom for prostration.
  • וַיְדַבֵּר is a Piel wayyiqtol. The Piel is the ordinary stem of דבר 'speak'; it does not mark a conversation as opposed to a command.
  • אִתּוֹ is the preposition אֵת 'with' with a suffix, not the object marker.
  • The subject is אֱלֹהִים, though verse 1 names יְהוָה as the one who appeared: the speaker is the same.
  • לֵאמֹר 'saying' is an infinitive construct with ל and introduces direct speech.

Rashi reads the fall as fear of the divine presence; Radak and Sforno as prostration of thanks for the covenant; Ramban as preparing himself for prophecy. The English keeps "fell on his face" without choosing.

Commentary (7)
Rashinormativerecords וַיִּפֹּ֥ל אַבְרָ֖ם עַל פָּנָ֑יו
Rashi: from fear of the divine presence; before he was circumcised he had no strength to stand while the holy spirit stood over him. The English keeps the physical action only.

17:4

As for me, here is my covenant with you: you shall become the father of a multitude of nations.

I behold my-covenant with-you and-you-shall-be to-father-of multitude-of nations

Grammar
  • אֲנִי stands first for emphasis, "as for me", with הִנֵּה calling attention to the covenant.
  • אִתָּךְ ends in pausal -ךְ (qamets under the tav under etnaḥta); this is the masculine pausal form of אִתְּךָ.
  • וְהָיִיתָ is weqatal, continuing the promise: "you shall become".
  • The pairing אַב הֲמוֹן is the explanation of the new name in verse 5.

The morphology table labels the suffix of אִתָּךְ as 2nd person feminine. I keep the data but note it as the pausal masculine form (cf. Genesis 17:4 context, addressee Abram). הֲמוֹן is chosen as "multitude" (sense 3). Ramban: this is the covenant of circumcision, as the text goes on to say.

Apparatus
  • The pack parses אִתָּךְ as 2nd person feminine; kept as data, flagged in the note.
17:5

No longer shall your name be called Abram; your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.

and-not will-be-called still [obj] your-name Abram and-will-be your-name Abraham for father-of multitude-of nations I-have-made-you

Grammar
  • Niphal יִקָּרֵא governs אֶת־שִׁמְךָ: an object marker after a passive, which Radak compares with יֵחָלֵק אֶת־הָאָרֶץ.
  • The explanation of the name is in כִּי אַב־הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם נְתַתִּיךָ; the wordplay is אַבְרָהָם with אַב הֲמוֹן.
  • נְתַתִּיךָ is qatal: God has already established Abraham as father of many nations (Sforno: the name starts today because he is already so).
  • The disjunctive tevir on עוֹד and the etnaḥta on אַבְרָם mark the first clause.

Per the decisions, the meaning of the name goes in the notes and not in the English line. Rashi reads כִּי אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם as a notarikon (abbreviation) of the name אַבְרָהָם: the resh, which belonged to the name when he was father only of Aram, was not removed now that he is father of the whole world. Ibn Ezra explains the resh, which אַב הֲמוֹן does not account for, as coming from אַבִּיר: 'mighty one of a multitude of nations'. He also says the change of name does not take a letter away but only adds one, the he.

Commentary (12)
Rashinormativerecords כִּ֛י אַב הֲמ֥וֹן גּוֹיִ֖ם
Rashi: כִּי אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם is a notarikon of the name אַבְרָהָם. The resh, which belonged to the name when he was father only of Aram, his homeland, was not removed now that he is father of the whole world. Even the yod taken from Sarai's name complained before the Shekhinah until it was added to Joshua's name (Numbers 13:16).
Hebrew

The change does not take a letter away from his name but only adds one. The English line does not render the name; the gloss gives the text's own explanation, and this reading is recorded in the note.

17:6

I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come forth from you.

and-I-will-make-fruitful [obj]-you in-muchness muchness and-I-will-make-you to-nations and-kings from-you will-go-out

Grammar
  • The Hifil of פרה is "make fruitful"; it echoes 1:28 and 9:1.
  • וּנְתַתִּיךָ לְגוֹיִם: נתן with ל "make into", a weqatal continuing the promise.
  • In וּמְלָכִים מִמְּךָ יֵצֵאוּ the plural subject comes first, which gives the kings emphasis.

Rashi: "nations" are Israel and Edom, since Ishmael already existed and was not being announced; Ramban rejects this, since Esau did not keep circumcision, and says Israel alone are called goyim and amim; Radak: Isaac, Ishmael and the sons of Keturah, or Jacob's seed alone. The English keeps "nations".

17:7

I will establish my covenant between me and you and between your offspring after you, throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you.

and-I-will-establish [obj] my-covenant between-me and-between-you and-between your-seed after-you to-their-generations for-covenant-of forever to-be to-you for-God and-to-your-seed after-you

Grammar
  • הֲקִמֹתִי is Hifil of קום: "set up, make stand", the verb for fulfilling an existing covenant.
  • The long string with לִבְרִית עוֹלָם and the infinitive לִהְיוֹת states the content of the covenant; Rashi: and what is the covenant? to be God to you.
  • זֶרַע is a collective singular; לְדֹרֹתָם has a plural suffix for it.
  • The accents (revia on וּבֵינֶךָ, zaqef qaton on לֵאלֹהִים) mark off the parties and then the content of the covenant.

Radak applies the covenant to the seed of Jacob; the English keeps "your offspring after you" for זַרְעֲךָ אַחֲרֶיךָ. Sforno: to bind my name to you without an intermediary.

17:8

I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession, and I will be their God.

and-I-will-give to-you and-to-your-seed after-you [obj] land-of your-sojournings [obj] all-land-of Canaan as-possession-of forever and-I-will-be to-them for-God

Grammar
  • The verse has two objects, each marked by אֵת: אֶרֶץ מְגֻרֶיךָ and כָּל־אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן. The second is in apposition and widens the first. Radak: not only the places where you sojourn but all the land of Canaan.
  • מְגֻרֶיךָ is plural, 'your sojournings': the places where Abraham has lived as a גֵּר, a resident alien.
  • לְךָ carries telisha gedola, a disjunctive accent written on the first letter of the word and repeated here on the stressed syllable. It marks a minor pause, not emphasis. The geresh on אַחֲרֶיךָ, the revia on מְגֻרֶיךָ and the etnaḥta on עוֹלָם divide the recipients, the land and the term.
  • וְהָיִיתִי לָהֶם לֵאלֹהִים repeats the formula of verse 7 (לִהְיוֹת לְךָ לֵאלֹהִים), now with the plural 'to them'.

Rashi: there I will be your God; one who lives outside the land is like one who has no God (a homily). Radak: even if they go into exile, the possession is everlasting and they will return. Sforno: so that you can do my will in it.

17:9

God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you, throughout their generations."

and-said God to-Abraham and-you ACC-covenant-my you-shall-keep you and-seed-your after-you to-generations-their

Grammar
  • The fronted pronoun וְאַתָּה before the verb is contrastive: 'and you, for your part'.
  • The yiqtol תִשְׁמֹר carries the force of a command or obligation.
  • The etnaḥta on תִשְׁמֹר divides the verse; the second half names the persons bound.
  • The plural suffix on לְדֹרֹתָם looks back to the singular collective זַרְעֲךָ.

The English follows Rashi, who takes the waw as joining a new clause to the earlier promise: 'I, behold, my covenant is with you; and you, keep it'.

Rashinormativefollows וְאַתָּ֖ה

כָּתַב רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ז:ט') ו' מוֹסִיף עַל עִנְיָן רִאשׁוֹן, אֲנִי הִנֵּה בְּרִיתִי אִתָּךְ, וְאַתָּה הֱוֵי זָהִיר לְשָׁמְרוֹ, וּמַה שְׁמִירָתוֹ, "זֹאת בְּרִיתִי אֲשֶׁר תִּשְׁמְרוּ" אַתֶּם שֶׁל עַכְשָׁו, "וּבֵין זַרְעֲךָ אַחֲרֶיךָ", הָעֲתִידִים לְהִוָּלֵד. וְצָדַק הָרַב בִּפְשׁוּטוֹ. וְאָמְרוּ (הרד"ק) בְּטַעַם הַמִּילָה, שֶׁשָּׂם זִכָּרוֹן בְּאֵבֶר הַתַּאֲוָה רַב הַמְּהוּמָה וְהַחֵטְא, לְבַל יִשְׁתַּמְּשׁוּ בּוֹ רַק בַּמְּצֻוֶּה וּבַמֻּתָּר. וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ הָאֱמֶת טַעַם "הִנֵּה בְרִיתִי אִתָּךְ" כְּטַעַם "הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי עִמָּךְ" (בראשית כ"ח:ט"ו), "וַיֹּאמֶר כִּי אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ" (שמות ג יב), "יְהִי ה' אֱלֹהֵינוּ עִמָּנוּ" (מלכים א ח נז), יֹאמַר כִּי הַבְּרִית יִהְיֶה עִמּוֹ וְלָכֵן יִפְרֶה וְיִרְבֶּה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ צִוָּה שֶׁיִּשְׁמֹר אַבְרָהָם הַבְּרִית הַזֹּאת, וְתִהְיֶה הַמִּילָה לְאוֹת בְּרִית. וְהִנֵּה הָאוֹת הַזֶּה אוֹת כַּשַּׁבָּת, וְלָכֵן יִדְחֶה אוֹתוֹ. וְהָבֵן זֶה (עי' זהר לך לך פט):

17:10

This is my covenant, which you shall keep between me and you and between your offspring after you: every male among you is to be circumcised.

this covenant-my which you-shall-keep between-me and-between-you and-between seed-your after-you to-be-circumcised to-you all male

Grammar
  • The infinitive absolute הִמּוֹל stands for an injunction, 'every male is to be circumcised'; Rashi and Ibn Ezra equate it with לְהִמּוֹל.
  • בֵּין is repeated before each term: 'between me and between you and between your offspring'.
  • The plural תִּשְׁמְרוּ addresses Abraham together with his descendants, after the singular of v. 9.
  • The gershayim on בְּרִיתִי and the etnaḥta on אַחֲרֶיךָ set the covenant and its parties apart from the command.

The English renders the infinitive absolute as a passive command. The pack parses it as nifal; Radak agrees, and Rashi and Ibn Ezra's equation with the infinitive construct supports the English.

17:11

You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of covenant between me and you.

and-you-shall-circumcise ACC flesh-of foreskin-your and-shall-be for-sign-of covenant between-me and-between-you

Grammar
  • וּנְמַלְתֶּם is a weqatal with imperative force, 'you shall circumcise'.
  • בְּשַׂר עָרְלַתְכֶם is a construct chain: 'the flesh of your foreskin'.
  • The zaqef gadol on וּנְמַלְתֶּם and the etnaḥta on עָרְלַתְכֶם close the command; the sign clause follows.
  • לְאוֹת בְּרִית 'for a sign of covenant' is a construct pair; the sign is the act itself.

Rashi: וּנְמַלְתֶּם is like וּמַלְתֶּם, the nun being a radical that drops at times, as in וּנְשָׂאתֶם. Ibn Ezra: like וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם, the nun a root letter. Both read it as active, 'you shall circumcise', though the pack parses it Niphal; the English follows them. The pack's entry נָמַל lists only Hithpo 'be cut off', which does not fit here, so the token has no sense.

17:12

At eight days old every male among you is to be circumcised, throughout your generations: the one born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring.

and-son-of eight-of days shall-be-circumcised to-you all male to-generations-your born-of house and-purchase-of silver from-all son-of foreign which not from-seed-your he

Grammar
  • וּבֶן־שְׁמֹנַת יָמִים is an age idiom, 'a son of eight days'; the yiqtol יִמּוֹל follows it with passive sense, 'shall be circumcised'.
  • The etnaḥta on לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם ends the general rule; the next clause names two classes of slaves, each a construct phrase.
  • יְלִיד בָּיִת and מִקְנַת כֶּסֶף are both constructs: 'one born of the house', 'a purchase of silver'.
  • The relative clause אֲשֶׁר לֹא מִזַּרְעֲךָ הוּא qualifies the foreigner: not of Abraham's line.

The English follows Rashi on both slave classes: born in the house to a maidservant, and bought at birth. Ibn Ezra reads the two clauses as covering everyone in Abraham's household, and the English is compatible. The fuller rabbinic reading of the repetition in v. 13 is recorded there.

17:13

The one born in your house and the one bought with your money must be circumcised, and my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant.

to-be-circumcised shall-be-circumcised born-of house-your and-purchase-of silver-your and-shall-be covenant-my in-flesh-your for-covenant-of everlasting

Grammar
  • הִמּוֹל יִמּוֹל is the infinitive absolute before the finite verb of the same root: it stresses the duty ('must be circumcised').
  • The verb stands first and the subject follows: 'must be circumcised, the one born ...'.
  • וְהָיְתָה is feminine because its subject בְּרִיתִי is feminine; the weqatal carries on from the command.
  • In לִבְרִית עוֹלָם the preposition לְ marks what the covenant becomes, 'as an everlasting covenant'; בְּרִית עוֹלָם is a construct pair, 'a covenant of perpetuity'.

The English follows Rashi's view that the doubling is deliberate: it includes a house-born slave circumcised later than the eighth day. This bears on the sense of the doubled form, which the English renders by 'must'.

17:14 · ס

Any uncircumcised male who does not circumcise the flesh of his foreskin, that person shall be cut off from his kin; he has broken my covenant.

and-uncircumcised male which not he-circumcises ACC flesh-of foreskin-his and-shall-be-cut-off the-person the-that from-peoples-her ACC covenant-my he-broke

Grammar
  • וְעָרֵל זָכָר is a casus pendens: 'and as for an uncircumcised male ...', picked up by הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא.
  • נִכְרְתָה is a weqatal Niphal (passive of 'cut off'), feminine because נֶפֶשׁ is feminine.
  • The fronted object אֶת־בְּרִיתִי before הֵפַר emphasizes what is broken.
  • The suffix of מֵעַמֶּיהָ is feminine singular agreeing with נֶפֶשׁ, and עַמִּים is plural: 'from her peoples'.

Rashi limits the punishment to the man who reaches the age of liability; Ibn Ezra says a boy who was not circumcised by his father must circumcise himself once he is of age, and the penalty of kareth is in God's hands. The English leaves 'cut off' unexplained and does not specify the penalty, which the commentators dispute.

הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי וּמֵת קֹדֶם זְמַנּוֹ (שבת כ"ד):

Ibn Ezra: יִמּוֹל is of the pattern יִפְעֹל, like יִדֹּר נֶדֶר (Num 30:3), from וּנְמַלְתֶּם: if he is of age and does not circumcise himself, he is liable to kareth at the hands of heaven, since a small boy's duty rests on the father. Those who think an uncircumcised child has no share in the world to come are wrong: נֶפֶשׁ means 'person', a body with a soul. Kareth is either death before fifty-two or the cutting off of his name at the death of his seed, hence 'from his kin'.

Apparatus
  • Variants: none noted in the pack.
17:15

God said to Abraham, "Sarai your wife: do not call her name Sarai, for Sarah is her name."

and-said God to-Abraham Sarai wife-of-you not you-call [object-marker] name-of-her Sarai for Sarah name-of-her

Grammar
  • שָׂרַי אִשְׁתְּךָ is a nominative absolute (casus pendens): the topic is named first and then taken up by the pronoun in אֶת־שְׁמָהּ.
  • לֹא־תִקְרָא with the imperfect is a prohibition ('you are not to call'), not a prediction.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׂרָי divides the verse: the prohibition, then the reason.
  • כִּי שָׂרָה שְׁמָהּ has no verb; the English supplies 'is'. Radak reads it as 'shall be her name', as in 17:5 וְהָיָה שִׁמְךָ אַבְרָהָם.
  • The change שָׂרַי to שָׂרָה echoes 17:5, where אַבְרָם becomes אַבְרָהָם.

The meaning of the new name is not given in the English line (decisions.md). Both names are rendered by transliteration, in the usual forms Sarai and Sarah. Radak notes that the husband, not the wife, is the one who 'calls' her name, which is why the order is addressed to Abraham alone.

כִּי הָאִישׁ הוּא הַקּוֹרֵא לְאִשְׁתּוֹ בִּשְׁמָהּ וְלֹא הָאִשָּׁה לְאִישָׁהּ, אֶלָּא דֶּרֶךְ כָּבוֹד בִּלְשׁוֹן אַדְנוּת קוֹרֵאת לוֹ לֹא בִּשְׁמוֹ, כִּי כָּל מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ מַעֲלָה עַל אַחֵר אֵין רָאוּי לַאֲשֶׁר לְמַטָּה הֵימֶנּוּ לִקְרֹא בִּשְׁמוֹ, כְּמוֹ אָבִיו אוֹ רַבּוֹ אוֹ אֲדֹנָיו. וְכֵן אָמַר עַל יָרָבְעָם ״זֶה הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר הֵרִים יָד בַּמֶּלֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹה אֲשֶׁר בָּנָה אֶת הַמִּלּוֹא״ (מלכים א יא:כז), קָרָא אוֹתוֹ מוֹרֵד בַּמֶּלֶךְ לְפִי שֶׁקָּרָא שְׁלֹמֹה בִּשְׁמוֹ, וְאָמַר ״שְׁלֹמֹה בָּנָה״ וְלֹא אָמַר ״אֲדֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ״. וְכֵן אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סנהדרין קט) הַקּוֹרֵא לְרַבּוֹ בִּשְׁמוֹ גּוֹרֵם לַשְּׁכִינָה שֶׁתִּסְתַּלֵּק מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל. וְכֵן הָאִשָּׁה לְבַעְלָהּ כִּי אֲדֹנֶיהָ הוּא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״וְהוּא יִמְשָׁל בָּךְ״ (בראשית ג:טז), וְכֵן אָמְרָה שָׂרָה ״וַאדֹנִי זָקֵן״ (בראשית ח:יב) וְלֹא אָמְרָה ״וְאַבְרָהָם זָקֵן״, וְאַבְרָהָם אָמַר ״וְאִם שָׂרָה״ (בראשית יז:יז). וְכֵן אָמַר הַכָּתוּב דֶּרֶךְ סִפּוּר (שופטים יט:כו) ״פֶּתַח בֵּית הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר אֲדֹנֶיהָ שָׁם״, לְפִיכָךְ אָמַר לְאַבְרָהָם לֹא תִקְרָא אֶת שְׁמָהּ שָׂרָי וְלֹא אָמַר כֵּן לְשָׂרָה עַל אַבְרָהָם, אֶלָּא אָמַר ״וְלֹא יִקָּרֵא״, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר בְּפִי הָאֲנָשִׁים הַקּוֹרְאִים בִּשְׁמוֹ. וְאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (ברכות יג) כִּי הַקּוֹרֵא לְשָׂרָה שָׂרַי אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר בְּלָאו וַעֲשֵׂה, כִּי אַבְרָהָם הוּא שֶׁנִּצְטַוָּה עָלֶיהָ וְלֹא אַחֵר, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר

וַאֲמַר יְיָ לְאַבְרָהָם שָׂרַי אִתְּתָךְ לָא תִקְרֵי יָת שְׁמַהּ שָׂרָי אֲרֵי שָׂרָה שְׁמַהּ:
17:16

I will bless her, and I will also give you a son from her. I will bless her, and she shall become nations; kings of peoples shall come from her.

and-I-will-bless [object-marker]-her and-also I-gave from-her to-you son and-I-will-bless-her and-she-will-be to-nations kings-of peoples from-her they-will-be

Grammar
  • וּבֵרַכְתִּי and וְהָיְתָה are weqatal forms: they continue the promise as future.
  • נָתַתִּי is a perfect that stands for the future (Ibn Ezra), a prophetic perfect, like נָתַתִּי כֶּסֶף הַשָּׂדֶה in 23:13.
  • The etnaḥta on בֵּן separates the gift of the son from the second blessing.
  • The pashta on וּבֵרַכְתִּיהָ is written twice because pashta is postpositive: the second sign stands on the last letter, and the first marks the stressed syllable (-תִּי-), which is not final.
  • מַלְכֵי עַמִּים: 'kings of peoples' is a construct chain. It comes first in its clause, before מִמֶּנָּה and the verb יִהְיוּ, so the kings are put forward.

וּבֵרַכְתִּי אֹתָהּ and וּבֵרַכְתִּיהָ are the same verb twice. Rashi gives each blessing a content (restored youth; milk for the nursing at Isaac's feast); Sforno reads the second as childbearing and rearing without pain. These readings are kept in the commentary entries and not added to the English. מִמֶּנָּה, 'from her', is kept as in the Hebrew.

Commentary (10)
Rashinormativerecords וּבֵרַכְתִּ֣י אֹתָ֔הּ
Rashi: the first blessing is that she was restored to her youth (Gen 18:12 'I have had pleasure'). Kept as an interpretation; the English says only 'bless'.
Hebrew
וּמַה הִיא הַבְּרָכָה? שֶׁחָזְרָה לְנַעֲרוּתָהּ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר הָיְתָה לִּי עֶדְנָה (בר' י"ח):
Rashinormativerecords וּבֵֽרַכְתִּ֙יהָ֙

בַּהֵרָיוֹן וּבַלֵּידָה וּבְגִדּוּל הַבֵּן שֶׁלֹּא בְּצַעַר, הֵפֶךְ קִלְלַת חַוָּה בְּאָמְרוֹ "בְּעֶצֶב תֵּלְדִי בָּנִים" (בראשית ג:טז). וְאָמַר שֶׁשָּׂרָה תַּהַר, תּוֹלִיד וּתְגַדֵּל אֶת בְּנָהּ שֶׁלֹּא בְּצַעַר, כְּאָמְרָם "אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם" (ישעיהו כט:כב) שֶׁפְּדָאוֹ מִצַּעַר גִּדּוּל בָּנִים.
17:17

Abraham fell on his face and laughed, and said in his heart, "Will a child be born to a man a hundred years old? And will Sarah, a woman of ninety years, bear a child?"

and-fell Abraham on face-of-him and-laughed and-said in-heart-of-him [question]-to-son-of hundred year will-be-born and-if Sarah [question]-daughter-of ninety year will-bear

Grammar
  • וַיִּצְחָק, 'and he laughed', uses the root of the name יִצְחָק (17:19) before the name is given.
  • הַלְּבֶן and הֲבַת open the questions with the interrogative ה; the second question continues with וְאִם ('and if / or').
  • The etnaḥta on וַיִּצְחָק separates the act from what he said in his heart.
  • יִוָּלֵד is Niphal ('be born') and תֵּלֵד is Qal ('bear'): the verbs are chosen to fit the subject.

Whether וַיִּצְחָק is laughter of joy or of mockery is the ambiguity of the verse. Rashi (and Onkelos וַחֲדִי, Radak, Ramban) take Abraham's laughter as joy, in contrast to Sarah's laughter in 18:12 as scorn; the English keeps the plain word 'laughed' and the reading goes in the commentary. The questions express wonder, not doubt: Rashi reads the first as a question that affirms (has such kindness been done for anyone else?), and Ibn Ezra as amazement. בֶּן מֵאָה שָׁנָה, 'a son of a hundred years', is the idiom for a man a hundred years old and is rendered 'a man a hundred years old'; the subject of יִוָּלֵד, 'a child', and the object of תֵּלֵד are not in the Hebrew and are supplied by the English.

Commentary (13)
Rashinormativefollows וַיִּפֹּ֧ל אַבְרָהָ֛ם עַל פָּנָ֖יו וַיִּצְחָ֑ק
Rashi: וַיִּצְחָק is the laughter of joy (Aramaic חֲדִי), unlike Sarah's laughter of mockery; Abraham believed and rejoiced, Sarah did not believe.
Hebrew
זֶה תִּ"אֻ, לְשׁוֹן שִׂמְחָה, וַחֲדִי, וְשֶׁל שָׂרָה לְשׁוֹן מָחוֹךְ; לָמַדְתָּ שֶׁאַבְרָהָם הֶאֱמִין וְשָׂמַח וְשָׂרָה לֹא הֶאֱמִינָה וְלִגְלְגָה, וְזֶהוּ שֶׁהִקְפִּיד הַקָּבָּ"ה עַל שָׂרָה וְלֹא הִקְפִּיד עַל אַבְרָהָם:
Rashinormativefollows הַלְּבֶ֤ן
Rashi: some questions are affirmations (תְּמִיהוֹת שֶׁהֵן קַיָּמוֹת), as הֲנִגְלֹה נִגְלֵיתִי (1 Sam 2:27) and הֲרֹאֶה אַתָּה (Ezek 8:6), and this is one: Abraham said in his heart, 'Has such kindness been done for anyone else, as the Holy One does for me?'
Hebrew
יֵשׁ תְּמִיהוֹת שֶׁהֵן קַיָּמוֹת, כְּמוֹ הֲנִגְלֹה נִגְלֵיתִי? (שמואל א ב'), הֲרֹאֶה אַתָּה (יח' ח'), אַף זוֹ הִיא קַיֶּמֶת; וְכָךְ אָמַר בְּלִבּוֹ, הֲנַעֲשָׂה חֶסֶד זֶה לְאַחֵר, מַה שֶּׁהַקָּבָּ"ה עוֹשֶׂה לִי?
Rashinormativefollows וְאִ֨ם שָׂרָ֔ה הֲבַת תִּשְׁעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה
Rashi paraphrases the question: 'is Sarah, at ninety, fit to bear?' Although the early generations begot at five hundred, by Abraham's time lifespans had shrunk and weakness had come into the world, as the ten generations from Noah to Abraham, who had children at sixty and seventy, show.
Hebrew
הָיְתָה כְדַאי לֵילֵד; וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁדּוֹרוֹת הָרִאשׁוֹנִים הָיוּ מוֹלִידִין בְּנֵי ת"ק שָׁנָה, בִּימֵי אַבְרָהָם נִתְמָעֲטוּ הַשָּׁנִים כְּבָר וּבָא תַּשּׁוּת כֹּחַ לָעוֹלָם, צֵא וּלְמַד מֵעֲשָׂרָה דּוֹרוֹת שֶׁמִּנֹּחַ וְעַד אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁמִּהֲרוּ תּוֹלְדוֹתֵיהֶן בְּנֵי ס' וּבְנֵי ע':
Ibn Ezranormativefollows הַלְּבֶ֤ן מֵאָֽה שָׁנָה֙ יִוָּלֵ֔ד
Ibn Ezra: Abraham marvels; the seed of an old man is cold, and the greater wonder is that a woman whose blood had stopped should bear.

תמה בעבור היות זרע הזקן קר על כן לא יוליד והתימא הגדול איך תלד אשה שנפסק דמה. והבן מהדם יבנה ויכונן וכאשר תסתכל ותרא כי דבר שרה נפלא מדבר אברהם כי הנה מצאנו אבות שכל אחד הוליד בן, והוא גדול יותר מתשעים שנה וחיי הדורות בימי אברהם ארוכים מחיי דור ודור וכאשר נסתלק המלאך מיד מל בנו וכל ילידי ביתו ומקנת כספו:

Apparatus

17:18

Abraham said to God, "If only Ishmael might live before you!"

and-said Abraham to the-God if-only Ishmael he-will-live before-you

Grammar
  • לוּ introduces a wish ('if only'), here with the imperfect יִחְיֶה.
  • The etnaḥta on הָאֱלֹהִים separates the speech from the introduction.
  • לְפָנֶיךָ is 'before you', the idiom of being in God's presence.

Rashi reads לוּ as 'would that' and takes it to mean that Abraham is unworthy of so great a reward. Ramban: לוּ is like אִם and Abraham fears that Ishmael may die. The English takes the wish plainly. Rashi's 'live in fear of you' is kept as a reading of לְפָנֶיךָ.

Commentary (6)
Rashinormativefollows ל֥וּ יִשְׁמָעֵ֖אל יִחְיֶ֥ה
Rashi: הַלְוַאי, 'would that Ishmael live'; Abraham says he is not worthy of such a great reward.

Rashinormativerecords יִחְיֶ֥ה לְפָנֶֽיךָ׃
Rashi: 'live before you' means live in fear of you, like הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי 'serve before me' (17:1). Ramban rejects this because God replies 'I have heard you' for Ishmael.

Grammar
  • אֲבָל here is 'truly' (Rashi), not 'but' (the Ramban reading: 'only').
  • יֹלֶדֶת is a participle: the future birth is spoken of as imminent.
  • וְקָרָאתָ is a weqatal in command sense: 'you shall call'.
  • וַהֲקִמֹתִי is the Hiphil of קוּם, 'cause to stand', used for confirming a covenant.
  • The word play: Isaac יִצְחָק is from צָחַק (17:17).

אֲבָל: Rashi 'truth of words', with 42:21 and 2 Kings 4:14; Ramban reads it as 'only'. The English follows Rashi with 'truly'; the 'only' reading is in apparatus. The covenant is established 'with him' and not 'with others' (Rashi), so that Ishmael is excluded from it.

Apparatus
  • אֲבָל: Ramban and Radak read 'but, only', not 'truly'.
17:20

As for Ishmael, I have heard you. Look, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and will increase him exceedingly. He will father twelve chieftains, and I will make him a great nation.

and-for-Ishmael I-have-heard-you behold I-have-blessed [object-marker]-him and-I-will-make-fruitful [object-marker]-him and-I-will-multiply [object-marker]-him in-very very twelve chiefs he-will-beget and-I-will-give-him to-nation great

Grammar
  • הִנֵּה is 'look', calling attention to what is already done: בֵּרַכְתִּי is a perfect.
  • The following weqatal verbs (וְהִפְרֵיתִי, וְהִרְבֵּיתִי) are future.
  • בִּמְאֹד מְאֹד is a doubled adverb for the superlative.
  • שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂר נְשִׂיאִם: the number precedes the noun. Rashi plays on נְשִׂיאִים 'clouds' (Prov 25:14) to say these princes will pass away like clouds; the plain sense 'princes, chieftains' stands.
  • The zinor on וּלְיִשְׁמָעֵאל and the segolta, written twice, on שְׁמַעְתִּיךָ set off 'As for Ishmael, I have heard you' as the first division of the verse's first half.

וּלְיִשְׁמָעֵאל שְׁמַעְתִּיךָ plays on the name יִשְׁמָעֵאל ('God hears'); the English cannot, so the point goes here. The verb שָׁמַע is Qal here, and the entry lists no Qal sense, so I give no sense for it. In the Hebrew שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר is a single number; the tokens for 'two' and 'ten' are combined in 'twelve'. נְשִׂיאִם is 'chieftains'; Rashi, citing נְשִׂיאִים וְרוּחַ (Prov 25:14), adds that these princes will pass away like clouds, a play on the word that leaves its sense in place.

Commentary (5)
Rashinormativenot-applicable שְׁנֵים עָשָׂ֤ר נְשִׂיאִם֙
Rashi: the twelve princes 'will pass away like clouds' (כַּעֲנָנִים יִכְלוּ), playing on נְשִׂיאִים 'clouds' in נְשִׂיאִים וְרוּחַ (Prov 25:14). He does not deny that they are princes; the comment is on their impermanence, a homily that leaves the plain sense 'chieftains' in place.

Grammar
  • The object וְאֶת־בְּרִיתִי is put first for contrast with Ishmael (17:20): 'but my covenant ... with Isaac'.
  • אֲשֶׁר is the relative 'whom', the object of תֵּלֵד.
  • לַמּוֹעֵד הַזֶּה, 'at this appointed time', means the same season a year on.
  • הָאַחֶרֶת is 'the other' and so 'the next'.

Radak: the time between prophecy and birth was a year; he does not say when the pregnancy began. The first word is וְ 'and', rendered 'but' because of the contrast. אֵת at 17:21.4 is a preposition (with), at 17:21.1 the object marker.

When he had finished speaking with him, God went up from Abraham.

Grammar
  • וַיְכַל לְדַבֵּר is 'he finished speaking'; the subject is God, from the previous verse.
  • וַיַּעַל is 'went up' and מֵעַל is 'from upon': the verb pictures God leaving Abraham's side.
  • The etnaḥta on אִתּוֹ separates the end of the speech from the departure.

The subject of וַיְכַל is God, 'he' in the English. Rashi calls מֵעַל אַבְרָהָם a respectful expression toward the Divine Presence, and from 'from upon' (מֵעַל) the Midrash learns that the righteous are God's chariot; Ramban cites the same. The English renders מֵעַל as 'from'.

Grammar
  • וַיִּקַּח, וַיָּמׇל are wayyiqtol forms: they carry the narrative forward.
  • בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה: עֶצֶם 'bone, substance' is used for 'the very' (same) day.
  • The zaqef gadol after זָכָר sets 'every male' apart as a summary of the groups just listed, closed by the etnaḥta on אַבְרָהָם.
  • כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר links the act to the command of 17:10-14: the obedience is exact.

The Piel perfect דִּבֶּר after a narrative verb is rendered as a past perfect in English ('had spoken'). עֶצֶם is rendered 'very' following Rashi's sense of the same day, not a later one. Parse note: lemma מוּל; the pack lists root מול and no Qal sense number is separate from 'Qal'.

Commentary (8)
Rashinormativefollows בְּעֶ֙צֶם֙ הַיּ֣וֹם
Rashi: בּוֹ בַּיּוֹם שֶׁנִּצְטַוָּה, on the very day he was commanded; by day and not by night. He feared neither the gentiles nor the scoffers, and he did it openly so that his enemies and his generation could not say 'had we seen him, we would not have let him circumcise and keep the command of the Omnipresent'. The English 'on that very day' follows.

Apparatus
  • Onkelos renders מִקְנַת כַּסְפּוֹ as זְבִינֵי כַסְפֵּיהּ, 'those bought of his silver', as the English does.
17:24

Now Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised, in the flesh of his foreskin.

and-Abraham son-of ninety and-nine year in-being-circumcised-he flesh-of his-foreskin

Grammar
  • בֶּן־תִּשְׁעִים וָתֵשַׁע שָׁנָה: age is given as 'son of ninety and nine year'.
  • בְּהִמֹּלוֹ is the Nifal infinitive construct with בְּ and a suffix: 'when he was circumcised'.
  • The Nifal is followed by בְּשַׂר עׇרְלָתוֹ, a noun phrase that functions as an adverbial accusative: 'as to the flesh of his foreskin'.
  • The etnaḥta on שָׁנָה separates the age from the circumstance.

The noun phrase after the Nifal is awkward; Radak explains it as an accusative of respect (like קְרוּעֵי בְגָדִים). The English keeps it as 'in the flesh of his foreskin'.

Hebrew
וְאַבְרָהָם בַּר תִּשְׁעִין וּתְשַׁע שְׁנִין כַּד גְּזַר בִּשְׂרָא דְעָרְלְתֵיהּ:
17:25

And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.

and-Ishmael his-son son-of three ten year in-being-circumcised-he [obj] flesh-of his-foreskin

Grammar
  • בֶּן־שְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה: thirteen is 'three ten', both feminine to match שָׁנָה.
  • The same phrase as 17:24 recurs, but with אֵת before בְּשַׂר: a deliberate difference.
  • אֵת after the Nifal בְּהִמֹּלוֹ: the particle can stand before the noun with a passive verb (21:5 בְּהִוָּלֶד לוֹ אֵת יִצְחָק); Radak reads it here as 'from' (like מִן): circumcised from the flesh of his foreskin.
  • The zaqef qaton on בְּהִמֹּלוֹ and tipḥa on אֵת set the object apart.

The English renders אֵת with 'in', as part of 'circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin', the same English as 17:24. Radak reads אֵת as 'from' (like מִן): 'circumcised from the flesh of his foreskin'. Rashi (from Bereshit Rabbah) explains why the particle is written here and not in 17:24: Ishmael needed uncovering (פְּרִיעָה) as well as cutting. The English is consistent with both and keeps them in the commentary.

Commentary (4)
Rashinormativerecords בְּהִ֨מֹּל֔וֹ אֵ֖ת בְּשַׂ֥ר עׇרְלָתֽוֹ׃
Rashi (from Bereshit Rabbah): of Abraham 'et' is not said because he lacked only cutting of flesh, already pressed by use; Ishmael, a child, needed cutting and uncovering (פְּרִיעָה), hence אֵת. A homiletic reading of the particle; not adopted for the English.

וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרֵיהּ בַּר תְּלָת עַשְׂרֵי שְׁנִין כַּד גְּזַר יָת בִּשְׂרָא דְעָרְלְתֵיהּ:
Apparatus
  • Radak 17:25:1 notes that Ishmael's age is derived from Abraham being eighty-six at his birth, and that thirteen is the age of obligation.
17:26

On that very day Abraham was circumcised, and Ishmael his son.

in-bone-of the-day the-this was-circumcised Abraham and-Ishmael his-son

Grammar
  • The adverbial phrase opens the verse, which gives it emphasis.
  • נִמּוֹל is parsed in the pack as the Nifal perfect of מוּל; Ibn Ezra and Radak (17:27) take it from a root נמל, with the root's first נ assimilated into the מ (hence the dagesh). It is singular and agrees with the first subject only.
  • The pashta is written on the last letter of its word; עֶצֶם is stressed on the first syllable, so the pashta is repeated there to mark the stress.
  • The etnaḥta falls on אַבְרָהָם, dividing the two subjects.

The verb is singular and the second subject follows after the etnaḥta as an addition, so 'and Ishmael his son' is joined to it by a comma.

Commentary (7)
Rashinormativefollows בְּעֶ֙צֶם֙ הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה
Rashi: בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה is the day on which Abraham completed (שֶׁמָּלְאוּ) ninety-nine years and Ishmael thirteen: the circumcision fell on the day they reached the ages just stated. The English 'on that very day' stands with this reading.

כָּתַב רַשִׁ"י (רש"י על בראשית י"ז:כ"ו) בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, שֶׁמָּלְאוּ לְאַבְרָהָם צ"ט שָׁנָה וּלְיִשְׁמָעֵאל י"ג, נִמּוֹלוּ. וּמָה טַעַם לְהַזְכִּיר זֶה, וְעוֹד שֶׁכְּבָר הִסְכִּימוּ (ר"ה י) לְדִבְרֵי רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר שֶׁבְּתִשְׁרֵי נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם וּבְתִשְׁרֵי נוֹלְדוּ אָבוֹת וּבְפֶסַח נוֹלַד יִצְחָק, וְהַכָּתוּב אָמַר "לַמּוֹעֵד הַזֶּה בַּשָּׁנָה הָאַחֶרֶת", וְהוּא כָּתַב בְּסֵדֶר וַיֵּרָא (יח י) כִּי הַבְּשׂוֹרָה הָיְתָה בְּפֶסַח וְלַפֶּסַח הַבָּא נוֹלַד יִצְחָק. אֲבָל "בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה", שֶׁנִּצְטַוָּה בַּמִּצְוָה הַזֹּאת נִמּוֹל הוּא וִילִידֵי בֵיתוֹ שְׁמֹנָה עָשָׂר וּשְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וְכָל מִקְנַת כַּסְפּוֹ. סִפֵּר הַכָּתוּב מַעֲלָתוֹ בְּיִרְאַת ה' וּמַעֲלַת כָּל בְּנֵי בֵּיתוֹ, שֶׁכֻּלָּם זְרִיזִים מַקְדִּימִין לְמִצְוֹת. וְאֵין טַעַם "נִמּוֹל אַבְרָהָם", שֶׁנִּמּוֹל הוּא בַּתְּחִלָּה, אֲבָל יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ נִמּוֹל מִתְּחִלָּה, וְכָל בְּנֵי בֵּיתוֹ, כִּי כֵן כָּתוּב (בראשית י"ז:כ"ג) "וַיִּקַּח אַבְרָהָם אֶת יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ וְאֵת כָּל יְלִידֵי בֵּיתוֹ" וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן "וְאַבְרָהָם בֶּן תִּשְׁעִים וָתֵשַׁע שָׁנָה בְּהִמֹּלוֹ", וְהַטַּעַם כִּי אַבְרָהָם נִזְדָּרֵז בְּמִצְוַת הַמִּילָה שֶׁלָּהֶם תְּחִלָּה וּמָל אוֹתָם הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ, אוֹ שֶׁזִּמֵּן לָהֶם מוֹהֲלִים הַרְבֵּה וְהוּא עוֹמֵד עֲלֵיהֶם, וְאַחַר כָּךְ מָל אֶת עַצְמוֹ, שֶׁאִלּוּ הִקְדִּים מִילָתוֹ הָיָה חוֹלֶה אוֹ מְסֻכָּן בָּהּ מִפְּנֵי זִקְנָתוֹ וְלֹא הָיָה יָכוֹל לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּמִילָתָם:

Apparatus
  • Ramban 17:26:1 disputes Rashi's note on the ages and says the verse tells the zeal of Abraham and his household.
17:27 · פ

And all the men of his household, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.

and-all men-of his-house born-of house and-purchase-of silver from-with son-of foreign were-circumcised with-him

Grammar
  • The subject is long and the verb stands last: נִמֹּלוּ אִתּוֹ closes the sentence and the paragraph.
  • יְלִיד בָּיִת and מִקְנַת כֶּסֶף are two appositional classes of household members.
  • מֵאֵת is a compound preposition, 'from with', that is 'from the possession of'.
  • The verb is plural, in agreement with the collective subject.

The English line adds commas to keep the two classes apart; the Hebrew has only the conjunction וּ on the second class.

Commentary (3)
Ibn Ezranormativefollows נִמֹּ֖לוּ אִתּֽוֹ׃
Ibn Ezra: נִמֹּלוּ is Nifal from the root נמל (like וְנִשְׁלוֹחַ סְפָרִים, Esther 3:13). The pack gives the root as מול; the data is kept, and the English reads the form as a passive.

Radakrecords נִמֹּ֖לוּ אִתּֽוֹ׃
Radak: נִמֹּלוּ אִתּוֹ means they were circumcised by Abraham's hand (עַל יַד אַבְרָהָם); the root of נִמֹּלוּ is נמ״ל. The English 'with him' keeps the plain sense of אִתּוֹ and does not take 'by him'.
